requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; WP; HLP._

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | Revision | Date | Notes |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 1.54 | 1993 | Last published 1.x specification; the universal interoperability baseline. See the [v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/README.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 2.00 A0-A4 | 1993-Dec 1994 | The five ALPHA drafts of the 2.0 specification, introducing ports, tables, world coordinates, UltraNums, and the rest of the modern architecture. Per-revision change logs are preserved in the [2.0 Introduction](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 2.0 / 2.1 / 2.2 | 1995-1997 | The undocumented "RIPscrip-2" product era: the engine as shipped in RIPterm Professional 2.0 (Jan 1995), 2.20.00 (Nov 19, 1995), 2.20.01 (Nov 28, 1995), and 2.30 (Oct 27, 1997), with **no specification published after ALPHA 4** (no product labeled "2.1" has surfaced). The shipping engine moved past the draft from day one - RIPterm Pro 2.0 already used the 26-character RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE argument block (SHADOW.RIP) rather than ALPHA 4's 13-character form, and v2.20.01 added the icon-transparency flag (`<flags2>` bit 128) to RIP_BUTTON_STYLE, absent from the ALPHA 4 table. Features often credited to "3.x" were already shipping in the January 1995 2.0 release - background **.WAV audio playback** (specified since ALPHA 3; HMI sound drivers), JPEG image display, SVGA/256-color modes, BMP icons, and Atech `.FF1` outline fonts (see the [RIPterm 2.30 font assets](../../2.0/assets/fonts/README.md)). See [4.5 Audio Files](4.5-audio-files.md). |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 3.0 | 1995-1996 | The 2.x design finalized and renamed. Publicly described by the Dec 1996 white paper; no language reference published. |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: | 3.0.7 | Oct 1997 | Driver shipped with RIPtel 3.1 "Visual Telnet" - the concrete engine this edition documents. |

requirements.heading: Revision History
requirements.text: One notable change between the 2.00a4 draft and the shipping 3.0: **GIF support was dropped.** The 2.A4 draft added GIF alongside JPEG for compressed images, but the white paper explains it had to be removed "due to outrageous licensing conditions for the compression algorithm LZW," leaving JPEG as the sole compressed image format (with PNG named as the intended successor). See [the white paper on image formats](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt).

requirements.heading: The 2.0 ALPHA Drafts and the Shipping Engine
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: The 2.0 ALPHA Drafts and the Shipping Engine
requirements.text: The 2.00 ALPHA 4 draft ("RIPscrip Graphics Protocol Language, Technical Reference" - Version 2.00, Revision ALPHA 4, December 13th 1994) is the last published specification of any kind, and its ALPHA lineage matters for reading this reference: the drafts were an ongoing culmination revised as A0 through A4, each sub-revision flagged in the document's margin (`_(v2.A3)_`-style markers, preserved throughout this reference on inherited material). The A0 draft defined the resolution-independent coordinate system, 24-bit color encoding, the 36-slot text-window/viewport/style tables, and base-math variation; A1 added the header command, save/restore protection, extended fonts, and UU-encoded data blocks; A2 added command grouping and borderless fills; A3 added drawing ports, WAV audio, and file deletion; A4 reworked text variables, data tables, and the extended text window. The complete per-revision change logs - creator-relevant history for understanding why commands look the way they do - are carried in full in the [2.0 Introduction](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md). The shipping 2.30-generation clients already diverged from the draft in documented places (auto-sense reply, the Base Math opcode, the extended-font layout - see the [2.0 reference's spec-status note](../../2.0/ripscrip/1.0-introduction.md)); the 3.0 engine this edition documents inherits those shipping resolutions, not the draft positions.

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus; HLP; WP._

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text: Relative to the last published specification draft, the shipping 3.0 engine differs as listed below. Note that these differences accumulated **across the 2.0-2.2 product releases as well as the 3.0 renaming** - with no specifications published after ALPHA 4, the exact release where each feature landed is mostly unrecorded; where evidence exists (e.g. WAV audio and the reworked extended-font-style block shipping in RIPterm Pro 2.0), the relevant section says so.

requirements.heading: Differences from 2.00 ALPHA 4
requirements.text:
- **Adds new drawing primitives** never documented in any spec: skewed ovals (`&`, `-`, `]`, `[`, `+`), the filled oval chord (`_`), markers (`;`), poly-polygons with even-odd fill (`<`), and bounded text (`"`). All are named or demonstrated in TeleGrafix's own NEWCMDS.RIP and companion demos - see [the script census](../../3.0/research/riptel-script-census.md) and the [2.2 Curves](2.2-curves.md) and [2.3 Shapes & Fills](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md) pages.
- **Resolves the 2.00a4 opcode collision**: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH is level-0 `J` on the wire, leaving `b` to RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW. See [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md).
- **Adds the flowed-text column system** - `1e` column regions, linked multi-column layouts, overflow paging, and RIP_SelectArticle - the "powerful column system" advertised for newspaper-style presentation. See [3.1 Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md).
- **Adds a conditional/macro layer**: `<<IF …>> <<ELSE>> <<ENDIF>>` inline conditionals, `<<NAME>>` macro expansion, the `$&VAR$` dereference form, and `ID=n:` mouse-field identities. See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md).
- **Adds web integration**: `$GOTOURL(var)$` launches a URL held in a text variable - 1997-era web/BBS convergence.
- **Formalizes scene header segments** - a per-scene header mechanism carrying data-table flags and entries, coordinate size, direct-RGB bit count, general flags, and a revision code. See [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#scene-header-segments).

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; corpus._

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: Everything the 2.00 ALPHAs introduced applies: ports, tables, backup areas, world coordinates, 256/direct-RGB color, base-math variation, and the expanded command levels - the fundamentals chapters of this edition cover each. For interoperating with 1.54-era content, 3.x provides the **`$COMPAT$`** text variable, which sets the environment to RIPscrip 1.54 settings - the classic 640×350 EGA coordinate space and defaults. TeleGrafix's own demo scenes issue `$COMPAT$` before playing 1.54-style artwork (21 uses in the corpus), making it the standard bridge between the two coordinate worlds. The driver also retains 1.54 `.ICN` icon handling, converting old icons to BMP on the fly ("Can't convert RIP 1.54 Icon %s to 2.0 BMP format!").

requirements.heading: Differences from 1.54
requirements.text: Two backward-compatibility subtleties inherited from the 2.0 redesign are worth restating for authors converting 1.54 material: XOR (and the other raster write modes) now apply to **all** primitives including curves and filled areas, where 1.54 limited XOR to simple line primitives _(v2.A1)_; and the resolution-independent fill model means filled rectangles inset one pixel from their right and bottom coordinate lines, which can open one-pixel gaps in 1.54 artwork replayed under a non-1.54 environment - see [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#the-mathematics-of-graphics-and-coordinates) for the full rules _(v2.A1)_. Filled objects' borders, always drawn in 1.54, can be turned off from 2.0 onward (they default on for compatibility) _(v2.A3)_. _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.text: _Evidence: SyncTERM; editorial survey._

requirements.heading: Implementation Status
requirements.text: No modern implementation covers RIPscrip 3.x in full:

requirements.text: | Implementation | Coverage |

requirements.text: | icy_tools, fTelnet, PabloDraw | RIPscrip 1.54 only (varying subsets). |

requirements.heading: Implementation Status
requirements.text: The practical takeaway: **1.54 is the interoperable floor**, SyncTERM is the only living implementation of anything beyond it, and the original RIPSCRIP.DLL 3.0.7 driver (via RIPtel under emulation) remains the reference behavior for the full language. See [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#ansi-sequences-auto-sensing) for version identification details.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:18516-18608)._

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: RIPscrip is organized into 10 levels of graphical commands (low Level-0 to high Level-9). Level-0 commands are the building blocks of RIPscrip. The basic graphics primitives of the system are all Level-0, including the commands Line, Rectangle, Circle, Color, Font, etc. Each level of RIPscrip gets progressively higher-level in concept. For example, Level-1 commands use Mouse Regions, Icons, and Formatted Text Regions.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: The basic syntax rules are as follows:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 1. A RIPscrip command line starts at the beginning of a line of text. A RIPscrip command line moved to the middle of a line of text is treated as literal text. This prevents people inserting mischievous things in teleconference messages, or similar pranks. The only exceptions to this rule is stated below under item 6, "continuation of long lines", and item 12 "alternate RIPscrip starting sequences".
requirements.reason: Reference adoption reopens this claim: the containing document changed in PR #71. Existing implementation/tests are historical evidence, pending reconciliation with the new contract. Previous review: Incremental framing preserves opaque command/quote bytes, recognizes line-start ! and anywhere SOH/STX, falls back to exact raw text for bogus/escaped introducers, chains at unquoted pipes, dispatches at CR, swallows mid-command LF and removes only the odd continuation slash. Every split and one-byte input, long commands, CP437/UTF-8 byte preservation, cursor-column callback, allocation-failure resynchronization, reset/destruction and nonfatal processing are independently tested. This is not active terminal routing, expansion, binary transfer or EOF dispatch.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 2. A RIPscrip command line begins with an exclamation mark `!` (ASCII code 33 decimal).
requirements.reason: Reference adoption reopens this claim: the containing document changed in PR #71. Existing implementation/tests are historical evidence, pending reconciliation with the new contract. Previous review: Incremental framing preserves opaque command/quote bytes, recognizes line-start ! and anywhere SOH/STX, falls back to exact raw text for bogus/escaped introducers, chains at unquoted pipes, dispatches at CR, swallows mid-command LF and removes only the odd continuation slash. Every split and one-byte input, long commands, CP437/UTF-8 byte preservation, cursor-column callback, allocation-failure resynchronization, reset/destruction and nonfatal processing are independently tested. This is not active terminal routing, expansion, binary transfer or EOF dispatch.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 3. Every RIPscrip command is preceded by the universal RIPscrip delimiter, vertical-bar `|` (ASCII code 124 decimal).

Existing implementation/tests are historical evidence, pending reconciliation with the new contract. Every split and one-byte input, long commands, CP437/UTF-8 byte preservation, cursor-column callback, allocation-failure resynchronization, reset/destruction and nonfatal processing are independently tested. This is not active terminal routing, expansion, binary transfer or EOF dispatch.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 7. RIPscrip makes provisions for multiple Graphical Windows and multiple Text Windows. A Graphical Window is where all RIPscrip graphics appear. A Text Window is where raw text appears. Raw Text includes ANSI color and cursor movement codes (a subset of VT-100 terminal emulation), and possibly other terminal emulations like VT-100, VT-102, VT-220, etc.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 8. The vertical bar (`|`) of a RIPscrip command can be followed by a level number. If the 1st character after (`|`) is a numeric digit (1-9), then that's the RIPscrip Command Level. If the very 1st character is NOT a digit 1-9, then it is the command type character and the command is a Level-0 command. If the 1st character is a digit 1-9, and the second character is also a digit, then that defines a sub-level of a RIPscrip level. For example:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
         !|L     RIPscrip Level-0 Command "L"
        !|1L     RIPscrip Level-1 Command "L"
       !|15L     RIPscrip Level-1, sub-level 5 Command "L"
   ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Each of the above examples are unique commands not to be confused with each other. You may continue the sub-levels up to a maximum level of 9 (e.g., `!|123456789<cmd>`").

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 9. Every RIPscrip command includes a command type character. In Level-0 commands, this character immediately follows the vertical bar. At all other levels, it follows the level digits. The command type character may be any of the following characters:

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text:
```text
   ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
   abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz
   @#$&*()[]{}<>:;'",.?-_=+!
   ```

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: 10. Following the command type character are 0 or more parameters. If the command requires a text-string, it is always the LAST parameter. Numeric parameters DO NOT have any delimiters (commas, dashes, spaces, etc.). A variable width numeric parameter may be used as the last parameter. This allows for maximum efficiency.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: If a RIPscrip command does not have a string parameter, but does have numeric parameters, the last parameter may be shortened to get a bit more efficiency out of it. If the last parameter is more than one digit long and the left-most digits are zeros, they may be omitted. At least one digit must remain though after all of the shortening is done (eg, "0001" can be shortened to "1" but "0000" cannot be shortened to "", it can only be shortened to "0"). _(v2.A3)_

In this case, the reserved parameter may be omitted completely, and the value should be assumed to be zero (`0'). Please take note that the previous paragraphs still apply! You can omit the reserved parameter AND shorten the last transmitted parameter so as to squeeze out as many unnecessary characters from the command as possible. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: RIPscrip Protocol - Syntax and General Structure
requirements.text: Numbers are normally represented in base-36 (unless altered by a RIPscrip command). This compacts numbers down to roughly 3/5 of their decimal form. This numbering system, technically called "Hexa-Tri-Decimal" or "MegaNums" is unlike Hexadecimal which uses 0-9 and A-F. MegaNums take advantage of the entire alphabet, using characters 0-9 and A-Z. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.text: 11. An exclamation mark (`!`) or vertical bar (`|`) character can appear in a RIPscrip text parameter by preceding it with a backslash (`\`). This is known as "quoting" a special character. A literal backslash is represented with a double-backslash (`\\`). Also, in some situations you need to quote specific characters so that they are not misinterpretted. For example, in a button host string, the characters `[`, `]`, `(`, and `$` are used as special host command characters and will need to be quoted (eg, `\[`, `\]`, `\(` and `\$` respectively). See rule #14 below for more details on quoting these special sequences. _(v2.A3)_

This prevents people from cluttering teleconference, or other areas of a host with spurious RIPscrip sequences.

requirements.heading: Command Syntax - Parser-Exact Behavior
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL; [primary traces, artifact identity, native buffer/RIP/ANSI probes and controlled-service limits](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md)._

requirements.heading: Command Syntax - Parser-Exact Behavior
requirements.text: These sections describe the original RIPtel 3.1 driver’s input pipeline. The original outer buffer consumer tries RIP framing first when RIP emulation is enabled; unconsumed/fallback bytes then enter the text path, where ordinary ANSI parsing remains available. Column-flow interception and disabled text/ANSI paths can consume text separately; the following ANSI examples assume the normal ANSI-enabled text path.

requirements.heading: Introducers
requirements.text: In idle RIP framing, SOH (0x01) or STX (0x02) can introduce a sequence between raw-text bytes. `!` (0x21) is accepted when the preceding byte is CR, LF or form feed and ANSI is idle, or when the client’s beginning-of-line callback returns true. Every introducer must then be followed by `|`; otherwise both the failed introducer and the following byte go through the raw-text fallback. A stray exclamation therefore remains ordinary text.

requirements.heading: Introducers
requirements.text: The client predicate is explicit: RIPtel supplies client-maintained line state. SyncTERM’s separate display-cursor-column rule is not established as this driver’s universal rule. SOH/STX acceptance is an idle-framing rule, not a promise to interrupt an already buffered RIP argument or reset pending ANSI. The [priority examples](#esc-priority-and-resumption) distinguish these states.

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text: The original parser accepts **up to nine consecutive digits `1`..`9`** after the initial/chaining pipe. All those digits form the level key; the next non-level digit/byte is the opcode. A **third digit is another level digit**, unlike SyncTERM’s two-digit parser. `0` is never a level digit at any position: `!|0X` attempts level-zero opcode `0`, not a level-zero form of command X. A tenth level digit discards the current command.

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text: The complete shipped dispatch table defines commands at level zero and single-digit keys 1, 2, 3 and 9 only. Recognizing a deeper key syntactically does not define commands for it: `!|123L…` is an unknown level-123 command, not opcode `3` under level 12. Unknown commands scan to a pipe or line ending. Opcode bytes need not be printable; ESC is the actual opcode in level-1 query, level-2 directory-switch and level-9 block-mode commands.

requirements.heading: Levels and Sublevels
requirements.text: **Shipped stale-prefix defect:** after a multilevel prefix, its second byte can remain in the parser’s reused key buffer. Level-zero lookup checks that stale byte and can skip all level-zero records even after a pipe or new line. Checked input `!|123L00000000|c01` plus CRLF dispatches neither command. A subsequent `!|1K|c01` plus CRLF dispatches both: the one-digit prefix clears the stale second byte. A full parser reset also clears it. Implementations that clear unused key bytes correct this defect; do not mistake the defect for a two-digit depth limit or reinterpret a third digit as an opcode.

requirements.heading: Parameters
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 rules 9-10._

requirements.heading: Parameters
requirements.text: Zero or more parameters follow the command character, with no delimiters between numeric fields. Numeric parameters are fixed-width [MegaNums or UltraNums](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md) per the current base math. A text parameter, if present, is always last. The last numeric parameter may be shortened by dropping leading zeros (`!|c01` → `!|c1`; at least one digit must remain), and a trailing _reserved_ parameter may be omitted entirely (assumed `0`).

requirements.heading: Chaining, Continuation, and Line Endings
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL, original byte parser; [checked streams](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md#distinguishing-streams-and-stages)._

requirements.heading: Chaining, Continuation, and Line Endings
requirements.text: An unquoted pipe dispatches/finishes the buffered command and starts the next command on the same line. **CR, LF and form feed terminate commands**; LF is not unconditionally swallowed inside a command. CRLF is accepted as a physical line ending. Thus `!|Tleft` LF `right` CRLF draws `left`, then routes `right` CRLF as raw text; it does not concatenate the two words.

requirements.heading: Chaining, Continuation, and Line Endings
requirements.text: A backslash at a physical line ending continues the current parsing state across CR/LF/form-feed bytes. In a string, `abc\` CRLF `def` becomes `abcdef`. A literal trailing backslash is doubled; two backslashes preserve the literal and allow the line to terminate, while a third continues it. These rules apply to the framing state, before macro/host interpretation.

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL, text escape branch RVA `0x3aa63–0x3aae2`; [framing capture and original-host-stage checks](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md#distinguishing-streams-and-stages)._

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: Framing does **not** globally remove every backslash. Within a RIP string, quoting SOH, STX or `|` removes the backslash and inserts that byte as data. Other quoted bytes retain both the backslash and the following byte in the string passed to the command consumer. In particular, `\$`, `\[`, `\]`, `\(`, `\!` and `\\` survive framing; continuation at a line ending is the separate rule above.

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: The subsequent consumer interprets its own text/macro/host syntax. In the ordinary dollar-code scanner, enabled backslash processing removes one quote and skips interpretation of the following character. Host response processing makes [two ordinary passes](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order), deferring backslash removal in the first and applying it in the second. The preprocessor and command-block parsers have their own scans, so quoting is stage-specific.

requirements.heading: Escaping in Text Parameters
requirements.text: Checked host text `\$SHIFT\$` transmits literal `$SHIFT$` and never queries SHIFT. Quoting only the opening dollar, `\$SHIFT$`, is insufficient in this two-pass path: the first pass evaluates SHIFT and the second removes the remaining quote; with Shift down the output is `1`. Preserve the quotes through framing and quote both dollar delimiters for the literal-variable example. SyncTERM’s global `\X` collapse before command consumption is a distinct implementation behavior.

requirements.heading: ESC Priority and Resumption
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL, original buffer consumer `0x57a2`, RIP parser `0x39e90`, ANSI parser `0x37b7c`, autosense `0x355d9`; [native derivation](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md)._

requirements.heading: ESC Priority and Resumption
requirements.text: ESC does not globally preempt all unfinished input. RIP framing runs before ordinary ANSI handling while enabled. In a pending RIP text argument, ESC is data; in numeric fields it can corrupt the command; in the opcode position it can be a valid level-1/2/9 opcode. Only bytes routed to the text path are candidates for ANSI interpretation.

requirements.heading: ESC Priority and Resumption
requirements.text: ANSI recognizes a new ESC sequence while idle. ESC received during its pending ESC/CSI sequence is handled by that state rather than universally restarting at ESC; the checked unsupported ESC final clears the pending sequence, leaving subsequent `[`/`!` as ordinary text. CAN (0x18) and SUB (0x1a) explicitly cancel a pending ANSI sequence. Starting RIP with SOH while ANSI is pending does not itself clear ANSI state.

requirements.heading: ESC Priority and Resumption
requirements.text: Disabling RIP skips RIP framing but leaves the normal ANSI path available. `ESC[2!` can therefore re-enable RIP, including for the next byte in the same buffer. Enable changes the emulation flag; it does **not** reset parser state or reinterpret bytes received while disabled. If an API/menu action disables RIP during a buffered string, re-enabling resumes that string with the disabled interval omitted. Send a new command at a valid framing boundary (for example CRLF then `!|`, or idle SOH followed by `|`); enable is not an implicit scene reset.

requirements.heading: Raw Text and Error Handling
requirements.text: A line with no accepted introducer is raw text, routed to the current text path (or consumed by active [column flow](3.1-column-text-system.md)). Malformed numeric input discards the command and scans toward a pipe or line ending. Surplus text after a complete fixed-field command can be ignored after that command has already dispatched, as the corpus’s inline commentary shows; this is not a universal “extra byte invalidates the command” rule. Recovery after multilevel prefixes remains subject to the [stale-prefix defect](#levels-and-sublevels).

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: As previously described, RIPscrip is composed of ten different levels of commands. The distribution of commands over different levels is done in a rather organized fashion based on command type. Each level of command in general, is progressively higher level in concept. For example, level 0 commands are the most basic building blocks of RIPscrip (eg, graphical primitives, protocol setup, etc). Level one commands are simple user interface objects. Level 2 commands are higher level still in that they deal with context swapping issues. At the highest level, level-9, we deal with binary transfer modes like file transfer protocols, etc. A more formal definition of the currently used levels are:

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels

requirements.heading: Description of RIPscrip Command Levels
requirements.text: | 1 | Simple user interface objects (buttons, mouse fields, clipboard slots, formatted text regions). This level consolidates one or more simple building blocks from level 0 and also introduces more abstract user interface objects (eg, mouse fields). |

requirements.text: Each level/character pair is a unique command: `!|L`, `!|1L`, and `!|15L` are three different commands. The consolidated 3.x inventory across all levels is [9.0 Command Reference](9.0-command-reference.md).

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | `ESC[!` or `ESC[0!` | When RIP is enabled, send exactly `RIPSCRIP030001` (14 ASCII bytes); no NUL, CR or LF |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | `ESC[1!` | Disable RIP framing; no reply; ANSI control remains available |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | `ESC[2!` | Enable RIP framing; no reply; parser state is preserved |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: | `ESC[3!` | When RIP is enabled, send `RIPSCRIP030001` followed by one CR |

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: Queries 0/3 while disabled produce no reply. The callback uses only the first ANSI parameter (later parameters are ignored); other selectors produce no reply. The ordinary ANSI decimal accumulator wraps to 16 bits, so `65536` reaches selector 0. Private-prefixed `ESC[?0!` does not invoke this callback. As described [above](#esc-priority-and-resumption), these sequences require the ANSI path; their printed bytes inside an unfinished RIP text argument do not become controls.

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: The phrase format is **`RIPSCRIPxxyyvs`**: two decimal major digits, two minor digits, one vendor code and one vendor subversion. The vendor allocation is 0 generic/unspecified, 1 RIPterm/TeleGrafix, 2 Qmodem Pro. Thus RIPtel’s `030001` means language 03.00, vendor 0, subversion 1; the last two digits are not a two-digit language revision. Product version RIPtel 3.1 and driver build 3.0.7 are separate identities.

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: A new compatible implementation may use the explicitly documented **generic profile `RIPSCRIP030000`** (language 03.00, vendor 0, subversion 0), with the same selector/terminator policy. This is an interoperability choice permitted by this reconstruction, not a claim to be TeleGrafix. The [complete byte/reply reference](9.2-versions.md#generic-implementation-profile) gives exact bytes and separates this profile from historical replies.

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: RIPTEL.HLP’s FAQ prints only `RIPSCRIP03000`; retain that as a documentary quote, not a complete executable reply. SyncTERM independently sends `RIPSCRIP030001` in its RIP 3 mode, but its documented one-way-disable bug does not establish RIPtel behavior. The original RIPtel pipeline demonstrably re-enables. Client-configured CR-to-CRLF translation may affect selector 3’s CR; default/0 have no line ending to translate.

requirements.heading: ANSI Sequences (Auto-Sensing)
requirements.text: > **Product-era note:** the recovered 2.x-generation RIPterm binaries report `RIPSCRIP020000` despite product-version changes; see the [2.0 identity record](../../2.0/ripscrip/9.2-versions.md). That string likewise uses the vendor/subversion allocation, not a separate product build field.

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL; [derivation and original-parser probes](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md)._

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments
requirements.text: The shipped [`RIP_HEADER`](#rip_header) is one `h` command with an eight-character base block and concatenated typed segments. The base fields are revision, global flags and segment count; each segment has a type digit and its own fixed fields. A pipe or line ending terminates the complete header. All header numbers use base 64. See the [complete field/flag tables and checked examples](#rip_header); the Alpha 4 flag list is not the shipped 3.0.7 layout. Audio is a stop-playback segment with no table slot.

requirements.heading: Wire-Format Observations from the Corpus
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: Wire-Format Observations from the Corpus
requirements.text: The 116 TeleGrafix-authored RIPtel demo scripts are the best available picture of real 3.x on the wire:

requirements.heading: Wire-Format Observations from the Corpus
requirements.text:
- **SOH marks scene start.** 111 of 116 files begin their _first_ command line with SOH + `|`, then use `!|` for every subsequent line - SOH apparently flags start-of-scene to the 3.0 stream parser, while `!|` remains the 1.54-compatible introducer. (Three files invert the pattern, nearly all-SOH.)
- **The standard prologue** opens 90+ files: `J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO` - base math 36, 2-digit coordinates, 8-bit palette color mode, 1280×960 world frame (see [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md)).
- **Trailing text after fixed-length arguments is tolerated** and used as inline commentary - the driver stops reading once the fixed fields are consumed: `!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960`. Chained `!|command|! comment` forms (the `!` comment opcode) are ubiquitous.
- **Typo tolerance is high.** A missing `!` introducer (`|1<ESC>0000$COMPAT$`, CURVES.RIP), separator lines `!|----` that accidentally parse as the `-` opcode with dash arguments (`-` reads as MegaNum 0), and bare `!|` no-op lines all pass through the shipping driver without visible failure. Robust parsers should degrade as gracefully.
- **Line endings are CRLF**, with `\` continuation across physical lines for long vertex lists (POLYPOLY.RIP). See [6.0 Writing 3.x .RIP Files](6.0-writing-rip-files.md) for authoring conventions.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: _Evidence: editorial; format follows 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: The chapters of this reference detail the reconstructed RIPscrip 3.x command set (the consolidated index is [9.0 Command Reference](9.0-command-reference.md)). Each command has these aspects:

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **SYMBOL** - the symbolic constant that is referenced in RIPscrip documents. This is the universal name for the command. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FUNCTION** - A short description of the command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **LEVEL** - The Command Level. Sub-levels (if any) are represented with decimal points (eg, 1.3.5 for Level-1, Sub-level 3, Sub-Sub-level 5). This is for discussion purposes only. The decimal points are never part of the actual command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **COMMAND** - The character identifying the command

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **ARGUMENTS** - The arguments or parameters for the command. Commands that do not require any parameters after the command type character are shown here as "\<none\>". Each parameter is shown in the order it appears in the command, and is represented by a name. If a parameter is numeric, it is followed by a width specifier indicating how many meganum or ultranum digits the parameter consists of (e.g., ":2" means a 2-digit number, or a value between 0 and 1295 for meganums, or 0 and 4095 for ultranums). If a parameter does not have a width specifier, it is by default a text parameter, and should be the last parameter of the command.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: If a command is variable length (see [POLYGON](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_polygon)), then it will appear with an ellipe (...), meaning that the command repeats the specific parameters a variable number of times. _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: If the parameter is a variable-width coordinate that can be set by the [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_coordinate_size), or via the [RIP_HEADER](#rip_header) commands, then the parameter will be followed by a coordinate specifier (e.g., ":XY" means that the parameter is a variable-width coordinate). _(v2.A2, revised v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: If the parameter is a color parameter whose format is determined by the [RIP_SET_COLOR_MODE](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_set_color_mode) command, (ie, the parameter switches between "color mapping mode" or "direct RGB encoding" mode), then a color mode specifier will come after the parameter name (e.g., ":CM" indicates this parameter uses the current color mode). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: Some commands do not allow color parameters to switch modes based on RIP_SET_COLOR_MODE. These exceptional commands document these exceptions and the :CM specifier will not be present. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FORMAT** - This represents the format of the command, with the starting `!|`, the level digits, the command type character, and the parameter list, with the parameter names in angle brackets. (These parameters are spaced apart, but these spaces never appear in the physical commands.)

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **EXAMPLE** - An actual example of the RIPscrip command. In this reconstructed edition, examples are drawn from the RIPtel corpus wherever one exists.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **DRAW COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Drawing Color.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **BACK COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses (or affects) the current background pen drawing color. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **LINE STYLE** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Line Style Pattern.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FILL COLOR** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Fill Color.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FILL PATRN** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Fill Pattern.

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **WRITE MODE** - If YES, then this command will take advantage of the current Write Mode (eg, COPY, or XOR).

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **FONT STYLE** - If YES, then this command uses or affects the current Font Style/size/orientation. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **VIEWPORT** - If YES, then this command adheres to the graphical viewport (draws inside it). Any RIPscrip command that adheres to the graphical viewport will be drawn (when received) only if the viewport is activated. If the viewport is deactivated, then the command is parsed, but completely ignored. _(v1.54, revised v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **USES PORT** - If YES, then this command adheres to, is affected by, or modifies the definition of a [port](7.0-drawing-ports.md). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: - **BASE MATH** - Indicates which base math this command responds to. The possible settings are N/A (does not apply), Meganums (uses meganums ONLY), Ultranums (uses Ultranums ONLY), and Current (uses current base math setting as set by either RIP_HEADER or [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_base_math)). _(v2.A2)_

requirements.heading: How commands are documented
requirements.text: In addition - because this is a reconstructed edition - every command entry carries an **_Evidence:_** line naming the sources for that command: `2.00a4`, `HLP` (the RIP_* name in the 3.0.7 inventory), `corpus` (with file names), and/or `SyncTERM` (with ripper.c line cites). Commands attested only by a single source, and argument layouts inferred rather than documented, are flagged in the entry.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: _Configure a scene using a base header and typed state segments_

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL (RIPtel 3.1’s RIPscrip 3.0.7 driver); [primary derivation and original-routine probes](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md). This shipped contract replaces the Alpha 4 header flag list previously reproduced here. It does not change the preserved 2.0 source edition._

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | **Command** | `h` |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `revision:2 flags:4 segments:2`, followed by typed segments below |

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|h <revision> <flags> <segments> <segment>…` **Example:** `!|h01000201502O2220`

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: All fields, including every segment, use **base 64 regardless of current base math**. Spaces shown in the grammar are explanatory and are not sent. `revision` accepts 0 or 1, `flags` accepts 0..31, and the declared segment count accepts 0..10. The accepted revision tags are the inherited 00/01 tags, not a client version number or a new `03` tag; the driver remembers the tag for the scene.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: The byte grammar for a well-formed header is:

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text:
```text
!|h RR FFFF NN S1 S2 … SNN terminator
RR:2, FFFF:4, NN:2                 all base 64
terminator = command pipe, CR, LF, or form-feed
```

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: Segments are concatenated **without pipes, commas, spaces or nested introducers**. A pipe ends the entire header and starts the next command. The segment count is not a byte-level terminator: the parser consumes typed segments until a command/line terminator, then validates the declared count and decoded argument length. Ordinary backslash line continuation works inside fields and between segments. Do not append unmarked prose after the final segment.

requirements.heading: RIP_HEADER
requirements.text: The driver validates the entire decoded header before performing global resets or segment actions. A bad revision, flag value, slot or segment count suppresses its application. Runtime failures in an individual operation do not roll back earlier operations. Segments run in wire order; repeats are permitted. A shipped validation exception is that a declared count of zero ignores parsed extra segments; those extras are not applied. Well-formed headers still send exactly the declared segments.

requirements.heading: Global header flags
requirements.text: These values may be ORed. The sequence is reset, remember revision, release a previous input lock, optionally lock input again, select table zeros, clear refresh state, then execute the segments.

requirements.heading: Global header flags
requirements.text: | Value | Shipped effect |

requirements.heading: Global header flags
requirements.text: | 1 | Hard reset, including protection and saved-state cleanup |

requirements.heading: Global header flags
requirements.text: | 2 | Drawing/soft reset, as `RIP_RESET_WINDOWS`; ignored when bit 1 is also set |

requirements.heading: Global header flags
requirements.text: | 4 | Lock mouse/keyboard input during scene receipt and select the wait cursor; `#` releases this lock |

requirements.heading: Global header flags
requirements.text: | 8 | Select slot 0 of text-window, button-style, graphics-style, drawing-port, palette and environment tables |

requirements.heading: Global header flags
requirements.text: | 16 | Clear refresh state |

requirements.heading: Global header flags
requirements.text: Zero requests no optional global operation, but still remembers the revision and releases an existing input lock. It does not imply the Alpha 4 default reset/coordinate flags. A later segment can change a state just selected/reset globally, including the cursor. This mechanism is separate from local-file start and from the `#` scene-end marker.

requirements.heading: Segment fields
requirements.text: The first field is a literal type digit `0`..`9`; it is also the first decoded numeric argument. Table slots are always checked 0..35, even if the operation flags do not use the supplied slot. Coordinate width/RGB fields are present in an environment segment even when their setting bits are absent.

requirements.text: The remaining two low-byte bits differ by object:

requirements.heading: Button, graphics-style, palette and environment flags
requirements.text: **Palette correction:** 64 scans entries but only uploads the current palette; it does not reset defaults or other slots. For 128, the original INUSE helper does not recognize the supplied -1/current sentinel and reads the flag word **two bytes before the palette array**. Bit 1 of that unrelated word gates the upload; the following current-protection check is valid. This is an out-of-bounds shipped defect with no reliable defined-slot semantics. Neither bit changes stored RGB values or definition flags. The earlier reconstruction's “reset defaults” description is withdrawn; use the explicit [PAL reset lifecycle](7.1-data-tables.md#palette-reset-lifecycle) when defaults are required. _Evidence: original upload/guard instructions and [controlled-canary native checks](../research/issue-16-table-lifecycle.md#header-correction-and-failed-hypotheses)._

requirements.heading: Button, graphics-style, palette and environment flags
requirements.text: **Environment validation defect:** when 1024 is set, the validator checks the **slot number**, rather than coordinate width, against 2..5. When 4096 is set it checks the **slot number**, rather than RGB bits, against 1..8. A header using these settings with slot 0 is rejected even if the fields are valid. The actual setters then silently ignore an invalid width/RGB field, while the other segment effects continue. Direct environment setters, including bit 128, do not consult environment protection; the all-environment reset under bit 64 does. These are distinct paths, not a uniform permission rule.

requirements.heading: Button, graphics-style, palette and environment flags
requirements.text: Global drawing/hard resets have a separate [image-style reset scope](4.1-jpeg-images.md#defaults-and-reset-scope): drawing reset changes port zero and the old current port even if protected, while other protected survivors retain image state. A header without a global reset does not implicitly reset image style. These global effects are distinct from the drawing-port segment operations below. _Evidence: [original outer reset/header tests](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#original-outer-resetheader-checkpoint)._

requirements.heading: Character-set descriptor defect
requirements.text: Type 9 advertises only `type:1 charset:2`; its consumer stores charset 0 or 1. However, validation and application advance **three decoded arguments**, while the byte parser supplies only two. A standalone type-9 segment therefore fails validation. A following segment can instead be read at the wrong offset: constructed `!|h01000002900200060` parses as type 9 followed by a port segment, but validates/applies as charset 0 followed by a mouse segment with flags 0; it performs no port switch. Other malformed combinations can read outside the intended argument structure. There is no independently usable, consistently framed character-set segment in this driver; do not invent a third reserved wire field. This discrepancy is preserved as a shipped defect, not an alternative grammar for well-formed scenes.

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: This command indicates that RIPscrip commands are complete. This allows the terminal program to activate Mouse Regions, or respond to queued up Mouse Clicks without disturbing the natural flow of the script transmission.

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: For noise-immunity, the Host should transmit three or more RIP_NO_MORE command consecutively to make sure the message gets to the terminal. The terminal should also time-out if no data is received for a while, and assume RIP_NO_MORE.

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: The actual duration of the "time-out" is entirely up to the implementor of their terminal program. A good recommended setting would be at least an entire second or more after the receipt of the last RIPscrip command. Raw ASCII/ANSI text does not contribute to the time-out in any way. Only an actual RIPscrip command could cause the time-out counter to be reset (thus starting the time-out countdown all over again). Timing-out is not a pre-requisite to supporting RIPscrip. It is a highly desirable feature to do this, but it is not required. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_NO_MORE
requirements.text: This command also re-activates user input previously disabled with a [RIP_HEADER](#rip_header) command. This is useful to prevent the user from clicking on buttons before the scene is completely drawn. See the RIP_HEADER command for more details on this mode of operation. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.text: The numeric foundations of RIPscrip 3.x: the base-36 [MegaNum](../../glossary.md) system carried forward from 1.54, the base-64 [UltraNum](../../glossary.md) system introduced by the 2.0 redesign, the global [Base Math](../../glossary.md) setting that selects between them, and the mathematics of the resolution-independent [world-coordinate](../../glossary.md) model.

requirements.heading: Numerical Parameters - Formats and Base-Math Variations
requirements.text: Throughout the RIPscrip specification, numeric parameters are used extensively to indicate where to draw things, how to draw things and various other pieces of information. For compactness, we do not use numbers that are normal decimal numbers (base-10). By default, RIPscrip uses base-36 numbers (Hexa-Tri-Decimal or more fondly, MegaNums) which use the digits 0-9 followed by A-Z. This was the original numbering system used in the 1.xx specification.

requirements.heading: Numerical Parameters - Formats and Base-Math Variations

A couple of the RIPscrip commands utilize specific base math values (eg, UltraNums, etc) under certain circumstances. Any commands that are exceptions like this will be clearly documented as being exceptions to the rule.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: Both systems are plain positional numerals in RIPscrip's own digit alphabets - **not** the RFC 4648 "Base32"/"Base64" encodings, which share nothing with these beyond the number 64.
requirements.reason: Representation terminology or worked-example table header; behavior is covered by the adjacent digit/value requirements.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text:
- **MegaNum digit alphabet (base 36):** `0`-`9` (values 0-9), then `A`-`Z` (values 10-35). Writers emit uppercase by convention.
- **UltraNum digit alphabet (base 64):** `0`-`9` (values 0-9), `A`-`Z` (values 10-35), `a`-`z` (values 36-61), `#` (value 62), `&` (value 63). Case is significant - `A` is 10 but `a` is 36.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Calculating multi-character values:** most-significant digit first, each position worth a power of the base - value = d₀·bⁿ⁻¹ + d₁·bⁿ⁻² + … + dₙ₋₁ (b = 36 or 64). To _decode_: MegaNum `1M` is 1×36 + 22 = 58; MegaNum `HR` is 17×36 + 27 = 639; UltraNum `R9a` is 27×64² + 9×64 + 36 = 111,204. To _encode_ a decimal value, take `value ÷ b^k mod b` for each position, highest power first: decimal 250 as a 2-digit MegaNum is 250 ÷ 36 = 6 remainder 34 → `6Y`; the same 250 as a 2-digit UltraNum is 250 ÷ 64 = 3 remainder 58 → `3w`; decimal 360 (a full circle in degrees) is `A0` in MegaNums.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Fixed widths and zero padding:** a `:2` width specifier means exactly two digits in the current base, zero-padded on the left (decimal 10 is `0A` as a 2-digit MegaNum, `0A` as a 2-digit UltraNum too). Numeric parameters have no delimiters between them - the fixed widths are what let the parser slice them apart, so a missing pad digit shifts every following parameter. `:XY` coordinate parameters are 2 digits by default, adjustable via [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](#rip_set_coordinate_size); `:CM` color parameters follow the current color mode ([2.0 Color Modes & Palettes](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_set_color_mode)). Per-command field widths are collected in [9.0 Command Reference](9.0-command-reference.md).

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Last-parameter rules:** a variable-width numeric parameter may be used only as the last parameter of a command, and syntax rule 10 allows the last numeric parameter to be shortened by dropping leading zeros (`!|c01` → `!|c1`); a trailing reserved parameter may be omitted entirely ([1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#ripscrip-protocol---syntax-and-general-structure)). A text string is likewise always last and never number-encoded.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: **Base Math switching:** the global setting starts at base 36, is changed with [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](#rip_set_base_math) or the [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) flags, and resets to base 36 on any [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows). Commands documented as exceptions ignore it - direct-RGB color values and drawing-palette RGB parameters are always UltraNums, and RIP_SET_BASE_MATH's own parameter is always a MegaNum.

requirements.heading: Working with MegaNums and UltraNums by hand
requirements.text: Parser-side edge cases (early termination behavior, out-of-alphabet bytes, and the like) are implementer material - see the [MegaNum encoding techspec](../../1.54/techspecs/1.1-meganum-encoding.md) and the [2.0 stream conventions delta](../../2.0/techspecs/1.0-stream-conventions-delta.md).

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus; SyncTERM (ripper.c:9107-9131)._

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text: Which base a command's parameters use is a **global mode**, not a per-command choice: after `!|J10` every base-math-governed field in every subsequent command reads as base-36; after `!|J1S`, base-64. Individual commands differ only in whether they _obey_ the mode - each command entry in this reference carries a base-math line, which is one of:

requirements.heading: Choosing MegaNums vs UltraNums
requirements.text:
- **current setting** - the common case: coordinates, dimensions, radii, vertex counts, and most numeric fields.
- **MegaNums only** - commands that must parse before the mode is knowable or that reset it: [RIP_SET_BASE_MATH](#rip_set_base_math) itself (its `10`/`1S` argument is always base-36), and anything that follows a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) (a reset silently returns the mode to base 36 - re-send `J` immediately if the scene needs otherwise).
- **UltraNums only** - direct-RGB color values and drawing-palette RGB parameters (see [2.0 Color Modes & Palettes](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md)).
- **not numeric** - text parameters (always last in a command) ignore base math entirely.

requirements.heading: Worked encodings
requirements.text: A field's value is `first_digit × base + second_digit` (and so on for wider fields). Digit values: `0`-`9` = 0-9, `A`-`Z` = 10-35, then (UltraNums only) `a`-`z` = 36-61, `#` = 62, `&` = 63.

requirements.text: So the ubiquitous corpus line `!|fZKQO` is a 1280×960 world frame in MegaNums - and note that TeleGrafix's chosen frame fits 2-digit MegaNums with 15 to spare (1295 max). A constructed UltraNum equivalent would be `!|J1S|fK0F0` _(constructed example - see the caution below)_.

requirements.heading: Decision guide
requirements.text: UltraNums earn one byte per coordinate over 3-digit MegaNums in the 1,296-4,095 band - meaningful at 2,400 baud when a scene is thousands of drawing operations.

requirements.heading: Interoperability caution
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus; SyncTERM._

requirements.heading: Interoperability caution
requirements.text: **No UltraNum usage has been observed in the wild.** All 116 TeleGrafix demo scripts run `J10` MegaNums, and SyncTERM cannot parse UltraNums at all - its number reader (`parse_mega`, ripper.c:9107-9131) treats `a`-`z` as _case-insensitive base-36 digits_, so a base-64 scene would silently mis-decode rather than fail. MegaNums are the only wire-proven encoding; treat UltraNums as documented-but-unexercised.

requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; WP §4.1; corpus._

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: Starting with the v2.0 specification of RIPscrip - carried unchanged into 3.x - the language is resolution independent through a "world coordinate system": you can alter the base coordinate system used to address the video's physical device coordinate system. Each coordinate system is called a "Coordinate Frame". There are two distinct levels of coordinate systems, from the lowest (least abstract) to the highest level (the drawing board):

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: 1. **DEVICE COORDINATE FRAME** - the resolution of the actual display device. This is not determined as part of the RIPscrip language itself, it is actually determined by the terminal - based upon whatever type of video hardware is present (and what mode the user has chosen).

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: 2. **[WORLD COORDINATE FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame)** - This is the master coordinate system. This is the global set of coordinates, set by [RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame) (wire opcode `f`). Ideally, it should be higher in dimensions than the Device Frame so that you do not lose resolution when "mapping" X/Y coordinates from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system. If the dimensions of the World Frame are the same as the Device Frame then the mapping operation between World and Device Frames are identical and can be skipped entirely since an X/Y coordinate in the World Frame directly corresponds to a pixel location in the Device Frame.

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: The white paper advertises a maximum **32,767 × 32,767** world frame, but that is **not the recovered RIPtel 3.1 setter limit**. The original [RIP_SET_WORLD_FRAME](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_set_world_frame) handler accepts **0..65535** in each dimension, including zero and 32768..65535, and stores/activates those unsigned word values. The [WORLD variable](5.1-text-variables.md#world) normally stores the same range and has an additional asymmetric oversized-value defect. Do not infer a signed-16-bit world-dimension validation gate from the white paper or confuse stored dimensions with the signedness of individual drawing coordinates. _Evidence: [original wire/macro handlers and native boundary matrix](../research/issue-23-environment-query-names.md#native-callback-activation-and-wire-checkpoint)._ Since versions of the RIPscrip specification prior to v2.0 were based on a 640x350 resolution without any World Frame, the World Frame defaults to 640 across and 350 high for backward compatibility; the `$COMPAT$` text variable restores that whole 1.54 environment (see [1.0 Introduction](1.0-introduction.md#differences-from-154)).

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: A real 3.x example, from the RIPtel demo prologue:

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text:
```text
!|fZKQO                 Set world coordinats to 1280x960
```

requirements.heading: World Coordinate Systems
requirements.text: (comment and spelling TeleGrafix's own, ONLINE.RIP): `ZK` = 35×36+20 = **1280**, `QO` = 26×36+24 = **960**. The demos thus run in a 1280×960 world regardless of the user's actual screen mode. Alternate frames observed in the corpus: `HSDC` = 640×480, `HR9S` = 639×352, `HRDC` = 639×480. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4 (the treatment carries into 3.x unchanged)._

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Mathematics, unlike graphics, is abstract in nature. Graphics on the other hand, is very discrete in nature. A pixel in graphics is the smallest displayable element on a graphics screen (Picture Element). The corresponding concept in mathematics is a single point. A pixel has a discrete size and shape in graphics whereas in mathematics, a point is infinitely small and occupies no physical space in the cartesian coordinate system in which it exists.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: In graphics we use the concept of coordinates and points to specify where a pixel is located. If graphics were like mathematics where a pixel was infinitely small, a graphics monitor wouldn't show anything other than black because a pixel would be infinitely small surrounded by blackness. But this is not the case. Graphics hardware has to have pixels defined as discrete areas of the screen - addressable areas of the screen that can be set to a particular color. This is how we see things on the screen, as individual pixels of data used together to represent some kind of image.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Just like the point in mathematics, a line is infinitely thin, but has length. A line is composed of an infinite number of points between the beginning and ending locations of the line.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Relating these two distinctly different concepts to each other though doesn't always lend itself to a simple situation to understand. On the surface, a pixel's coordinate location appears to be the same thing as it is in mathematics. But, when you get into deeper issues of graphics theory this isn't truly the case because of the difference in sizes of a point compared to a pixel. In math, points don't have to be on even integer boundaries - they can be fractional. A point can be at (2.53,1.295), whereas in graphics, a pixel cannot be at a fractional location - there's no such thing as a part of a pixel!

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: A graphics screen is designed so that every pixel location on the screen has a unique location specified (in human terms) as an X/Y coordinate pair. This is called the Cartesian Coordinate System. It is by far one of the easiest ways of representing a coordinate in a two-dimensional world like a monitor. If you zoom in closely on a monitor and look at the layout of pixels and their relationships to coordinates, you might see something like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look at the previous diagram, you can see that there is a grid of pixels that is 24 pixels wide (the X direction) and 10 pixels high (the Y direction). Each of the squares is a black pixel. The pixels contain a "#" are considered white pixels. There are four pixels that are ON in this diagram, at locations (11,2), (12,2), (11,3) and (12,3). This is how graphics hardware addresses graphics pixels, by specifying an X/Y coordinate location for a pixel to turn it on or off (or more generally, to set it to a particular color).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the locations of the coordinates in the previous diagram, the X/Y coordinates address the physical pixel cells themselves. Each pixel cell is separated by infinitely thin lines - the pixel cells' borders so to speak. Now, each pixel is physically adjacent to the ones next to it and there are no gaps between them. This is the way graphics hardware works.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now that we've described the way graphics hardware addresses pixel locations, let's look at why it's not really the best way of describing graphics mathematically. For the hardware, this is the best way of handling things, but mathematically, it's not.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: The world of graphics hardware has many different facets. One graphics display device can often times display graphics at different resolutions. A typical video card on the IBM-PC can display graphics at 320x200, 640x350, 640x400, 640x480, 800x600, 1024x768 and even as high as 1280x1024 and higher. That's quite a bit of difference in pixel grids (like the one shown earlier). Not only can the number of pixels change horizontally and vertically, but when the resolutions get higher, the pixels get smaller and harder to see. When graphics hardware can achieve a resolution of infinity by infinity, then we will have achieved perfect sight (like what we see around us). But obviously, this will probably never happen in our lifetimes (or our great granchildren's for that matter).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: What would happen if you had a line drawn on a graphics screen from coordinates (0,0) to (639,349) at 640x350 resolution? You would have a nice little line on the screen that stretches from the upper-left corner to the lower-right corner. Now, if you drew the same line at 800x600 resolution? Your line would no longer go all the way to the bottom of the screen or to the far right of the screen. It would stop about 2/3'rds of the way down and over.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: The problems start to come up with mathematics and graphical representations when we try to make something look the same at one resolution as it does in another (resolution independence). Sure you can translate a coordinate in one resolution to some other coordinate in a different resolution. All you need to know are the dimensions of each resolution and a bit of algebra. But pixels aren't the same thickness! The line described previously could still be drawn properly to the lower-right of the screen, but it would appear a lot thinner. You could try drawing two lines offset by one pixel location and you would come "close" to the original thickness of the line at 640x350 resolution, but it wouldn't be a perfect match. A perfect match is a rare thing when dealing with different resolutions.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, on to the real issue at hand here: translation of coordinates. We won't worry about the size of pixels, but will concentrate on getting the locations of points correct at different resolutions. Let's say you have a screen at 640x350 resolution with two filled rectangles drawn on it. The first rectangle is drawn from (2,1) to (4,3) and the second one is drawn from (5,1) to (7,3) like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, you notice that both rectangles are right next to each other. There are no gaps between them. Now, if you tried to draw these same two rectangles on a graphics screen that was 1280x700 pixels in size, and tried to make it appear in the exact same location and size on the monitor, you would have to translate the corners of the rectangles to the new resolution and re-plot the rectangles. Now, 640x2 is 1280 and 350x2 is 700 so our new resolution is exactly twice as large in both the X and Y directions (this is RARELY the case!). So, in order to translate our original coordinates to this resolution we simply multiply the numbers by 2. Pretty simple. Our previous rectangles in their old untranslated state and the newly translated ones would be:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |             | Untranslated  | Translated      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Now, let's plot these two rectangles on our new graphics screen at the newly translated coordinates:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: What happened? We now have a black line in between the two rectangles. That's definitely not what we wanted to happen. Why did this happen? It's partly because of the nature of graphics hardware in the way they address pixels, and partly the way we humans think of pixels mathematically from a programming standpoint. What we need is a better mathematical representation of pixels and graphics coordinates so that when we translate coordinates these things don't happen.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: As we mentioned earlier, the lines on the above diagram represent the borders around each pixel. Each of these lines, like their mathematical counterparts, are infinitely thin. The only thing in the above diagram that has any size (or area) physically are the pixels themselves. Since the boundary lines around the pixels are defining the area that the pixel will occupy, it makes sense that we should think of those lines as the actual coordinates. If we think of the areas in between the pixels as the actual coordinates, we can think of pixels as the areas in between coordinates that are filled in with color. So, if we said to draw a filled in rectangle like we did earlier, we would actually be saying "fill in this rectangle's interior". Just like coloring books as a child, you have to stay inside the lines (or at least we're supposed to). Think about pixels as spots between the lines that get filled in with color just like a coloring book - the only difference is, a pixel cannot go outside the lines (don't you wish you were a pixel when you were younger?).

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Using this new way of thinking of graphics is not very difficult, it just seems a bit odd -especially if you've been working with graphics for awhile. To draw the previous two rectangles properly the coordinates for them would have to be changed somewhat - like this:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **(old method)**

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |             | Untranslated  | Translated      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **(new method)**

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: |             | UNTRANSLATED  | TRANSLATED      |

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Notice that the untranslated rectangles' coordinates are almost the same. In fact, the upper-left coordinates haven't changed at all. The only coordinates that have changed are the lower-right coordinates, and only by one pixel location. Now, if we draw these two rectangles using our new mathematical model for graphics, we would get the following (in both resolution examples:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the two graphs above you may notice a subtle difference in the numbering of the coordinates. The numbers are all there, but instead of labeling the cells themselves with coordinates, we have labeled the lines in between as the coordinates. When we say to draw a rectangle from (2,1) to (5,4) we are saying to draw a filled in area "between" coordinate lines 2 and 5 in the X direction and 1 and 4 in the Y direction. If you look closely at the upper left diagram, you will notice that is exactly what we have done. Now look closely at the upper right diagram. There are no gaps between the rectangles now. Also if you look at the translated coordinates, the right edge of the first rectangle is at X coordinate 10, and the left edge of the second rectangle is also at X coordinate 10. But they don't overlap each other. That's the part about this new way of thinking about things that gives people the hardest time.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: So far so good. Let's look at another example - one which draws the same two rectangles but this time, let's not fill them in. The diagram below shows the two at both example resolutions:

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Not what you thought would happen, was it? This example illustrates a key point in our mathematical model of graphics: that there is a difference between filled objects and outlined objects. Filled objects fill everything inside an enclosed area whereas an outline (one or more lines) uses pixels to approximate an infinitely thin line. When lines and points are plotted on the video device, they are "rounded up" to the next highest pixel location. So, a point at (4,2) would not be on the intersecting lines at (4,2), it would be a pixel activated between 4 and 5 on the X axis and 2 and 3 on the Y axis. Look at the upper right diagram to convince yourself this is the case. Filled-in areas on the other hand, do not round up to the next highest pixel locations. They always fill in an area in-between the boundary lines. This means that in a filled-in rectangle, the right and bottom edges are "off by one" so to speak.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: To better illustrate these two different situations, we will draw a filled-in rectangle and a non-filled rectangle both using the same dimensions at the same resolution, then we will superimpose them on top of each other to better show the differences;

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Notice that the two rectangles are not the exact same size. Both the left and top edges are at the exact same locations, but in the case of the unfilled rectangle, the right and bottom edges are one pixel over and down. This shows that lines and points are rounded up to the next highest pixel location (the first pixel after the coordinate), but filled areas fill between the boundary lines. This seemingly odd way of doing things becomes extremely important when you deal with one image at different resolutions - as you saw with the case of translating two filled-in rectangles earlier from one resolution to another.

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: In a very real sense, you could easily think about coordinates and graphics in two different ways. The way to think about them depends on the type of graphics operation being performed. If you are dealing with a fill operation of some kind, then you think about the drawing surface with coordinate lines "in between" the physical pixel cells. If you are dealing with a line drawing situation (or drawing points, circles, etc), then you can think of coordinates directly addressing the pixel cells themselves (just like when we began this conversation at the beginning of this section). When dealing with line drawing operations, there is no difference in mathematical models - there's only a difference when you get into filling areas in. Whichever method of thinking of things works best for you, use.

requirements.text: Other filled objects work the same way as do filled rectangles. For example, consider an unfilled polygon with the following vertices: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.text: With this polygon we would have a polygon that looks like the left diagram below. The right diagram is what it would look like if it were filled and had a border drawn at the same time (the different shaded blocks indicates which is border, fill-color, or both): _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: Taking a second example. Let's consider an unfilled oval centered at (7,3) with a horizontal radius of 8 and a vertical radius of 4. The unfilled oval is depicted in the left diagram below. The diagram on the right is the same oval with the border drawn and also filled in. Notice how the border is drawn in relation to the filled-in interior and how it adheres to resolution independence. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: If you look closely at the right diagram, you will notice that the oval isn't "balanced". This is because in this situation, the oval is centered about a particular point, but the filled oval is partially offset on an odd-boundary - the filled interior is 8 pixels to the left of the center point (inclusive), and 7 pixels to the right of the center point (inclusive). This is due to the resolution independent nature of filled regions. If you need to draw a perfectly smooth filled oval, draw one with a solid fill and with borders enabled, both with the same drawing and fill color. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: The Mathematics of Graphics and Coordinates
requirements.text: **Practical summary:** for fills, think "coordinates between pixels"; for lines, points, and curves, think "coordinates address pixels" - the models only diverge for filled interiors. Filled polygons and curved regions follow the same fill-between-lines rule, with their borders (optional since 2.0, see [2.3 Shapes & Fills](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md)) rounding up like lines. _Evidence: 2.00a4 (the treatment carries into 3.x unchanged)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BASE_MATH
requirements.text: This command sets the Base Math used extensively throughout the RIPscrip language. By default, the RIPscrip language uses Base-36 math for all of its numeric parameters. This number can be changed to accomodate larger values for numeric parameters. For example, a two digit base-36 number can hold a number from 0-1295. A two digit Base-64 number can hold a number from 0-4095 which is considerably larger.
