requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER
requirements.text: _Draw a chain of cubic Bézier curves and lines, closed_

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `z`                                |

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `num:2 count:2 [type:1 record]...` |

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|z <num> <count> [<type> <record>]...` **Example:** See the annotated original below.

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Draw Color, Back Color, Line Style, Write Mode, Viewport, Port, Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** original special byte parser, handlers 0x1e449 / 0x2cda0, type-class table 0x7ef48, and complete SHAPES.RIP samples; [derivation](../research/issue-15-bezier-contracts.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER
requirements.text: The header contains **only `num` and `count`**, each fixed width 2 in the current base. There is **no separate `x_base y_base` header pair** in the shipped 3.0 grammar. The first typed record supplies the first point. This corrects the inherited [2.0 draft layout](../../2.0/ripscrip/2.2-curves.md#rip_poly_bezier); it is not a special second grammar for the census examples.

requirements.heading: Typed records
requirements.text: `num` is the number of records, including the terminal record, and must be at least 1. Each record begins with one literal digit. All coordinates have the active XY width and current base; they are absolute world coordinates.

requirements.heading: Typed records
requirements.text: | Type digits | Following fields | Rendering meaning |

requirements.heading: Typed records
requirements.text: | `0`, `3`, `4` | `x:XY y:XY` | A point on the connected outline; a straight edge leads to the next record's start |

requirements.heading: Typed records
requirements.text: | `1`, `2`, `5`, `6` | `x:XY y:XY cx1:XY cy1:XY cx2:XY cy2:XY` | Cubic start P0=(x,y), controls P1/P2, endpoint P3 taken from the **next record's first pair** |

requirements.heading: Typed records
requirements.text: All three point types render identically; all four curve types render identically. The draft calls 1 “smooth” and 2 “jointed” as authoring distinctions, but this renderer neither synthesizes missing controls nor enforces a smooth join. Types 3..6 are accepted directly on the wire, including 5/6 in the shipped demos.

requirements.heading: Typed records
requirements.text: For a **last curve record**, z takes P3 from the **first record's first pair**. A **last point record** need not repeat that first pair: the closed polygon consumer adds the final straight edge. The command does not append a separate closure vertex. This same closure rule applies to filled [`x`](2.3-shapes-and-fills.md#rip_filled_poly_bezier). Only open [`t`](#rip_poly_bezier_line) prohibits a terminal curve.

requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text: `count` is the requested point count **per curve**, using the same sampling as [`Z`](#rip_bezier). Let C be the number of curve records and L the number of point records, so `num=C+L`. The complete decoded input occupies **2+7*C+3*L numeric values**, including both headers and every type. This must fit the original parser's **8193-value** collection capacity; each header is also bounded by its two-digit encoding. For example, no more than 1170 all-curve records fit, while base-64 permits 2730 all-point records. This input limit is separate from the generated limit below.

requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text: If C>0 and count is zero, RIPtel rejects the whole primitive without drawing. If C=0, count is unused and may be zero. For C>0, calculate the effective N as follows:

requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text:
```text
N = count
if C*N + L + 1 > 4095:
    N = floor((4094 - L) / C)
if N == 0:
    reject whole primitive
submitted_points = C*N + L
```

requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text: Thus **4094 is the maximum actual submitted point count**, not 4096, and reduction applies uniformly to every curve. For example, two curves and one point requested at 2047 use N=2046 and submit 4093 points. Each curve's N-point output includes its next record's start when N>=2; that following record also supplies its own start, so join duplicates are retained. N=1 contributes only the curve start to the submitted array. The generator's extra scratch endpoint for N=1 is not an additional drawn point.

requirements.heading: Counts, limits and rejection
requirements.text: Invalid types, incomplete records or disagreement with `num` reject the whole primitive; they do not draw a prefix or silently omit a bad terminal record. Most common-consumer failures are silent, while `num=0` reports “Too few segments”. Oversized numeric input is truncated by the byte parser and rejected when its resulting vector fails validation. See the [consumer contract](../techspecs/2.2-bezier-consumer-contract.md) for the exact numerical and capacity boundaries.

requirements.heading: Annotated original z example
requirements.text: The first z at physical line 70 of the original **SHAPES.RIP** is complete below. The file sets `J10` (base 36) and `n2000` (XY width 2). The census's 60-character preview truncates its tail; the original payload is valid.

requirements.heading: Annotated original z example
requirements.text:
```text
!|z081428KGC8KESASF85CGF8E4F8BCGC5DKGCEOGCE4GW5DKHGD0I0BWI06ASI0BWGWASFS09OGW09OI008KI0
```

requirements.heading: Annotated original z example
requirements.text: | Field / record | Exact grouped bytes | Decoded world coordinates |

requirements.heading: Annotated original z example
requirements.text: | Header | `08 14` | 8 records, requested N=40 |

requirements.heading: Annotated original z example
requirements.text: | 3: curve | `5 DK GC EO GC E4 GW` | Start (488,588); controls (528,588), (508,608) |

requirements.heading: Annotated original z example
requirements.text: | 5: curve | `6 AS I0 BW GW AS FS` | Start (388,648); controls (428,608), (388,568) |

requirements.heading: Annotated original z example
requirements.text: Each curve ends at the next listed start. The last point closes straight to (308,588). C=5 and L=3 produce **203 submitted points** without budget reduction. The original parser produces 46 numbers, exactly `2+7*5+3*3`; the apparent `28 KG` header and invalid type `C` arise only from applying the draft's nonexistent base-point header. Artifact identity and native vectors are preserved in the [research note](../research/issue-15-bezier-contracts.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER_LINE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Draw Color, Back Color, Line Style, Write Mode, Viewport, Port, Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** original handlers 0x1e4a4 / 0x2cda0, mode-2 terminal check 0x2ce98, and original CURVES/SHAPES samples; [derivation](../research/issue-15-bezier-contracts.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER_LINE
requirements.text: Use the [same header, typed records, sampling and limits as z](#rip_poly_bezier). The outline remains open. Its **last record must be a point type 0/3/4**; a terminal curve type 1/2/5/6 causes rejection of the **entire command**, without a drawing call. The help string “The last segment of a poly-bezier cannot be a curve” applies to this open form, not to closed z or filled x. No terminal point is required to repeat the first point, and t adds no closing edge.

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER_LINE
requirements.text: The original example decodes as follows; it too has no separate base-point header:

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER_LINE
requirements.text:
```text
03 14                         # 3 records, N=40 in base 36
2 JA 62 HA 62 JE A6            # start (694,218), controls (622,218),(698,366)
6 HU A6 JG A6 HC EE            # start (642,366), controls (700,366),(624,518)
0 JC EG                       # terminal point (696,520)
```

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_BEZIER_LINE
requirements.text: The two cubics end at (642,366) and (696,520), respectively. C=2, L=1 gives **81 submitted points**. The original parser produces the 19-number vector `3,40,2,694,218,622,218,698,366,6,642,366,700,366,624,518,0,696,520`.

requirements.text: This command fills a rectangle using the current fill style and, when [borders](#rip_set_border) are enabled, draws its border with the **current logical pen and current write mode**. RIPtel 3.1 does **not** force that border to solid COPY. (x0,y0) and (x1,y1) are any two opposing corners of the rectangle. If x0=x1 or y0=y1 then the command can draw a single line or pixel; with borders off the degenerate region draws nothing. _Evidence: original K consumer, line-pen producer and native border/ROP captures; [derivation](../research/issue-33-filled-rectangle-borders.md)._

requirements.heading: RIP_FILLED_RECTANGLE
requirements.text: The pen producer maps line types 0/1/2/3/4 to GDI SOLID/DOT/DASHDOT/DASH/DASHDOTDOT. Therefore a width-one dotted border keeps its dotted pen, while **custom type 4 uses fixed DASHDOTDOT rather than the stored arbitrary 16-bit custom mask** in this K path. Thickness is the stored device value described by [LINE_STYLE](2.1-lines.md#rip_line_style). GDI makes patterned CreatePen styles solid when width exceeds one; width zero requests one device pixel. This API limitation explains wide solid borders, but does not change their selected write mode. For example, K with a width-one dotted pen and XOR uses DOT plus XOR; width three uses a solid GDI pen plus XOR. _Evidence: original pen requests/selection and Microsoft's [CreatePen contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-createpen); [derivation](../research/issue-33-filled-rectangle-borders.md)._

requirements.heading: RIP_FILLED_RECTANGLE
requirements.text: With borders enabled, ordinary line flags draw the fill first with no pen, then a border with the current pen, no fill brush and transparent pattern gaps. Line flags **exactly 1** combine fill and current pen in one pass with opaque background gaps; flags 0/2/3 take the separate-pass route. Borders off uses the fill brush with no pen. In all cases K retains the current write operation for its drawing passes and leaves stored pen/mask/write-mode state unchanged. _Evidence: complete original K execution across all five modes, line types, border states and flags; [derivation](../research/issue-33-filled-rectangle-borders.md)._

requirements.heading: RIP_FILLED_RECTANGLE
requirements.text: This command operates similarly to the [RIP_BAR](#rip_bar) command when borders are disabled, however the lower-left and lower-right edges of the filled rectangle obey the resolution independent method of performing fills (see [1.2 Math & Coordinates](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md) for details on how this works). _(v2.A3)_ Under that rule a filled interior fills _between_ the coordinate lines - one pixel short of the right and bottom border.

requirements.text: Draws the outline of a rounded rectangle using the current logical pen and write mode, with no fill brush. N's filled-object border setting does not suppress this outline. Both opposing axes are normalized before conversion, so reversed corners are accepted. Radius is an **XY-width unsigned X-world distance**, converted once using the X scale; the usual corner diameters are equal device values. requirements.heading: RIP_FILLED_ROUNDED_RECT
requirements.text: Draws the same rounded geometry with the current fill brush. N0 selects no pen; N1 adds the current logical pen. As with [K](#rip_filled_rectangle), ordinary line flags use separate fill and border passes, while flags exactly 1 combine them. Both retain the current write mode: the inherited promise of a forced COPY border is not the shipped behavior. Fill geometry and brush phase do not change when borders are disabled. _Evidence: original u consumer and native pen/brush/ROP captures; [derivation](../research/issue-38-rounded-rectangle-geometry.md)._

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: **Wire fields:** U and u each contain **five XY-width unsigned numbers**, including `rad`. Supported XY widths are 2..5 in the current base math. There is no signed negative-coordinate/radius form and no fixed two-character radius exception. For example, after selecting XY=3, all five fields occupy three characters; a two-character radius leaves an incomplete command. _Evidence: original dispatch descriptors and complete byte-parser captures at both bases/all four widths; [derivation](../research/issue-38-rounded-rectangle-geometry.md)._

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: For ordinary values, first normalize each opposing coordinate pair, then convert the two corners with their respective world-to-device X/Y ratios. Let the converted inclusive corner lines, after viewport origin, be `(L,T)` and `(R,B)`. The driver requests **RoundRect(L,T,R+1,B+1,2r,2r)**, where **`r=floor(rad × device_width / world_width)`**. It does not convert radius with Y, apply another aspect correction or clamp it against the rectangle before that request.

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: On a **640×350 world / 640×480 canvas**, radius 20 becomes **20 device pixels on both axes**, giving a 40×40 corner ellipse. World corners `(20,35)` and `(100,105)` become `(20,48)` and `(100,144)` with zero viewport origin; the request is `(20,48,101,145,40,40)`. Thus Y placement scales by 480/350 while the corner's ordinary radius stays 20. On a 1280×960 world / 640×480 canvas, radius 20 instead becomes 10 device pixels and the corner ellipse is 20×20. These are device-coordinate circles before any oversize fitting; the inherited unrestricted claim of truly circular corners is too broad.

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: **Oversize fitting:** the RIP driver neither rejects nor pre-clamps an oversized radius; it forwards the corner ellipse to GDI. In the ordinary compatible device-coordinate geometry, GDI fits the ellipse's absolute diameters **independently** to the available X/Y spans: `dx=min(abs(ellipse_width),R-L)`, `dy=min(abs(ellipse_height),B-T)`. Semiaxes are dx/2 and dy/2. This happens after coordinate/radius conversion and compatible-mode far-edge adjustment; it is not a common circular-radius clamp to half the smaller dimension. For example, an 8×6 span and r=5 fits to an 8×6 ellipse, rather than a circle of radius 3. Fine curved-edge rounding remains a canvas raster decision. _Evidence: original unchanged requests, Microsoft's [RoundRect diameter contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-roundrect), and separately identified [GDI conformance vectors](../research/issue-38-rounded-rectangle-geometry.md#gdi-boundary-reconciliation)._

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: **Zero and degenerate cases:** radius 0 requests square corners (ordinary rectangle geometry). Equal source X or Y coordinates are accepted; far+1 makes the corresponding API extent one device unit, including for u with N0. There is no RIP-level early rejection or empty-object skip; U still requests its pen, and u still requests its fill/optional pen. Do not expand a degenerate shape by the radius: fitting is constrained by its resulting span. A one-unit API box has a zero centerline span on that axis. Whether it changes a digital edge pixel depends on pen/fill rasterization. The driver ignores the drawing service's success/failure return, including oversized requests, and does not report a new RIP argument error on that basis. _Evidence: original branches and normalized/zero-extent/success/failure captures; [derivation](../research/issue-38-rounded-rectangle-geometry.md)._

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: **Shipped high-radius defect:** the actual request is `ellipse_width=2r` using the full converted DWORD, but `ellipse_height=2×(int16_t)(r & 65535)`. Thus r=32768 produces height -65536, r=65535 height -2, and r=65536 height 0. GDI's ellipse handling uses the magnitude for negative dimensions and treats a zero dimension as square-corner geometry; this is not a second radius unit. Modern geometry code should distinguish the normal X-world radius rule from this original truncation/sign defect. Extreme DWORD multiplication/doubling overflow is also original fixed-width arithmetic, not an additional advertised coordinate range. _Evidence: original U/u argument preparation, exhaustive WORD-radius native captures and the separately sourced [GDI boundary](../research/issue-38-rounded-rectangle-geometry.md#gdi-boundary-reconciliation)._

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: **Filled interior:** u uses the same converted bounds with or without its pen. There is **no extra one-pixel inset or shrink** when N0 is selected. The original K path also constructs far+1 bounds; the inherited prose about filling strictly between all coordinate lines must not be interpreted as an additional inset applied to u. The brush fills the rounded region with the established [device-context pattern phase](#fill-pattern-bitmaps). Removing the pen removes a separate border operation, not the region's geometric contour. Microsoft's [RoundRect contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-roundrect) and the bounded conformance observations establish the drawing boundary; these native probes capture requests and do not execute Windows rasterization.

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: For a device-space rounded contour `(0,0)`..`(8,6)` with r2, this grid distinguishes strictly interior samples from its contour. **F** samples are inside the fill region in either N state, **B** marks the straight geometric border, **.** is outside, and **?** leaves curved-edge pixel selection unspecified:

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text:
```text
      x 012345678
    y
    0   .?BBBBB?.
    1   ??FFFFF??
    2   BFFFFFFFB
    3   BFFFFFFFB
    4   BFFFFFFFB
    5   ??FFFFF??
    6   .?BBBBB?.
```

requirements.heading: Rounded-Rectangle Geometry
requirements.text: This is a geometry/interior illustration, not a Windows pixel oracle. With N0, B is not separately stroked; the grid does not promise that removing the pen paints or erases every integer sample on that contour. Exact corner scan conversion is deliberately left to the canvas. The resolved wire fields, device radius, independent oversize fitting and unmodified filled bounds are sufficient to construct the shape without choosing an unspecified RIP policy. _Evidence and inference boundaries: [complete derivation](../research/issue-38-rounded-rectangle-geometry.md)._

requirements.heading: RIP_PIE_SLICE
requirements.text: This command draws a "pie slice". The slice is circular. It obeys all of the same commands as the [RIP_ARC](2.2-curves.md#rip_arc) command. The ends of the arc are connected to the Center-Point of the Arc with two straight lines. These two lines converge at the Center-Point. The interior of the Slice is filled with the current Fill Color and Pattern. The exterior (outline) of the Slice is drawn using the current drawing color and line thickness. The Line Pattern feature does not apply to this command.

requirements.heading: Polygon counts and wire limits
requirements.text: **Reconstructed from RIPtel 3.1:** [RIP_POLYLINE](2.1-lines.md#rip_polyline), RIP_POLYGON and [RIP_FILLED_POLYGON](#rip_filled_polygon) consume a **two-character count in the current base math**, followed by exactly N pairs of XY-width coordinates. Increasing coordinate size changes the coordinates' widths, not the count's width.

requirements.heading: Polygon counts and wire limits
requirements.text: | Base math | Largest count prefix | Supplied vertices | Open polyline segments |

requirements.heading: Polygon counts and wire limits
requirements.text: The exact maximum-command prefixes are `!|J10|lZZ` and `!|J1S|l&&`, respectively, followed by 1295 or 4095 XY coordinate pairs. Replace `l` with `P` or `p` for the closed or filled commands. J's own parameter always uses MegaNum. For example, keeping default XY=2, the UltraNum command supplies 8191 numeric values (one count plus 8190 coordinates). Do not transmit a separate closing vertex unless it is intentionally part of the N supplied vertices; Polygon closes the last-to-first edge automatically, while Polyline stays open.

requirements.heading: Polygon counts and wire limits
requirements.text: The historical readme/HLP advertisement of **4096 vertices** does not establish a reachable wire count. Two digits have no representation for 4096 and the original parser has no special count encoding. The original handlers actually convert **N+1** pairs from scratch storage while passing **N** to Polygon/Polyline; at the maximum UltraNum count, that is 4096 scratch conversions and 4095 drawn vertices, even for an open polyline. The extra pair comes from stale argument slots, not an implicit closing point supplied by the host. A new implementation should read exactly N pairs and validate the complete count/length relationship before drawing.

requirements.heading: Small counts and drawing state
requirements.text: The count is direct at the lower boundary too: **`00` means zero, never 4096**. The byte parser accepts the count-only form, but the original P/l/p handler reports `Insufficient parameters` and returns before coordinate conversion or any drawing call. This is a diagnosed command with no pixels, not a special maximum-count encoding.

requirements.heading: Small counts and drawing state
requirements.text: | Supplied vertices | `P` (closed outline) | `l` (open polyline) |

requirements.text: | 1 | Calls Polygon with count 1; GDI rejects it, with no point drawn | Calls Polyline with count 1; GDI rejects it, with no point drawn |

requirements.text: | 2 | Accepted ordinary two-vertex closed outline between those vertices; no enclosed area | Accepted single segment between the two vertices |

requirements.heading: Small counts and drawing state
requirements.text: RIPtel does **not** enforce a three-vertex minimum for P or turn a one-vertex shape into POINT. The one-vertex GDI failure is ignored by the driver; no additional RIP error is reported. Microsoft’s [Polygon](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-polygon) and [Polyline](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-polyline) contracts require at least two points, and neither changes the GDI current position. A two-vertex closed outline uses the ordinary selected pen/write operation; this does not promise a renderer-independent pixel mask or override line style, thickness or write mode.

requirements.heading: Small counts and drawing state
requirements.text: These counts leave the RIP pen/style selection and stored drawing cursor unchanged, including the zero- and one-vertex cases. For positive counts the handler performs its usual temporary drawing selections, restores background mode/objects and may invalidate a region even when GDI draws nothing. Its stale N+1 scratch conversion still occurs for a one-vertex command, but **only the declared N points** reach GDI; the stale pair does not make a second visible vertex. Filled p shares the zero/one-count guards; two vertices enclose no fill area, with any outline still controlled by its ordinary border state. _Evidence: original parser/handlers,0..3 counts at every supported width/radix with state snapshots and [223,367 native checks](../research/issue-13-polygon-counts.md#post-pr-small-count-results), reconciled with the GDI contracts above. The native probe captures original calls and API-failure cleanup; it does not execute Windows rasterization._

requirements.heading: Small counts and drawing state
requirements.text: **Evidence:** original count/coordinate descriptors, byte parser, J/n handlers and l/P/p drawing consumers, including all maximum prefixes at XY widths 2–5 and a trailing-sentinel test; see the [derivation and native probe](../research/issue-13-polygon-counts.md#exact-counts-and-single-contour-closure). These are RIPtel 3.1 wire findings; they do not change the earlier editions' 512-vertex limits or require reproducing GDI rasterization.

requirements.heading: RIP_POLY_POLYGON
requirements.text: A multi-contour polygon: an initial contour count and first vertex count, followed by coordinate pairs and later contour counts/pairs using the exact [width and aggregate rules below](#multi-contour-widths-and-aggregate-limits). Contours are filled by the even-odd rule - POLYPOLY.RIP places a colored circle behind the figure "so you can see the transparency aspect" through the holes - and the border is switched via [RIP_SET_BORDER](#rip_set_border) ("With borders:" / "Without borders:"). The example above encodes 3 contours (a 4-vertex outer box and two triangular holes). Vertex lists may be split across physical lines with the standard `\` continuation. This is a genuinely new object type: 2.00a4 has nothing comparable, and the single-contour [RIP_FILLED_POLYGON](#rip_filled_polygon) even-odd overlap behavior is only an accident of its fill rule.

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: **Reconstructed from RIPtel 3.1:** the initial contour count C and the **first** contour's vertex count N1 each occupy **two digits** in the current base math. Every coordinate occupies XY digits. A shipped descriptor quirk makes **every later contour's vertex count occupy XY digits too**. The exact sequence is:

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text:
```text
C:2 N1:2 (x:XY y:XY repeated N1 times)
N2:XY (x:XY y:XY repeated N2 times)
...
NC:XY (x:XY y:XY repeated NC times)
```

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: At default XY=2, all these counts are two digits. At XY=3, however, first-contour count 3 is `03` and second-contour count 2 is `002`. For example, this exact stream gives the first contour three (1,2) pairs and the second two (1,2) pairs; the coincident points deliberately isolate parsing from rendering:

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: The original parser collects at most **8193 numeric values in one command**, including all count fields. For a well-formed multi-contour command with total V vertices, use the aggregate constraint **1 + C + 2V <= 8193**. Each contour must have at least two supplied vertices. C and N1 must fit two digits; later Ni must fit XY digits. All contours share the point/argument budget.

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: | Base math | Maximum contours C | Count encoding | Construction reaching that maximum |

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: | MegaNum (36) | 1295 | `ZZ` | Two vertices in each contour; 6476 numbers |

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: | UltraNum (64) | 1638 | `Pc` | Two vertices in each contour; 8191 numbers |

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: These maxima are `min(base²-1, floor(8192/5))`: each minimal contour costs one count and four coordinates, in addition to the initial C. Increasing C can reduce the remaining vertex allowance. With XY=2, the maximum **aggregate** V is 4094 in MegaNum (counts 1295,1295,1295,209) or 4095 in UltraNum (counts 4093,2, or one contour of 4095). With XY>=3, MegaNum also reaches 4095, using first-contour count 2 and later-contour count 4093. All three multi-contour vertex-boundary constructions use 8193 numbers and are verified through the original parser and PolyPolygon consumer. There is no separate 4096-vertex allowance for every contour.

requirements.heading: Multi-contour widths and aggregate limits
requirements.text: **Shipped malformed-input behavior:** after collecting 8193 values, RIPtel discards further numeric fields but still dispatches the collected prefix. Its contour/length guards are incomplete, and its single-contour handlers also perform the stale extra read described [above](#polygon-counts-and-wire-limits). These defects are not a safe rejection policy for oversized input. Implementations should enforce the full grammar, declared counts and aggregate budget before drawing, rather than forwarding truncated or inconsistent arrays to a renderer.

requirements.heading: Fill-pattern origin and scaling
requirements.text: **Reconstructed from RIPtel 3.1:** predefined and custom patterns tile from **(0,0) of the drawing device context**, with an **eight-device-pixel period** in each direction. Onscreen ports share the master screen drawing context; each offscreen bitmap has its own bitmap-local origin. This is the graphics drawing surface's origin, independent of where the application window sits on the desktop. Changing the port, viewport, clipping rectangle or primitive does not restart the tile within that context. World scaling converts shape coordinates to device coordinates but does not resize the 8×8 mask.

requirements.heading: Fill-pattern origin and scaling
requirements.text: For a covered device-context pixel `(x,y)`, use `M[y mod 8] & (0x80 >> (x mod 8))`, with modulo residues 0–7. A nonzero result selects the fill color; zero selects the pen background color, subject to the current write mode. Evaluate this after world conversion and geometry placement, using the final context coordinates. [RIP_VIEWPORT's original placement behavior](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport) determines those coordinates; do not separately add a screen port's origin a second time. Adjacent primitives sample the same tile continuously.

requirements.heading: Fill-pattern origin and scaling
requirements.text: For example, let a screen port start at `(2,1)` and its stored viewport start at device-context `(5,3)`, with world and device sizes both 640×480. Set custom rows `80 00 00 00 00 00 00 00` (MegaNum command `!|s3K0000000000000001`, fill-color index 1). Draw filled objects over neighboring world-coordinate ranges `x=0..8` and `x=8..16`, both spanning `y=0..8`. Their placement starts at context X=5 and X=13. Interior samples `(8,8)` and `(16,8)` both select foreground, while `(9,8)` and `(10,9)` select background. Restarting at the viewport would instead put a set bit at `(5,3)`; restarting at the port would put one at `(10,9)`. The native probe captures the original placement and unchanged brush; these sample colors follow from the context-origin rule, independently of exact shape-edge rasterization.

requirements.heading: Fill-pattern origin and scaling
requirements.text: **Evidence and limits:** the original brush builder creates a fixed 8×8 monochrome bitmap; the ordinary filled-shape paths select that brush directly into their drawing context without changing its origin. The [derivation](../research/issue-12-fill-masks.md#consumers-and-exact-phase-derivation) combines those original calls with Microsoft's [default brush-origin contract](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/gdi/brush-origin). This establishes RIPtel's default phase, rather than leaving it to a new implementation's choice; it does not claim exact Windows shape-edge rasterization or historical 1.x/2.x phase parity. The legacy [RIP_FILL defect](../techspecs/2.0-fill-defects-delta.md) remains an exception: its affected border-color branch fills solid instead of applying the pattern.

The other pixels in the fill area are set to the current pen background color.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BORDER
requirements.text: The inherited ALPHA 4 draft claims all filled-object borders use COPY and that only polygon borders honor line patterns. **That blanket rule does not describe RIPtel 3.1's K path.** [RIP_FILLED_RECTANGLE](#rip_filled_rectangle) selects its current logical pen, including dotted/dashed styles at supported widths, and uses the current write mode for both fill and border. Its GDI pen mapping, custom-mask limitation, width behavior and background-gap/pass rules are specified in that command's entry. N controls whether that border is present; it does not force a solid pen or COPY. Do not derive K's rendering from the draft's generic exception list. _Evidence: original N state setter and K producer/consumer captures; [derivation](../research/issue-33-filled-rectangle-borders.md)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_BORDER

requirements.heading: RIP_FILL
requirements.text: This command performs a "flood fill" emanating from the given `<x,y>` point. The fill "oozes" in all directions up to `<border>` color, but the border itself is not changed. If the border color does not completely enclose the `<x,y>` point, the fill will continue to the edges of the viewport; if the fill point is already the border color, no fill is performed. _(1.54 semantics, never restated for 2.x or 3.x)_

requirements.heading: RIP_FILL

Their actual [angle and closure behavior](2.2-curves.md#angle-ordering-and-sweeps) remains command-specific.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT
requirements.text: This command displays text at the current graphics cursor of the selected port. For RIPtel 3.1, every accepted nonempty TEXT call advances stored X by the signed low-word width returned by the selected font's metric routine and leaves Y unchanged. **There is no orientation or justification gate.** The inherited horizontal/left-only rule does not describe this driver. Classic text uses the classic width routine; outline text uses the cached outline width routine. The update is not conditional on pixels being produced. _Evidence: [original handler and native cursor matrix](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#text-cursor-stores)._

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT
requirements.text: The cursor belongs to the [port](7.0-drawing-ports.md#the-port-table), independently of the selected graphics style. MOVE stores a world-to-device converted point plus viewport origin. The [TEXT_XY compatibility rules](#rip_text_xy) include a different classic path; stored coordinates must not be assumed to remain in world units. Empty TEXT and a disabled viewport leave the cursor unchanged. A RIP_ERASE_VIEWPORT does not reset it; drawing reset initializes the current cursor.

requirements.text: This command draws at an explicit anchor using the current font settings. In RIPtel 3.1 it is **not fully equivalent to MOVE followed by TEXT**. Every accepted nonempty call with an enabled viewport replaces both stored cursor coordinates, for vertical, centered and right-justified text as well as horizontal left-justified text. requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_XY
requirements.text: The classic branches use the unconverted input `(x,y)` in these **cursor stores**. Font zero also wrongly chooses the outline metric: the branch tests the classic **font number**, not direction. These are shipped state-update defects; the classic drawing helper's own geometry is a separate operation. Orientation and justification do not change this table.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_XY
requirements.text: For a concrete outline case, take viewport origin (5,7), a 1:1 world/device ratio, explicit anchor (100,80), previous cursor (300,400) and a string whose outline width is 37. A vertical, centered or right-justified TEXT_XY leaves the cursor at **(142,87)**. A following TEXT of width 37 leaves **(179,87)**. At a 2:1 ratio, outline TEXT_XY instead stores **(92,47)**; the classic paths still add raw (100,80) before the selected metric. The [native fixtures](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#text-cursor-stores) deliberately supply distinct classic/outline widths 13/37 to prove every branch, without claiming a particular real font/string has those widths.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_XY

Accepted calls update state even if the rendering helper does not produce text. _Evidence: DLL; [complete original handler, source addresses and controlled-service limits](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md)._

requirements.text: This is the workhorse text command of the corpus (638 uses, versus zero bare `T` commands). In 3.x scenes it renders in whichever font was last selected - very often an [RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE](#rip_extended_font_style) outline font - and the text argument may contain `<<NAME>>` macros (`!|@809U<<LAB1>>` labels buttons from `.DEF`-file [text variables](../../glossary.md)) or `$&VAR$` dereferences. requirements.heading: RIP_BOUNDED_TEXT

requirements.text: The physical pixel dimensions of any particular font cell at a given magnification level vary depending on resolution in such a way that they appear to be the same size on the screen. For example, if a font at magnification level 4 is 35 pixels tall at 640x350 resolution, at 640x480 resolution, the font would be the same width, but would be 48 pixels tall. This makes sure that the fonts are resolution independent. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.text: Flag values 1 and 2 are mutually exclusive. This means that either one of them may be specified, but not both! If both are omitted, then the text is "left justified". Flags 4, 8 and 16 are also mutually exclusive. If either of them are omitted, then the text is drawn with "top" justification. If both flags 1 and 2 are specified, or more than one of the flags 4, 8 and 16 are specified then the command is considered an error and is completely ignored. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Graphics Style, World Frame (font sizing and optional baseline conversion), Viewport (optional baseline conversion). **Numeric base:** every numeric field is **always UltraNum (base 64)**, independent of Base Math and coordinate size. **Evidence:** DLL 3.0.7 (dispatch slot 75; handler RVA `0x1adc0`; text consumer `0x42870`; renderer `0x40ed0`) · corpus (FONTS.RIP, SHADOW.FN, TELLISTS.MNU). The [derivation and original-instruction probe](../research/issue-3-extended-font-style.md) identify the binary, give exact locations and reproduce the results.

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE
requirements.text: The command selects outline-font mode in the current graphics-style record. Subsequent [RIP_TEXT](#rip_text) and [RIP_TEXT_XY](#rip_text_xy) use it; [RIP_FONT_STYLE](#rip_font_style) selects the alternative legacy font mode. Buttons and flowed text also use outline fonts but their placement routines can supply their own alignment or suppress rotation; the ordinary graphics-text rules below do not override those commands' placement policies.

requirements.heading: The Shipped 3.x Wire Layout
requirements.text: **26 fixed characters precede the font-name string.** TeleGrafix's comment in FONTS.RIP is a width crib, not a definition of every field's meaning:

requirements.heading: The Shipped 3.x Wire Layout
requirements.text:
```text
sfFFFFZZOOSSCCBBCCWWRRRRRR
```

requirements.heading: The Shipped 3.x Wire Layout
requirements.text: Offsets below are zero-based from the first character after `y`. All ranges and defaults are decimal. The default column records the dormant outline fields initialized by the exported SDK `RIP_SetDefaultSettings`; these are not optional command arguments and do not imply that normal startup/reset invokes that routine or selects outline-font mode. Normal [style-table defaults](7.1-data-tables.md#initial-and-per-slot-defaults) instead have an empty dormant outline name, size/shadow distance zero and spacing 100.

requirements.heading: The Shipped 3.x Wire Layout
requirements.text: The six-character reserved value has no semantic numeric range: the shipped parser uses a 32-bit accumulator, so values exceeding 32 bits wrap, with no effect on this command. The common `1a1a` idiom is therefore **100% spacing followed by an ignored field**, not an X/Y scale pair. UltraNum `a` is 36, so `1a` = 1×64+36 = 100; a base-36 reader produces the wrong value.

requirements.heading: The Shipped 3.x Wire Layout
requirements.text: The initial `s` and `f` bytes have no active selector semantics in this driver. Their historical intended names need not be guessed to implement them. Their values remain part of the stored graphics style.

requirements.heading: Flags, Justification and Shadow
requirements.text: These are the shipped flag assignments. In particular, underline and strike-through differ from the draft table, and the draft's separate vertical-justification field has no counterpart in `y`. The two apparent alignment validation branches in the DLL are ineffective: they mask to `0x30`/`0xc0` and compare against larger, unreachable bounds. Do not invent command rejection or flag normalization for these combinations.

requirements.heading: Flags, Justification and Shadow
requirements.text: Shadowing draws one displaced copy of the glyph bitmap in the current background color, then the foreground glyph; it does not extrude the outline through intermediate offsets. For distance `d > 0`, the device displacement is `max(1, trunc(d * canvas_width / world_width))` on each shadow axis. The direction bits select the signs independently of the string and character rotations.

requirements.heading: Size, Rotation, Baseline and Spacing
requirements.text: Font size is a whole nominal point count. The renderer gives the font engine `10 * size` tenths of a point and derives separate effective X/Y DPI as `trunc(72 * client_dimension / world_dimension)`. Consequently it follows the world frame rather than physical monitor DPI: at matching world and client dimensions, one nominal point corresponds to one device unit before the font's own metrics are applied. It does not use the current Base Math to reinterpret size, and arbitrary glyph rasterization need not match the original engine pixel for pixel.

requirements.heading: Size, Rotation, Baseline and Spacing
requirements.text: The two rotation fields are independent and absolute; they are not added together. All sixteen pairs are valid:

requirements.text: | `S8` | 1800 | 180° | Left | Half turn |

requirements.heading: Size, Rotation, Baseline and Spacing
requirements.text: For example, `!|y0000B00W04E400001a1a000000Dixon` selects an upward string with upright glyphs; `!|y0000B00W0400E4001a1a000000Dixon` selects a rightward string with quarter-turned glyphs. Decode the actual bytes rather than relying on the corpus's comments: FONTS.RIP includes a `00`/`E4` pair labelled “180 x 90”.

requirements.heading: Size, Rotation, Baseline and Spacing
requirements.text: The shipped baseline-displacement branches are irregular. Let `B` be the stored displacement, negated when `0x0100` is set. The table gives the additional device offset relative to the same command with a zero displacement; positive X is right and positive Y is down. Do not replace this with a general perpendicular-to-baseline rule.

requirements.heading: Size, Rotation, Baseline and Spacing
requirements.text: | String rotation | Character 0° | Character 90° | Character 180° | Character 270° |

requirements.heading: Size, Rotation, Baseline and Spacing
requirements.text: With `0x0200`, conversion happens once at definition time, so later world-frame changes do not retroactively rescale the stored displacement.

requirements.heading: Size, Rotation, Baseline and Spacing
requirements.text: For spacing percentage `P` and normal glyph advance `w`, the adjustment helper returns `trunc((P - 100) * reference_width / 100)`, using truncation toward zero. Normally the reference is `w`; with `0x0400` it is the realized font’s device-space bounding-box width. The ordinary glyph advance is first converted from the font engine’s 1/1440-inch units to device units; the bounding-box width is already in device units. The adjustment is added to the ordinary advance. The flag does not make glyphs monospaced: at `P=100` it changes nothing. For a glyph advance of 8 and a font bounding-box width of 12, `P=125` adds 2 normally, or 3 with `0x0400`. `P=50` and a reference width of 7 produce an adjustment of −3.

requirements.heading: Size, Rotation, Baseline and Spacing
requirements.text: The [FastFont rendering contract](../techspecs/3.2-fastfont-additions.md#riptel-31-rendering-contract) additionally specifies nonzero glyph-interior fill, hollow device-space stamp selection independent of horizontal style percentage, per-glyph masked COPY and direct raw-byte character indexing. These come from the original RIPtel 3.1 engine, not an inference from Type 1 ancestry or a modern font library.

requirements.heading: Exact Decode of the Example
requirements.text:
```text
s f flags size shadow str char baseline spacing unused reserved font
0 0 00BW  1Q   08     00  00   00       1a      1a     000000   Marin
```

requirements.heading: Exact Decode of the Example
requirements.text: `00BW` = 736 = `0x02e0`: centered text, lower-right shadow, and world-unit baseline conversion. `1Q` = 90 nominal points; `08` = shadow distance 8; both rotations and the baseline displacement are zero; spacing is 100%. The second `1a` and the six reserved characters have no effect. No bold, italic, underline or strike-through bits are set.

requirements.heading: State, Errors and Font Names
requirements.text: A successful command selects extended mode and replaces the current style's outline fields and expanded typeface name. A protected graphics style, invalid rotation, zero spacing or missing input name rejects the command before those fields change. Size zero is stored successfully and fails only when text is rendered. No command argument means “retain the old field”; provide the complete block.

requirements.heading: State, Errors and Font Names
requirements.text: Names resolve case-insensitively against the `.RFF` catalogue. The [shipping fonts](../assets/fonts/README.md) include BRUSH, COBB, DEFAULT, DIXON, EUREKA, MARIN, OAKLAND and SYMBOL, with thin, condensed, wide, expanded and hollow variants. The name may be a variable, as in SHOWFONT.FN's `…000000$&FONT_NAME$`. Name expansion can produce an empty or unavailable name after the initial presence check; a failed lookup produces no outline text and leaves the selected extended style intact. **RIPtel 3.1 does not switch to RIP_FONT_STYLE's default at size one on a failed outline-name lookup.** Font-load failure likewise does not install that fallback.

requirements.heading: State, Errors and Font Names
requirements.text: The [2.00a4 draft entry](../../2.0/text/RIPScrip-2.0-alpha-4.txt) describes a superseded 13-character layout, facings and alignment fields. It is not a second accepted `y` form in the shipped 3.0 driver. Earlier shipping clients already used a 26-character block, but this derivation establishes **RIPtel 3.1 / driver 3.0.7**; it does not silently assert every semantic detail for RIPterm 2.x.

requirements.heading: RIP_FONT_ATTRIB
requirements.text: _Add outline-font attributes to the current graphics style_

requirements.heading: RIP_FONT_ATTRIB
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `q`            |

requirements.heading: RIP_FONT_ATTRIB
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `attributes:2` |

requirements.heading: RIP_FONT_ATTRIB
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|q <attributes>` **Example:** `!|q01`

requirements.heading: RIP_FONT_ATTRIB
requirements.text: **Numeric base:** current Base Math. **Evidence:** DLL 3.0.7, dispatch slot 55, handler RVA `0x1c799`; [derivation and original-handler probe](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_FONT_ATTRIB
requirements.text: The current graphics style must be unprotected and use an extended/outline font selected by [`RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE`](#rip_extended_font_style). System-font mode rejects the command. Accepted values are 0..15; bits 1, 2, 4 and 8 mean bold, italic, underline and strike-through respectively. The handler **ORs** these bits into the existing extended-font flags, preserving all other flags. Zero changes nothing; it does not clear attributes. Use a new `y` definition to replace the flags. There is no shadow bit in this command.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: _Return measurements of text in the current graphics font_

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `r`                               |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `mode:1 domain:1 reserved:4 text` |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|r <mode> <domain> <reserved> <text>` **Example:** `!|r010000Hello`

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: **Numeric base:** current Base Math; the four reserved digits are consumed and ignored. **Evidence:** DLL 3.0.7, dispatch slot 57, handler RVA `0x20371–0x209ce`, output helper `0x6947`; [derivation, controlled metric oracles and client-output trace](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md).

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: This is a host query using the current graphics style’s font, not a text-window mode setter. It supports both legacy/system and extended/outline font modes. It prepares the font and measures text without drawing the supplied string. Mode and domain are checked before text processing or a reply:

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | Mode | Result                                  |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | 0    | Width of the complete string            |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | 1    | Height of the complete string           |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | 2    | Width of each byte measured separately  |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | 3    | Height of each byte measured separately |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | Domain | Units |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | 0 | World units: convert device width by world-width/device-width and height by world-height/device-height, with integer truncation |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: | 1 | Device units |

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: Other mode/domain values reject the command. Per-byte results are independent character measurements, not cumulative positions or Unicode code-point measurements. Full-string measurements use the driver’s current font metric routines, so they need not equal a sum of independently measured bytes.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: Except for a case-insensitive exact `$TEXTDATA$` argument, the handler copies at most 1023 input bytes, NUL-terminates the copy, expands text variables with a 1022-byte expansion limit and stores the result as the retained `$TEXTDATA$`. The exact sentinel instead measures the previously retained text without replacing it.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: The engine replies with signed decimal numbers, independently of Base Math. Each result is narrowed to signed 16 bits; world conversion also uses signed 16-bit values. Modes 0/1 return `number\r`. Modes 2/3 return `number:number:…\r`, with no trailing colon. Here `\r` denotes one CR byte. RIPtel’s client output layer can add LF after CR according to its line-ending configuration; this translation is separate from the engine’s reply format.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: A literal empty text argument in extended-font mode produces **no reply**. In system-font mode it follows the metric routines normally: width mode returns zero, height mode returns that font’s empty-string height, and per-byte modes return a bare CR. A nonempty expression expanded to empty text still reaches the metric/reply path in extended-font mode; the early empty check tests the original argument. The outline-font initialization call’s return value is not checked before metric queries, so a reply alone is not proof of successful font loading.

requirements.heading: RIP_TEXT_METRIC
requirements.text: For a controlled font with width 3 per byte and height 7, querying `ab` in device domain returns `6\r`, `7\r`, `3:3\r` or `7:7\r` for modes 0..3. With world/device ratios of 2, world-domain replies are `12\r`, `14\r`, `6:6\r`, `14:14\r`. These are original-handler test oracles with synthetic font metrics, not pixel measurements of a shipped typeface.

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: _Define a rectangular text region_

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `T`                             |

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x1:XY y1:XY x2:XY y2:XY res:2` |

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Viewport, Port, Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_begin_text)) · HLP (`RIP_BeginText`) · corpus (12 uses in N2_TITLE.RIP, NEWS.RIP) · SyncTERM (ripper.c:16581)

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: This command defines a rectangular portion of the graphics viewport that is to display text, usually a long stream of text. Following this command should be a number of [RIP_REGION_TEXT](#rip_region_text) commands with the text to be displayed. The [RIP_END_TEXT](#rip_end_text) terminates this stream of text, something like this:

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text:
```text
RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
     RIP_REGION_TEXT
     RIP_REGION_TEXT
     RIP_REGION_TEXT
     :
     RIP_REGION_TEXT
RIP_END_TEXT
```

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: There must be at least one RIP_REGION_TEXT command in between the header and the footer. There may be as many as needed.

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: These commands ignore the current font "direction"; all text is always displayed horizontally in the current font type, style and size. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: NOTE: The `res` parameter is two bytes wide and is RESERVED for future use and should be set to "00".

requirements.heading: RIP_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: **3.x extension (DLL-confirmed):** The trailing digits are separate one-digit global column and article identifiers, each 0..35. NEWS.RIP uses `01`, `11`, `21`, `31` for columns 0..3 of article 1. Definition retains existing overflow/search settings; fresh state has overflow off. The same rectangle/column helper serves [`1e`](3.1-column-text-system.md#defining-a-column-region---1e). See [the legacy form in 3.1 Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md#the-legacy-form---1t-with-columnstream-digits).

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: _Display a line of text in rectangular text region_

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `t`                         |

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `justify:1` and text-string |

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1t <justify> <text-string>` **Example:** `!|1t1Southern California was pounded`

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Draw Color, Write Mode, Font Style, Viewport, Port, Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_region_text)) · HLP (`RIP_RegionText`) · corpus (42 uses in N2_TITLE.RIP) · SyncTERM (ripper.c:16623)

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: A number of these commands may come sandwiched between the [RIP_BEGIN_TEXT](#rip_begin_text) and [RIP_END_TEXT](#rip_end_text) commands. The `<text-string>` should already word-wrapped in such a way that it will fit inside the rectangular region based on the current font, font size, and drawing color.

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: There are four possible settings for the `<justify>` parameter: _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: | Justify | Description                         |

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: | 0       | Left justify this line              |

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: | 1       | Right/left "full" justify this line |

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: If a text line falls off the bottom of the region, it is discarded -- the rectangular Text Region does not scroll.

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: This command is intended to import some sort of text file document directly into a RIPscrip scene and format it nicely to fit inside a simple rectangular area. If the `<justify>` parameter is set to a value of "1" for a given RIP*REGION_TEXT line, then that line will be justified to both the left and right margins (the RIP_BEGIN_TEXT boundaries). This is so that the displayed text aligns on both sides with the invisible boundaries. This "justification" is done by splitting each RIP_REGION_TEXT line up into chunks of word-groups, broken up at their "white-space" locations. Each spacer is then padded by however many pixels are necessary to keep each spacer of approximately equal size. Only enough spare pixels are added to make sure that the right-edge of the text region aligns with the right border of the boundary. The result is a nicely formatted text block. *(v1.54)\_

requirements.heading: RIP_REGION_TEXT
requirements.text: The corpus uses justify `1` for body lines and `0` for each paragraph's final line - N2_TITLE.RIP's article, quoted in full in the [census](../../3.0/research/riptel-script-census.md), is a TeleGrafix pitch for RIPscrip's JPEG/sound/24-bit future.

requirements.heading: RIP_END_TEXT
requirements.text: _End a rectangular text region_

requirements.heading: RIP_END_TEXT
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `E`      |

requirements.heading: RIP_END_TEXT
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `<none>` |

requirements.heading: RIP_END_TEXT
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1E` **Example:** `!|1E`

requirements.heading: RIP_END_TEXT
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Viewport, Port, Base Math (N/A) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_end_text)) · HLP (`RIP_EndText`) · corpus (20 uses in 8 files) · SyncTERM (ripper.c:16090)

requirements.heading: RIP_END_TEXT
requirements.text: This command indicates the end of a formatted text block. Only one of these "end" commands is necessary for each block.

requirements.heading: RIP_END_TEXT
requirements.text: In 3.x it flushes pending text, closes the selected article’s overflow outputs and deactivates flow for both the [RIP_BEGIN_TEXT](#rip_begin_text)/[RIP_REGION_TEXT](#rip_region_text) form and the [`1e` column-region](3.1-column-text-system.md#defining-a-column-region---1e) form. It retains definitions, selection and paging state; it is not an overflow reset. The scene-end `#` also reaches this operation. _Evidence: DLL; [derivation](../research/issue-4-column-overflow.md)._

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.reason: PR #71 documentation answers are adopted at a9e0c2f490714d82a0827675ffbc074aa5ae00e6; implementation and independent expectations must now be reconciled. Previous blocker review:

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | **Command** | `e` |
requirements.reason: PR #71 documentation answers are adopted at a9e0c2f490714d82a0827675ffbc074aa5ae00e6; implementation and independent expectations must now be reconciled. Previous blocker review:

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x0:XY y0:XY x1:XY y1:XY column:1 article:1 flags:4 highlight:2 reserved:8` followed by an optional search-word string |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1e <x0> <y0> <x1> <y1> <column> <article> <flags> <highlight> <reserved> <search-words>` **Example:** `!|1e4L3D919K0100010000000000`

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: All numeric fields use the current base math; each `XY` uses the current coordinate width. With two-character coordinates the fixed block is 24 characters. The driver normalizes each pair of corner coordinates into ascending order, records inclusive widths (`x1-x0+1`), and converts the rectangle from world to device coordinates when it is defined. Text uses the current font and drawing attributes when flowed; a definition does not capture a private font or copy of the article’s prose.

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: FONTS.RIP’s crib is `xxyyxxyycaffffccrrrrrrrr`. Its previously unknown `cc` field is the highlight palette index:

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | Field | Meaning and validation |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | Four `xx`/`yy` coordinates | Opposite rectangle corners in world coordinates |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | `c` | Global column slot, 0..35 |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | `a` | Article, 1..35; defining a region also selects it |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | `ffff` | Only 0..3 accepted; bit 0 enables this article’s overflow retention; bit 1 enables search-word highlighting in this column |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | `cc` | Highlight color index, 0..255 when bit 1 is set; ignored otherwise |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | `rrrrrrrr` | Consumed but ignored |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: | String tail | Search words when bit 1 is set; otherwise ignored |

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: Search words are expanded as text variables, trimmed, split on whitespace, and compared case-insensitively against complete text tokens. Matching changes the drawing color to `cc`; it does not paint a highlight rectangle. Up to eight words of at most sixteen bytes each are stored. An empty/whitespace-only list, an overlong word, or an out-of-range highlight index rejects the definition. A ninth word reports “Too many search words (8 max)” but installs the first eight. Unknown flag bits reject the command. Numeric identifier/flag errors are checked before modifying the definition. A protected drawing port suppresses the operation.

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: Bit 0 belongs to the **article**, while bit 1, color and search list belong to the **column**. Every successful `1e` definition overwrites its article’s overflow-enable setting: the last column definition for that article wins. Use consistent bit 0 settings across a chain.

requirements.heading: RIP_EXTENDED_BEGIN_TEXT
requirements.text: The example decodes in base 36 to rectangle (165,121)-(325,344), global column 0, article 1, overflow enabled, highlighting disabled, ignored color 0 and reserved zero. It does not append or render text by itself.

requirements.heading: Column Content - Raw Text Lines and `1E`
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL; corpus (NEWSPAPR.RIP, N2_HORO.RIP, NEWS.RIP)._

requirements.heading: Column Content - Raw Text Lines and `1E`
requirements.text: After defining/selecting a nonzero article, raw text flows into its columns. Lines without a RIP command introducer are prose; RIP commands can still set attributes, add regions or read a file. Ordinary line endings are reflowed; blank lines separate paragraphs. An example inline block is:

requirements.heading: Column Content - Raw Text Lines and `1E`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1e0F3M434G0100000000000000
Southern California was pounded
with nearly two weeks of rain.
Hundreds left homeless as a result.
!|1E
```

requirements.heading: Column Content - Raw Text Lines and `1E`
requirements.text: [`1E`](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_end_text) flushes the pending line, closes that article’s overflow output streams and deactivates text flow. It retains the selected article, column definitions, page counters and saved files. The scene-end `#` also reaches this end operation. Neither operation is an overflow reset.

requirements.heading: Chained Columns and Streams
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL; corpus (DEMO-01.COL, N2_HORO.RIP, NEWSPAPR.RIP)._

requirements.heading: Chained Columns and Streams
requirements.text: There are **36 global column slots**, each assigned to one article, and 35 nonzero articles for raw text flow. Flow visits defined slots in increasing numeric order, skipping holes and columns assigned to other articles. Neither definition order nor rectangle position sorts the chain. A chain may begin at any slot and need not be contiguous.

requirements.heading: Chained Columns and Streams
requirements.text: The horoscope page uses slots 0,1,2 of article 1:

requirements.heading: Chained Columns and Streams
requirements.text: The newspaper’s secondary story uses global slot 3, article 2 (`1eA17FH48Y3200010000000000`). Defining slot 0 for article 2 would replace slot 0’s previous assignment to article 1; it would not create a second article-local slot 0.

requirements.heading: Redefinition and selection
requirements.text: A definition replaces the chosen slot, reassigns its owner, closes the target article’s overflow output handles, and resets its current column to “before the first column.” Its next prose starts at the lowest matching slot. Existing drawn pixels are not a retained text model and are not reflowed automatically.

requirements.heading: Redefinition and selection
requirements.text: The article’s current page, known forward-page limit and “complete source already captured” flag survive redefinition. Thus a continuation template can redefine its rectangles and re-read the current saved page without returning to page zero. Reassignment affects the new owner’s state; it does not reset the previous owner’s page counters.

requirements.heading: Redefinition and selection
requirements.text: Selecting a different article first flushes the old article’s pending line. Selecting the same article clears the pending word/line buffers without flushing them; a same-article redefinition can therefore discard unfinished prose. Define the complete chain before feeding its text, as the demos do. Selection alone does not rewind an already established article cursor; a definition is what resets it to the first column. The selector operation observed in NEWS.RIP is `1A`; its separate wire-layout reconciliation remains in [issue #2](https://github.com/bbs-land/remote-imaging-protocol/issues/2).

requirements.heading: The Legacy Form - `1T` With Column/Stream Digits
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL; corpus (NEWS.RIP, N2_TITLE.RIP)._

requirements.heading: The Legacy Form - `1T` With Column/Stream Digits
requirements.text: The inherited [`1T`](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_begin_text) uses the same rectangle/column helper. Its trailing two digits are separate one-digit column and article numbers, not one reserved two-digit number. Both accept 0..35; article zero is accepted for this compatibility form, but the raw-byte article feeder requires a selected article greater than zero, and the end-text helper returns immediately for article zero. Use articles 1..35 for the raw-flow and pagination contract. `1T` does not set the article’s overflow-enable flag or install/reset extended search settings; it retains those settings. On fresh state, overflow is disabled.

requirements.heading: Flowing Whole Files - `1R` on Plain Text
requirements.text: The demos’ `.TXT` targets are ordinary prose with no RIP introducers. Their text is wrapped into the selected article’s columns. A variable such as `$&MAIN_STORY$` supplies the filename; `$OVERFLOW(1,CUR)$` supplies a saved-page filename. These expressions return filenames, not the text content itself. requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL; corpus (DEMO-01.COL, DEMO-02.COL, NEWSPAPR.RIP)._

requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: Overflow is **lazy file-backed retention**, not an eagerly computed page list. When enabled, the first source feed at page 0 saves the complete incoming source as page 0. Text beyond the last column is saved as the remainder for page 1. Rendering page 1 can create page 2, and so on. With overflow disabled, prose beyond the last column is discarded.

requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: For each article let `P` be the zero-based current saved-page index and `H` the known forward limit. Both start at 0. Creating a remainder while rendering P sets H to P+1; reaching the end of the source without creating a remainder leaves H unchanged. Re-rendering an earlier page may reduce H by replacing it with that earlier page’s newly generated remainder index. H is not an eagerly measured total or a permanent maximum of all files ever created. Displayed page numbers are P+1.

requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: Saved-page names use `%03hu%c%04ld.OVR`: an instance identifier, a one-character article number (`1`..`9`,`A`..`Z`), and the zero-based page number with at least four decimal digits. For instance identifier 7, article 1, page 0 is `00710000.OVR`. Treat the returned name as an opaque local read-scene target; formatting a name does not establish that its file exists.

requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: The macro accepts zero to three parameters. No parameters means current filename of the selected article; one means current filename of that article. An explicit article is decimal 1..35, or `CUR` for the selected article. Names are case-insensitive. `CUR` can resolve to article zero after a reset, in which case a filename query returns `<NONE>`.

requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: The numeric page assignment has a shipped signed-16-bit truncation: accepted values 32768..65535 become negative, and 65536 becomes 0. Use 0..32767 for a valid nonnegative page index. This truncation follows the k≤H test. Numeric parameters must consist of decimal digits; negative spellings reject.

requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: For NEXT/PREV, an absent or empty third parameter acts as SET. Other third parameters reject; CUR/PAGE allow only QUERY when a third parameter is present, and numeric selection/RESET require exactly two parameters. Too many parameters, invalid article/operation/mode, disabled overflow for a modifying operation, or a numeric page beyond H report an error. No navigation occurs on these errors.

requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: A NEXT at P=H or PREV at P=0 **aborts the surrounding macro evaluation**, retaining the current page and skipping the rest of that response, including a following `$>template$`. SETVERBOSE additionally displays a `Cannot Continue` notification with `End of document.` or `Beginning of document.`. The boundary path returns no string; it is not the same as a successful empty-string expansion. This abort is local to the evaluation: the next evaluation clears it.

requirements.heading: Pagination - `$OVERFLOW$` and `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$`
requirements.text: `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$` is a **global layout and overflow-state reset**: close all article output handles, remove all column definitions, deactivate flow, select article 0, clear pending text and all page/source-capture state. It does not call file deletion: old physical files may remain, but are no longer represented by live paging state. Redefine the columns to start another article. The drawing reset `*` also removes columns and disables overflow, but retains page counters/source-capture flags; do not substitute it for `$RESET(OVERFLOW)$` when starting new copy.

requirements.heading: The `.COL` Page Template - Worked Example
requirements.text: A deterministic original-routine oracle in `run/riptel-column-probe` uses a ten-unit column, ten-unit line advance, unit character widths and a sixteen-word source. It observes eight pages, complete source retention at index 0, one new remainder per replay, all sixteen words in order, boundary abort, and a forward limit reduced from 7 to 1 when page 0 is rendered again. This checks state semantics with controlled metrics; it does not claim to reproduce the newspaper’s pixels.

requirements.heading: The Newspaper Demo - Showcase
requirements.text: The front page then draws a masthead in outline fonts, an "INSIDE" sidebar of four inline teaser columns (each an independent `1e` … `1E` block), the main headline as `@4L2L$&MAIN_TITLE$`, bylines as `By $&MAIN_AUTHOR$`, three chained columns flowing `$&MAIN_STORY$`, a boxed secondary story on stream 2 flowing `$&SUB_STORY$`, three captioned JPEG photographs (`1i`/`1p` - see [4.1 JPEG Images](4.1-jpeg-images.md)), and a navigation strip of mouse fields into the section pages - weather map, horoscopes (chained inline columns), business, and a JPEG photo gallery. Overflow from both stories pages into DEMO-01.COL and DEMO-02.COL. Swap two `.TXT` files and two title variables and it is _your_ newspaper - layout, pagination and navigation come free. Nothing else in the RIPscrip corpus, of any era, demonstrates this much of the 3.x design working together.

requirements.heading: 4.0 Icons & Bitmaps
requirements.text: Raster imagery on the terminal: capturing screen regions to a [clipboard](../../glossary.md) port, pasting them back with logical put modes, loading and writing disk-based [icons](../../glossary.md), and the block-move commands. Under the 2.0 engine that 3.x inherits, icons are Windows **BMP** bitmaps - `.BMP` for icons, `.BMH` for [hot icons](../../glossary.md), `.BMM` for [icon masks](../../glossary.md) - replacing the 1.54 `.ICN`/`.HIC`/`.MSK` formats.

requirements.heading: Capture Failure and Geometry
requirements.text: Replacement is **not transactional**. An unprotected assigned target is deleted before bitmap-port allocation. If budget, DC creation, bitmap creation or bitmap selection fails, the clipboard pointer becomes undefined and the target remains undefined; its former pixels/definition are **not restored**. Unrelated port definitions/pixels survive. Current selection changes only if deletion removed the current port, in which case it remains **#0** even after failure. With a previously unused target, allocation failure leaves it undefined and retains the original current source. Failure to delete a protected target is the earlier rejection case and retains the previous clipboard pointer instead of clearing it.

requirements.heading: Capture Failure and Geometry
requirements.text: The wire handler normalizes opposing corners and converts world coordinates to device coordinates, then adds one to both converted far coordinates. The shared clipboard helper adds another unit when deriving allocation extents, using low-WORD arithmetic. For ordinary nonwrapping bounds, bitmap width/height are therefore converted far-minus-near **plus two**. The actual source rectangle has only the first far increment and is offset by the source viewport. This can select a **stretch** copy rather than a verbatim transfer: at unit scale, `(1,1)`..`(3,3)` allocates **4×4** and requests a **3×3** source copied into that 4×4 destination. This is shipped caller/helper behavior, not a request to infer exact Windows interpolation. Clipping still uses the port viewports. _Evidence: original handlers and captured StretchBlt dimensions; [derivation](../research/issue-42-clipboard-capture-state.md)._
requirements.reason: Wire far increment plus shared low-WORD allocation increment and source viewport offset are implemented. The unit 3x3 -> 4x4 case, scaled WORLD/radix/width cases, clipped/outside capture and nonzero low-WORD wrapping are independently tested. Wrapped zero allocation counts remain unsupported before capture mutation: the pinned primary derivation explicitly does not establish a zero-dimensional native allocation result. This edge still needs reconciliation; ordinary nonwrapping captures are not a claim of whole-block completion.

requirements.heading: Capture Failure and Geometry
requirements.text: The clipboard pointer connects the earlier GET_IMAGE/PUT_IMAGE/WRITE_ICON family to the multi-port table. A normal [RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) selects port 0 and deletes unprotected nonzero ports. If it deletes the clipboard port, that pointer clears; a **protected clipboard port and its pointer can survive**. The inherited unconditional statement that every reset leaves no clipboard is too broad. Use the [table lifecycle rules](7.1-data-tables.md) for protection/reset and [data backup areas](7.2-data-backup-areas.md) for whole-port backup semantics. _Evidence: original SOFT call order and native port-deletion component; [derivation](../research/issue-42-clipboard-capture-state.md)._

requirements.heading: RIP_PUT_IMAGE
requirements.text: The image that is retrieved from the clipboard port does so based on the port's viewport (the entire contents of the viewport are copied to the active drawing port). If the clipboard port is only used with the RIP*GET_IMAGE command, then the viewport will be the full size of the port. If however, some port related commands are used on this clipboard port, then it is possible to alter the viewport inside this port. This gives you the ability to paste sub-areas of the port's actual image onto the destination drawing port. *(v2.A3)\_

The image written to disk is the image contained inside the viewport of the clipboard port (see the [RIP_PUT_IMAGE](#rip_put_image) command for more details about viewports and the clipboard port). If the clipboard pointer indicates that there is no clipboard in use, then this command does nothing. _(v2.A3)_
