requirements.heading: RIP_LOAD_ICON
requirements.text:
1. The image is loaded onto the current drawing port, truncated to the viewport if necessary.
2. Original RIPtel 3.1 calls the [GET_IMAGE shared helper](#rip_get_image) with the renderer-returned **unclipped device rectangle**. Its normal target selection, protection, extra far-coordinate increment and failure behavior apply. In particular, an assigned clipboard equal to current is **not skipped**: the documented destructive same-source defect applies. Viewport clipping of the initial paint does not shrink the rectangle passed to this helper. _Evidence: [loader and clipboard derivation](../research/issue-42-clipboard-capture-state.md#integration-review-loader-failures-and-completely-clipped-images)._
requirements.reason: Shared GET_IMAGE selection, first-unused scan, protected/zero target rejection, destructive current-target fallback, explicit pixel-budget accounting and nontransactional allocation/copy failure are implemented with independent state/index expectations. Wire 1C performs normalization/current ENV decoding/world projection and both far-edge increments; LOAD_ICON calls the same helper after paint with its unclipped returned rectangle. Ordinary LOAD_ICON failures retain pointer/resources and request a placeholder instead. All three canvases, documented target examples, source viewport offsets, radix 36/64 and widths 2..5, allocation/copy faults and byte-split recovery are covered. Wrapped zero allocation handling, reset/backup/port-coordinate producer integration, legacy conversion, other callers and active application routing remain separately pending; no Windows interpolation/native-device claim is made.

requirements.heading: RIP_LOAD_ICON
requirements.text: The `<scale>` parameter indicates whether the icon should be scaled to the device coordinates when it is loaded. A `1` indicates that it should be scaled, and a `0` indicates that it not should be scaled. This is important when dealing with older RIPscrip 1.54 icons. Icons that are loaded with RIPscrip 1.54 need to be resolution independent. This is performed when this command has a 1 in the scale parameter's position. All scaling is performed in this command as if the icon were created in a 640x350 environment. So, if an icon is loaded that is 35 pixels tall, and it is displayed in a 640x480 environment, it will be stretched vertically to make it 48 pixels tall. This makes sure that icons loaded in this mode are displayed at the correct size so that they are resolution independent. _(v2.A3)_

On ordinary lookup or renderer failure, RIPtel 3.1 attempts a missing-resource placeholder on the **current drawing port** and retains the current selection, clipboard pointer and port definitions/resources. This applies to both `<clipboard>=0` and 1, whether the assigned target is protected, screen/offscreen, current or already undefined. The inherited claim that failure clears the clipboard/pointer is false for this driver: neither deletion, pixel erasure nor pointer-only clearing occurs. If the clipboard port is itself current, ordinary placeholder drawing can change its pixels; different screen ports can also share drawing pixels. A different offscreen clipboard keeps its pixels. The placeholder may itself fail to render; clipboard state still survives. This failure path never reaches GET_IMAGE, unlike the separate GET_IMAGE allocation-failure path that really clears its pointer. _Evidence: [original failure/placeholder branches and native state matrix](../research/issue-42-clipboard-capture-state.md#load_icon-failure-retains-clipboard-state)._
requirements.reason: Shared GET_IMAGE selection, first-unused scan, protected/zero target rejection, destructive current-target fallback, explicit pixel-budget accounting and nontransactional allocation/copy failure are implemented with independent state/index expectations. Wire 1C performs normalization/current ENV decoding/world projection and both far-edge increments; LOAD_ICON calls the same helper after paint with its unclipped returned rectangle. Ordinary LOAD_ICON failures retain pointer/resources and request a placeholder instead. All three canvases, documented target examples, source viewport offsets, radix 36/64 and widths 2..5, allocation/copy faults and byte-split recovery are covered. Wrapped zero allocation handling, reset/backup/port-coordinate producer integration, legacy conversion, other callers and active application routing remain separately pending; no Windows interpolation/native-device claim is made. PR #73 source changes here are formatting-only; independent prior review/evidence is retained.

requirements.heading: RIP_LOAD_BITMAP
requirements.text: This command instructs the terminal to read a bitmap from disk and display it at the given upper-left (x0,y0) location. If the (x1,y1) values are non-zero, then it specifies the lower-right corner on the screen for the bitmap's display region. If the bitmap differs in size than the destination rectangle, then it is scaled (stretched) to fit into the proper region. If the values of X1 and Y1 are zero, then the bitmap is shown verbatim in whatever resolution of the disk based file (this is more like the RIP*LOAD_ICON command above). *(v2.A3)\_

requirements.text: The `<flags>` parameter is a bit field. Public processing stays void. PR #73 source changes here are formatting-only; independent prior review/evidence is retained.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Flag 1 - duplicate the initial image.** First draw/process the image on the current port, then copy its composited pixels to another port. The renderer returns its **unclipped requested device rectangle**, not the intersection of painted pixels with the viewport. `duplicate_port=0` calls the [GET_IMAGE shared helper](#rip_get_image), including its selection/protection, extra far increment and destructive same-source behavior. Explicit 1..35 equal to current skips duplication. A different explicit target is deleted if defined, then created as an offscreen bitmap of the returned rectangle's width/height and copied with COPY. An explicit port above 35 skips duplication. Without flag 1 the duplicate argument is ignored.
requirements.reason: Post-draw duplication now uses the original full requested rectangle. Explicit current and >35 selectors skip only duplication; a different defined target is deleted before full-size creation/COPY. Duplicate0 uses the shared helper, including extra allocation unit, selection/protection and same-source deletion/fallback. Independent wire tests cover these routes, assigned/first-unused slots, protected screen/offscreen targets, partial/outside source clipping and allocation/copy failures on all three canvases. Wrapped zero allocation counts remain unsupported in the shared helper, and complete port-coordinate producer reconciliation remains pending, so the entire block is not yet accepted. requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Protected explicit target:** the initial image/palette processing has already happened when deletion checks protection. Rejection preserves the target definition/resources, clipboard pointer and current selection, skips replacement and wallpaper, and leaves the initial draw/palette effects in place. There is no DEFINE_PORT-style fallback selection to 0. An independent offscreen target keeps its pixels; a screen target can share pixels affected by the initial draw. _Evidence: [original protected deletion and native caller checks](../research/issue-42-clipboard-capture-state.md#protected-explicit-load_bitmap-duplicate)._

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Completely outside the viewport:** a valid nonempty bitmap can finish the initial draw with no visible pixels and still return its full requested rectangle. Flag 1 then performs normal target selection/replacement; absence of visible pixels does not preserve the previous duplicate automatically. After successful allocation the compositor can reject the outside source, leaving the new port defined with its initialized background; the caller ignores that copy failure. For requested 4×2, an explicit target is 4×2, while the clipboard helper's extra far increment allocates 5×3. Successful explicit deletion of the assigned clipboard clears its pointer and this explicit route does not reassign it; duplicate 0 assigns the newly created clipboard. Protected-target rejection and actual decoder/resource/render failures retain their separate behavior. _Evidence: [original rectangle producer/consumer and native outside-image cases](../research/issue-42-clipboard-capture-state.md#completely-clipped-is-not-a-zero-size-returned-rectangle)._

Successful deletion of a defined explicit clipboard target clears its pointer and does not reassign it; an undefined explicit target skips deletion and retains a dangling assignment. Copy failures after allocation retain the new clear resource. PR #73 source changes here are formatting-only; independent prior review/evidence is retained.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Flag 2** - This flag indicates to take the color palette in the bitmap file and activate it in the current color lookup table. This means that the color palette in the bitmap is copied into the video device's color palette (and into RIPscrip's). This means that if any graphics are already on the screen when this happens, they might change in color as soon as the bitmap is loaded (this is due to the fact that the color palette is changed). If the number of colors in the bitmap exceeds the number of colors in the active display device, then the actual color palette in use is used for the bitmap instead of the internal bitmap palette. If the number of colors in the bitmap is equal or less than the number of colors for the active video mode then the image will be displayed exactly as it was intended. If this is the case, then no dithering is necessary on the image so the dither flag (see below) parameter is ignored. If the terminal is running in a mode that doesn't allow for a color palette in the video hardware, then dithering is ignored and the color palette inside the bitmap file is ignored - this is because the system is already running in a 32K, 64K or 24-bit color mode and there are more than plenty colors to represent the bitmap perfectly. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: In the separate engine's 256-entry palette device model, 1b flag 2 copies the decoded indexed BMP palette into the corresponding prefix of the bound current lookup table. Source indexes remain exact even when distinct indexes share RGB values, so transfer/transparency semantics survive adoption; unused table entries and other slots remain unchanged. Successful adoption suppresses flag-4 dithering. Protected palettes reject the complete load before painting, and staging failures commit neither palette nor pixels. True-colour images ignore adoption. Independent authored 1/4/8-bit BMPs cover all three canvases, five transfer modes, transparency, background recolouring, shortened palette tables, protected rejection and staging OOM. Other device models/application integration remain tracked separately. The complete row stays pending because lower-capacity/no-hardware-palette device fallback/bypass policy is not supplied by this fixed 256-entry renderer. Ordered dithering is now available for non-adopted sources in the current device model; successful adoption still suppresses it.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: If this flag is omitted, then the bitmap will use the current screen's color palette. Typically this will be the default color palette for use with RIPscrip but it might be different. This means that any pixel of the bitmap that is drawn to the screen is shown in whatever actual color is the absolute closest to the color palette number corresponding to that pixel in the bitmap (dithering may still apply - see below). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Flag 4** - This flag enables auto-dithering mode. This is an intelligent way of determining if dithering should be performed or not. If there are more colors in the bitmap than in the video device or if the bitmap's color palette is not used to set the video device, then dithering is used to get the image as close to the original color scheme as possible. If the bitmap's palette is committed to the video device then no dithering is necessary because the color palette in use has all (or more) of the necessary colors to display the image. 24-bit images will always enable dithering if this mode is used unless the terminal is running in 24-bit mode. Dithering slows down image drawing so it should only be used for images that really need it. _(v2.A4)_
requirements.reason: The adopted depth-specific color-key selection and translation are implemented:1-bit zero/nonzero, mapped 4/8-bit, exact 24-bit RGB,16-bit keyed rejection and 32-bit no-selection defect. Wire keys translate through the current drawing palette before adoption; all documented profiles are tested in the translator and the current device uses limit 236. Independent all-canvas mode/scaling/clipping, dither/adoption, explicit BMM and nonfatal failure/duplication/recovery tests cover this subset. Complete true-color RGB raster/device behavior, port-coordinate producer reconciliation and active application routing remain pending; no new documentation is needed for these answered contracts.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: If this flag is omitted, then no dither is performed at all. If the number of colors in the bitmap is higher than the number of colors in the display device then this will yield a lower quality image. But if there are more colors in the display device than the bitmap then the quality of the image will be close to the actual bitmap (or exact). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Flag 8** - Select a color of the explicitly loaded image as transparent; `<trans_color>` must be 0..255 and is translated through the current drawing palette. It does not request a same-named BMM. The original renderer generates an internal equality mask, computes the chosen put mode against the old background, retains that background at keyed pixels and uses the computed result elsewhere: `T ? D : F(S,D)`. Selection depends on depth: source bit versus zero/nonzero key for 1-bit, palette-mapped indices for 4/8-bit, exact current-palette RGB for 24-bit. The shipped 16-bit key path fails before drawing, and the shipped 32-bit classifier selects no transparent pixels. See the [complete color-key contract](../techspecs/3.0-bitmap-mask-delta.md#flag-8-is-a-separate-color-key-operation), including key translation and scaling. _Evidence: original DLL and [4,975 native checks](../research/issue-8-bmm-masks.md#full-original-renderer-with-controlled-drawing-boundary); corrects the inherited draft's blanket description._

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Flag 16 - wallpaper.** After displaying the bitmap at the requested position/size and performing any flag 1 duplication, repeat its **rendered device rectangle** across the **then-current port's viewport**, clipped to that viewport. The original helper copies horizontally and vertically from pixels already on the same drawing device using **COPY/SRCCOPY**, regardless of the initial `<mode>`. It does not reopen the bitmap, scale again, adopt another palette, dither again or test transparency at each repetition. If initial transparency retained background pixels inside the seed rectangle, those retained pixels are tiled too; the key is not applied to each new background. The initial requested ROP is evaluated once to form the seed, rather than repeated against each destination's old pixels.
requirements.reason: Wallpaper snapshots and repeats raw composited device indexes with COPY. Initial source ROP, transparency, mapping/dithering and palette commit run once. Independent XOR/keyed-background wire scenes capture the entire screen and palette on all three canvases, verifying repeated retained background pixels and untouched margins. Wallpaper staging failure leaves the initial draw and completed duplicate in place. PR #73 source changes here are formatting-only; independent prior review/evidence is retained.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Flag 32 - staggered rows.** This modifies flag 16 only. Relative to the row containing the seed, alternate rows start **floor(tile_device_width/2)** pixels to the left of aligned rows. Both directions from the seed use the same alternating phase, including odd tile widths. With 16 absent,32 is accepted and has no effect. This is an offset of existing pixel copies, not another stretch or a different palette/dither mode.
requirements.reason: Positive-modulo horizontal phase and floor-divided tile rows implement left half-width shifts in both directions from the seed row. Authored 3x2,4x2 and 1x1 cases cover odd/even widths and rows above/below the seed; a separate wire case proves 32 without16 does not repeat. PR #73 source changes here are formatting-only; independent prior review/evidence is retained.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: The tile starts at the renderer-returned image position, with the resulting device width/height. The wallpaper helper trims its far bounds to the viewport before repeating and rejects nonpositive/irreconcilable rectangles. A tile already covering the viewport requires no visible extra copy. This is a post-draw operation, separate from loading/scaling a bitmap to cover the viewport in one stretch. _Evidence: original `imageWallpaper()`0x3ea2e, rectangle reconciler 0x3f0a6, complete wire/renderer runs and [native tile/phase grids](../research/issue-58-load-bitmap-flags.md#native-matrix-and-wallpaper-geometry)._
requirements.reason: The wallpaper service trims far edges to the live viewport before snapshotting; invalid near origins/reversed rectangles reject without painting. A literal clipped 3x3 tile grid checks the trimmed period, while a full-viewport seed and inactive viewport bypass staging even under injected allocation failure. This is repetition of device pixels, without an additional stretch. PR #73 source changes here are formatting-only; independent prior review/evidence is retained.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: **Duplication precedes wallpaper.** Flag 1 captures the initial image rectangle, after its palette/dither/key/ROP processing, **before** wallpaper fills the viewport. It does not capture the completed wallpapered viewport. An explicit duplicate equal to the current port skips only duplication. The clipboard route (`duplicate_port=0`) uses [GET_IMAGE](#rip_get_image); if that helper changes the current port, wallpaper re-reads and uses that new current port/viewport. The handler does not save and restore the original selection around the copy.
requirements.reason: Duplication runs before wallpaper and retains the original requested extent. Explicit same-current skips only duplication. Shared capture reselects port zero when it deletes the current clipboard source; independent success and allocation-failure cases prove wallpaper then uses zero and its different viewport. Full screen index/palette captures on all three canvases retain source/margin provenance. PR #73 source changes here are formatting-only; independent prior review/evidence is retained.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: On renderer failure, the placeholder/error path returns before duplication and wallpaper. The later duplicate paths are not transactional: failure to delete an existing explicit duplicate returns before wallpaper; failure to create its replacement skips that copy but still reaches wallpaper. The [derivation](../research/issue-58-load-bitmap-flags.md#original-flags-and-ordering-checkpoint) records original branches and the controlled native failure cases.
requirements.reason: Initial load/render failure requests the error sink and exits before duplication/wallpaper. Explicit protected deletion retains the initial draw/adoption and prevents wallpaper; post-deletion budget/allocation failure leaves the target undefined and still wallpapers. Copy failure retains a newly clear allocation. Fault-injected wire tests verify these nontransactional effects, selection/pointer state, placeholder counts and later parser recovery. Public wire entry points remain void.

requirements.heading: Bitmap Flags
requirements.text: The original DRAGON.RIP first sets world 1280×960 and creates/activates port 1. STRIP6.BMP is 320×17 pixels. The example draws it into the world box 640×34, using the current world/device conversion, **then tiles that resulting rectangle throughout the viewport**. With a 640×480 device and that 2:1 world ratio, the initial rectangle is 320×17 device pixels. Bit 16 does not itself request that scaling, and the result is not merely a single stretched header band. _Evidence: original scene/BMP bytes, hashes and [decode](../research/issue-58-load-bitmap-flags.md#canonical-example-and-source-bytes)._

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: _Copy a screen area to a new location (bit blit)_

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `g`                                            |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x0:2 y0:2 x1:2 y1:2 dx0:2 dy0:2 mode:1 res:1` |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Draw Color, Back Color, Fill Style, Port, Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_copy_blit)) · HLP (`RIP_CopyBlit`) · corpus (88 uses in 6 files) - not in SyncTERM

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: This command is similar to the [RIP_SCROLL](#rip_scroll) command but is more generic in nature - it can move a rectangle of graphical information on the screen from one position to another - not just up or down. It does this with high-speed bit-blit operations. The rectangle contained in (x0,y0) to (x1,y1) is copied so that its upper-left corner is now at the location (dx0,dy0).

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: Some, part, or none of the original source image might be covered up by the moved screen data. The parts of the original image which are still on the screen (unobscured) can be cleared to some color or state if you wish by using the `<mode>` parameter (like RIP_SCROLL does). The possible settings for `<mode>` are:

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | Mode | Description |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | 0 | Do nothing - leave the old graphics on the screen |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | 1 | Fill the old graphical area with the current drawing color (solid fill in COPY mode). |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | 2 | Fill the old graphical area with the current background drawing color (solid fill in COPY mode). |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | 3 | Fill the area with the current fill color (solid fill in COPY mode). Fill pattern/styles are not used for this. |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | 4 | Fill the old graphical area with the current fill style/pattern in the current fill color. |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: | 5 | Erase the affected area entirely to black. |

requirements.heading: RIP_COPY_BLIT
requirements.text: The corpus uses it as a _within-screen_ slide primitive in the wipe/transition library (WIPE00-02.FN, DL.FN, DR.FN): the preserved example selects a 1200×960 world-coordinate slab and moves it 80 world units right in one step of a push transition. _Evidence: corpus (WIPE00.FN, WIPE01.FN, WIPE02.FN, DL.FN, DR.FN)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x0:XY y0:XY x1:XY y1:XY mode:1 res:1 dest_line:2` |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1G <x0> <y0> <x1> <y1> <mode> <res> <dest_line>` **Example:** `!|1G080G140M0005`

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Port, Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_scroll)) · HLP (`RIP_Scroll`) · SyncTERM (ripper.c:16246 - **documentation-only stub**: full 1.54 spec comment, then a bare `break;`) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: This command physically "copies" a rectangular region of the graphics screen up or down. The `<dest_line>` parameter is the Y position that is the destination scan line to receive the region. The Destination of the copy can overlap the original region, but cannot be on the same line. You cannot move the image area left or right at all. This command is designated for vertical scrolling of graphical data either up or down.

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: This is one of the only graphical output commands that DOES NOT adhere to the [RIP_VIEWPORT](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport) command. In other words, you can scroll graphical data outside the current graphical viewport (even over the text window!). However, it does adhere to the boundaries of the current drawing port. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: The `<mode>` parameter instructs the terminal what to do with the part of the source rectangle that isn't covered up by the scrolled data. You may specify several things to happen as defined by the mode values below: _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | Mode | Description |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | 0 | Do nothing - leave the old graphics on the screen |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | 1 | Fill the old graphical area with the current drawing color (solid fill in COPY mode). |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | 2 | Fill the old graphical area with the current background drawing color (solid fill in COPY mode). |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | 3 | Fill the area with the current fill color (solid fill in COPY mode). Fill pattern/styles are not used for this. |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | 4 | Fill the old graphical area with the current fill style/pattern in the current fill color. |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | 5 | Erase the affected area entirely to black. |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: | 6 | Fill the affected area with the color of a pixel from one of the corners of the affected rectangle. If the image area was scrolled up, then the color is taken from the lower-right most pixel from the old graphical rectangle (left exposed). If the data is scrolled down, then the rectangle is filled in with the color of the pixel in the upper-left most pixel. This is mode is used so that if the area is a multi-colored graphic, that a suitable fill color is used. |

requirements.heading: RIP_SCROLL
requirements.text: It is the one command SyncTERM documents in-source but does not implement - recognized and swallowed. The corpus does all of its region moving with [RIP_COPY_BLIT](#rip_copy_blit) and level-2 [RIP_PORT_COPY](7.0-drawing-ports.md#rip_port_copy) instead. _Evidence: SyncTERM (ripper.c:16246); corpus (absence)._

requirements.heading: Masks and transparency
requirements.text: The 1.54 technique of explicitly stamping a mask in AND mode and the image in OR mode remains available. The original RIPtel 3.1 image/button paths do **not** automatically fetch a BMM companion. An explicitly loaded BMM is an ordinary BMP: resolved white pixels preserve the background under AND and black pixels clear it, independent of their stored palette index. See the [bitmap-mask contract and four-pixel oracle](../techspecs/3.0-bitmap-mask-delta.md) for depths, mode order and missing/different-size cases. [RIP_LOAD_BITMAP](#rip_load_bitmap) flag 8 is a separate single-image color-key operation, used by DBACK.FN. _Evidence: [original driver routing/renderer trace and native observations](../research/issue-8-bmm-masks.md)._

requirements.heading: 4.1 JPEG Images
requirements.text: Photographic images - a capability of the 2.0/3.x generation with no 1.54 counterpart: a host delivers a compressed image file to the terminal and displays it scaled into an **image area**, a sub-region of the current viewport established by [RIP_IMAGE_STYLE](#rip_image_style). JPEG is the only compressed image format in shipping 3.x - the ALPHA 4 draft also added GIF _(v2.A4)_, but GIF was dropped over LZW licensing before shipping, and PNG was announced but never shipped (see the [white paper](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt)) - and SyncTERM's `RIPSCRIP030001` mode has no raster support at all, making JPEG display a clean 3.x-only differentiator.

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: **An inactive viewport does not block this wire setter.** Valid `1i` immediately replaces the stored per-port image area/flags while inactive, including on a protected current port. Reactivation retains that new configuration, so `deactivate; 1i new-area/new-flags; activate; 1p existing-jpeg` displays using the **new** style. An intervening `1p` while inactive skips image lookup/decoding/painting. The IMGSTYLE macro setter has a separate inactive-target gate and does not provide the same exception. _Evidence: [original setter/activation/display sequence and native checks](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#integration-review-inactive-viewport-wire-setter)._
requirements.reason: Wire 1i replaces the current stored record while inactive, including protected screen/offscreen ports. Independent radix/width/canvas state matrices and port-service deactivation/reactivation around byte-split 1i/1p commands prove the exception. An intervening inactive 1p skips allocator, file and decoder services even when bindings are absent; reactivation retains the newly stored style, with independent full-screen index/palette captures. Native and JPEG-disabled fixtures cover capability/error recovery. The separate IMGSTYLE inactive/protection gates are tested rather than inferred from the wire setter.

requirements.heading: RIP_IMAGE_STYLE
requirements.text: **All-zero coordinates do not disable JPEG viewing in RIPtel 3.1.** The inherited ALPHA 4 claim that they disable viewing is not implemented by this driver: the command stores (0,0,1,1), and subsequent display reaches the decoder through a lower-level size fallback. In the full-viewport fixture this uses the physical display dimensions. Do not implement an all-zero “ignore and delete” branch as shipped behavior. A separate internal raw-zero rectangle sentinel suppresses explicit IMAGE/playback before lookup, but is not produced by all-zero IMAGE_STYLE; the client’s received-image export bypasses that guard. _Evidence: [full original presentation chain and zero-area checks](../research/issue-21-image-style.md#full-presentation-and-zero-area-checkpoint)._
requirements.reason: Wire zero input stores enabled (0,0,1,1), distinct from raw-zero inhibit. Native 1i/1p sequences reach physical-size JPEG fallback on all canvases; flags 16/48 then wallpaper the actual stored 1x1 seed, yielding its top-left pixel across the viewport rather than repeating the full fallback image. The source image is not deleted. Disabled decoding remains a nonfatal capability diagnostic. Complete sub-viewport/offscreen fallback geometry and received-image/export routing remain pending; those pixels are not inferred from the full-viewport observation.

requirements.heading: File deletion and received files
requirements.text: The client has a separate transfer flag that registers completed files in a temporary-file list for **later purge**. requirements.heading: Clearing, aspect margins and write mode
requirements.text: JPEG rows use **COPY (SRCCOPY)**, independently of the current vector Write Mode. Unless NOCLEAR is set, the initial fill uses a **black replacement fill**, not the current background color or XOR/OR/AND mixing. With ASPECT, the driver first fits the image, then clears only that fitted rectangle. It leaves the surrounding margins unchanged. Thus **XOR + ASPECT + NOCLEAR** leaves the margins exactly as they were and copies the JPEG into the fitted rectangle; no black margins are XOR’d or otherwise combined with their previous contents. Wallpaper is a separate subsequent COPY operation when bit 16 is set.
requirements.reason: The complete named rendering sequence is implemented in the separate engine: initial black COPY clear over only the fitted rectangle unless NOCLEAR, JPEG COPY independently of vector mode, retained aspect margins, then optional COPY wallpaper from raw stored image-area pixels. Literal independent fill regions, complete index/palette captures, all 64 flags under every vector mode and post-draw staging/error recovery prove these effects. Native and JPEG-disabled fixtures distinguish actual decoder coverage. Full device/port-coordinate and delivered-image/application integration remain separate acceptance work.

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: [Mouse fields](../../glossary.md) - host-defined rectangular hot regions that transmit a [host command](../../glossary.md) when clicked - the commands that delete them, and control of the mouse pointer shape.

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: _The 1.54 record is [4.1 in the v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/4.1-mouse-fields.md); the 2.0 record is [4.2 in the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md), which added world-coordinate placement, the region-selective [RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS](#rip_kill_enclosed_mouse_fields), and [RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR](#rip_set_mouse_cursor)._

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: Two global rules apply to all mouse regions (fields and buttons alike):

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text:
- Up to 128 mouse fields, 128 mouse buttons, or any combination may exist simultaneously, but combined their total number cannot exceed 128 - they share the mouse field [data table](7.1-data-tables.md#mouse-field-table). _(v1.54)_
- When the user clicks the mouse on the screen, all mouse regions (whether mouse fields or mouse buttons) are scanned from most recent to the least recent ("last in, first out"): if regions overlap, the newest one wins the click. _(v1.54, revised v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: 4.2 Mouse Fields & Pointer
requirements.text: Mouse fields exist only on the screen (port #0) - they cannot be placed on offscreen [drawing ports](7.0-drawing-ports.md). The corpus confirms both rules operate as documented in the shipping 3.0 driver. _Evidence: 2.00a4; corpus._

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: This command ties together three things:

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text:
- A region on the screen
- A mouse-click event
- A string of text to be transmitted by the terminal.

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: This command defines a rectangular region on the screen that functions as a "hot" mouse area. If the user clicks the [left] mouse button while pointing inside the region, then the terminal must transmit the `<text>` string to the Host. The (x0,y0) parameter MUST be the upper-left corner, and (x1,y1) MUST be the lower-right corner of the region.

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: The `<num>` parameter used to be used in the older RIPscrip v1.0 specification but is now obsolete. For upwards compatibility, it should be set to "00". _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: The `<clk>` parameter, if 1, indicates that the region should be visibly inverted while the mouse button is down. This offers visual feedback. If `<clk>` is 0, the region will not be inverted while clicked.

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: The `<clr>` parameter, if 1, will physically zoom the text window to full screen size and clear the screen. This is useful if the `<text>` parameter instructs the host to enter an area of the System that doesn't support RIPscrip graphics.

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: The `<text>` parameter is a Host command that gets sent when the field is clicked. You may use a caret (^) or a backquote (`` ` ``) to represent control characters, (e.g., ^M for carriage return, `` `G ``, ^C, etc.). Mouse fields may use Data text variables, active text variables, pick lists, control characters and local file playback directives. At no time are templates permitted in simple mouse fields. See the section on [host commands](5.0-host-commands.md) for more details about these types of features of RIPscrip. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: Mouse fields are always created relative to port #0 (the screen port). Under no circumstances are mouse fields allowed in offscreen drawing ports - you can't have a clickable mouse area in a region that cannot be clicked (ie, off the screen). If the current drawing port is an offscreen port, or even a port other than port #0, then the mouse field is defined relative to screen port #0 for the purposes of defining its position. The same applies to mouse-based buttons (see the [RIP_BUTTON](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) command). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: Mouse fields that extend partially outside of a viewport are truncated to fit inside the viewport. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: When this command is stored in-memory, it is converted to global screen coordinates (for internal storage only). This makes it so that if you have mouse regions defined in multiple different viewports, that each field will be properly inverted at the right location regardless of the currently defined viewport. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_MOUSE
requirements.text: NOTE: All Mouse Fields are scanned in "last in, first out" order. This means that the last-most received Mouse Field will be the first one scanned for a mouse click. You are limited to a maximum of 128 Mouse Regions or Mouse Buttons (128 total). _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: 3.x extensions to the `<text>` parameter
requirements.text: The 3.x corpus reveals two undocumented extensions to the `<text>` parameter. Both live at the host-command layer - they are documented in full in chapter 5 and only summarized here:

requirements.heading: 3.x extensions to the `<text>` parameter
requirements.text:
- **`ID=n:` prefix** - assigns a numbered mouse-field identity, readable back through the `$FIELDID$` [text variable](5.1-text-variables.md) and used by the `.MSE` overlay scenes' entry/exit queries to drive hover status lines and cursor changes (the example above, from NEWSPAPR.RIP's navigation, is field ID 2). The prefix is not transmitted to the host. The mechanism - and RIPtel's canonical nine-field menu built on it - is documented in [5.0 Host Commands](5.0-host-commands.md#mouse-field-identities---idn). _Evidence: HLP (`$FIELDID$` - "current mouse field ID"); corpus (NEWSPAPR.RIP, MENU.MNU/MENU.MSE)._
- **Inline conditionals and macros** - `<<if $RETURN$!="">>$<<RETURN>>$<<else>>$NULL$<<endif>>` as a host command (BUTTONS.RIP), and [`$GOTOURL(WEBURL)$`](5.0-host-commands.md#launching-web-urls---gotourlname) launching a web URL from a variable (TELLISTS.MNU/.MSE - 1997-era web integration). The conditional/macro layer is [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md). _Evidence: corpus (BUTTONS.RIP, TELLISTS.MNU, TELLISTS.MSE)._

requirements.heading: 3.x extensions to the `<text>` parameter
requirements.text: Hover (entry/exit) behavior is not part of this command itself: the corpus wires deferred [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) modes 5/6 to mouse-field _entry/exit_ events - a 3.x extension of the documented click modes - to run `.MSE` overlay status-line updates and `$MCURSOR(n)$` pointer changes. _Evidence: HLP ("mouse-field entry/exit queries"); corpus (MENU.MSE) - mode numbering (hypothesis)._

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: This command will "forget" all Mouse Regions. Use it at the beginning of each Scene, so that one scene's Mouse Regions don't get used in another.

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: The corpus's TELKILL.FN ("Kill all mouse fields and entry/exit queries") wraps it as a reusable subroutine scene. _Evidence: corpus (TELKILL.FN)._

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A0._

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: _Destroys any Mouse Fields inside a region_

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `k`                               |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x0:XY y0:XY x1:XY y1:XY flags:4` |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Fill Style (see below), Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_kill_enclosed_mouse_fields)) · HLP (`RIP_KillEnclosedMouseFields`) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: This command will destroy any Mouse Fields or Mouse Active Buttons that are contained inside the given rectangle or that intersect the rectangle. The exact operation of this function is dependent on the setting of the `<flags>` parameter. The `<flags>` parameter can combine any of the following flags to determine the exact mode of operation:

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **Region Specific Flags**

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | Flags | Description                                              |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 1     | Kill only fields completely contained (non-intersecting) |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 2     | Kill only fields that intersect bounding rectangle       |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 4     | Kill fields entirely outside bounding rectangle          |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: > If 1, 2 and 4 are not present, then NO fields are deleted. One of these flags must be supplied for any mouse fields to be deleted.

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **What Types of Fields not to Destroy**

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | Flags | Description                              |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 8     | Don't destroy simple Mouse Fields        |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 16    | Don't destroy active Mouse Button fields |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: > If 8 and 16 are not present, then all types of mouse fields are destroyed.

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: **What to do With the Affected Region(s)**

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | Flags | Description |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 32 | Clear the affected field(s) to black (color 0) |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 64 | Fill the affected field(s) with current fill color and fill pattern (64 overides 32 in the case that both of 32 and 64 are present). |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: | 128 | Perform the 32/64 operations on the whole bounding rectangle (based on Region Specific Flags). |

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: > If 128 is omitted but 32 or 64 are used, then the mouse field's affected are cleared with the appropriate method. If 128 is present as well, then instead of clearing the individual mouse fields with the given method, the entire region specified by the Region Specific Flags is affected (ie, the entire interior of the bounding rectangle is cleared, etc). If 32, 64 and 128 are omitted, then the affected region/fields are left on the screen visually, but their mouse field definitions are destroyed internally. If 128 is used, but 32 and 64 are omitted then nothing is done visually either.

requirements.heading: RIP_KILL_ENCLOSED_MOUSE_FIELDS
requirements.text: The demos always clear all fields at once with [RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS](#rip_kill_mouse_fields) instead. _Evidence: corpus (absence)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: This command allows you to alter the current mouse cursor shape that is shown on the screen. This feature lets you change the cursor to another shape to give the user of the terminal an idea that something is going on. For example, changing the cursor to the shape of an hourglass or a watch could give the idea that they should wait for a moment because something is going on.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: The `<cursor_style>` parameter is an ID number that specifies which cursor style should be activated. The possible values for this parameter are: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | Style | Description                                    |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 00    | Standard "left-leaning" arrow cursor (default) |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 01    | Wrist watch cursor                             |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 02    | Cross-hair cursor                              |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 03    | I-bar cursor (for text editing)                |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 04    | Pointing finger cursor                         |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 05    | Hand held up cursor                            |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: | 06    | Hourglass cursor                               |

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: **State ownership (RIPtel 3.1):** the number is stored in the current environment, not in the graphics style. This wire command checks current environment protection; style protection is irrelevant. [`MCURSOR`](5.1-text-variables.md#mcursor) performs the same state change without that protection check. Style switching does not restore a mouse number; environment switching selects the stored number for the next refresh. _Evidence: [original handlers/setter and native cases](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#ownership-and-switching-observations)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: A [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) resets the mouse cursor to the default pointer. [`RIP_HEADER`](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) has selective cursor behavior: resets can restore defaults, input lock selects the wait cursor, and environment flag 32768 selects the arrow. A zero-flags header does not unconditionally reset the cursor.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR
requirements.text: FXSHWIMG.FN brackets its slow JPEG display with `!|1c06` / `!|1c00` - hourglass on, arrow back - omitting the reserved digits entirely, which the shipping driver's truncation-tolerant parser accepts. Most corpus cursor changes go through the `$MCURSOR(n)$` variable inside [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) commands instead ([5.1 Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md)), typically wired to field entry/exit for hover pointer changes. _Evidence: corpus (FXSHWIMG.FN, DEMO-01.COL, MENU.FN)._

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: [Buttons](../../glossary.md) - styled interactive controls with plain, icon (BMP), or clipboard faces, optional [hot-icon](../../glossary.md) pressed states (`.BMH`), special effects (bevel, chisel, recess, sunken), labels, hotkeys, and radio/check-box grouping. A style is defined once ([RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_button_style)) and then instantiated by [RIP_BUTTON](#rip_button) commands; up to 36 styles live in the button style [data table](7.1-data-tables.md#button-style-table) and are switched with [RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_switch_button_style).

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: Reference tables: [Label Orientation](#label-orientation) · [Button Types](#button-types) · [Size & Color Parameters](#size-and-color-parameters) · [Flags Field 1](#flags-field-1) · [Font Metrics & Descenders](#font-metrics-and-descenders) · [Chisel Effect Insets](#chisel-effect-insets) · [Flags Field 2](#flags-field-2)

requirements.heading: 4.3 Buttons
requirements.text: _The 1.54 record is [4.2 in the v1.54 reference](../../1.54/ripscrip/4.2-buttons.md); the 2.0 record is [4.3 in the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.3-buttons.md), whose changes were `.BMP`/`.BMH` faces, world-coordinate placement, the `<other_port>` clipboard-port parameter, and style slots._

requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; corpus._

requirements.text: _Button style definition_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: This RIPscrip command is probably one of the most complex in the entire protocol. It defines how subsequent [RIP_BUTTON](#rip_button) commands will be interpreted. The purpose of this command is to define what a Button is and how they operate. Buttons can have many different configurations, flags, and styles. With the diversity of modes that the Button can take on, complexity is a necessary evil.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: There are 36 separate button style slots that can be defined simultaneously. This command allows you to alter the current button style slot. This button style slot is used by the RIP*BUTTON command to define buttons of particular types. Button style slots can be used to avoid retransmitting button styles over and over again. *(v2.A4)\_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: This command does not actually do anything visibly on the screen. Simply put, this creates an internal definition for the Button mode which will be used with RIP_BUTTON commands after the definition is created.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: TeleGrafix left the positional crib for its 36-character argument block as a comment in the corpus's SHOWFONT.FN:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text:
```text
!|! wwhhooffffssffbbBBddssgg22uuccprrrrr
```

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: HLP's "snapshot" button type corresponds to the 2.00a4 clipboard button. _Evidence: corpus (SHOWFONT.FN); HLP._

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 starts with current button-style slot **0**, only slot **0** in use and every slot unprotected. All 36 records contain this fixed default. Selecting an undefined nonzero slot installs the same default, marks it in use and selects it; it does not copy the previously selected style.

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Field                        | Default                                 |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Width, height                | 0, 0 (dynamic sizing)                   |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Label orientation            | 2 (CENTER)                              |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Flags                        | 768 = PLAIN 256 + BEVEL 512             |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Bevel size                   | 3 device pixels                         |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Label foreground, background | 15, 0                                   |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Bright, dark, surface        | 15, 8, 7                                |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Group number                 | 0                                       |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Flags 2                      | 0                                       |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Underline, corner colors     | 15, 7                                   |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: | Other-port storage           | 0; wire argument ignored by this driver |

requirements.heading: Initial and Reset Style
requirements.text: Specific unprotected-slot reset restores these fields; zero stays in use and a nonzero slot becomes undefined. Table reset restores unprotected records and clears their nonzero in-use flags, retaining protected records. **Shipped defect:** resetting the current entry (`$RESET(BUT,CUR)$`, or the current-entry default) instead copies the default bytes into selection/in-use metadata: the records remain unchanged, current becomes zero and the first 26 in-use bytes are overwritten. It does not overwrite protection bytes. A protected current entry rejects the reset unchanged. This corrupt current-reset path must not be mistaken for a different default style. _Evidence: original initialization/selection/reset and bounded native matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Validation and Flag Precedence
requirements.text: The shipped style definition validates orientation **0..4**, group **0..35**, flags 2 **0..255**, the seven colors and current-style protection. A protected current style rejects an explicit definition. At least one of CLIPBOARD 1, ICON 128 or PLAIN 256 must be set; no type bit rejects the command without changing the record. More than one type bit is accepted. Other low-word flags, including combinations marked N in the compatibility tables, are retained: those tables describe applicability, not an additional definition-time rejection or normalization matrix. BEVEL absent is the exception: its stored size becomes zero. The wire `other_port` field is ignored.

requirements.heading: Validation and Flag Precedence
requirements.text: Rendering chooses **ICON first, otherwise CLIPBOARD, otherwise PLAIN**. Creation checks for an existing clipboard whenever CLIPBOARD is set, even if ICON is also set and would win rendering; an undefined clipboard rejects creation. HOT applies to the icon path, and mouse interaction options require a mouse field. These retained combinations do not make a nonmouse decoration interactive. The separate rule against mixing radio and checkbox groups still applies.

requirements.heading: Validation and Flag Precedence
requirements.text: For top/center/bottom labels, flags 2 LEFT 8 wins when RIGHT 16 is also set. NOFILL 32 wins over PATTERN 64: both set means no interior fill; PATTERN alone uses the current fill pattern, neither uses solid surface color. These decisions do not clear the stored flags. _Evidence: complete 65,536-value definition matrix, all flags 2 byte values and original creation/renderer captures; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: Every Button can have an optional text label. It can appear in several different locations compared to the Button itself. This is specified in the `<orient>` parameter. The actual text of the label is not specified with this command, it is specified when you actually create a Button (see RIP_BUTTON below). The value that `<orient>` can be is as follows:

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | Value | Description of Orientation                |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 00    | Display label above button                |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 01    | Display label to the left of button       |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 02    | Display label in the center of the button |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 03    | Display label to the right of button      |

requirements.heading: Label Orientation
requirements.text: | 04    | Display label beneath the button          |

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: There are three basic "types" of Buttons. There are Icon buttons, Clipboard buttons and Plain buttons. Each of these differ in the way that they create the button's image. A description of each type is as follows: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **ICON BUTTON (flag 128)** - An Icon Button means that the actual image of the button will be created by loading a bitmap icon image from the disk and load it at the given locatino. Any special effects (see below) can be applied to the Icon to further enhance the image. The filename for the Icon is supplied with the RIP*BUTTON command, as is the Icon's upper left X/Y coordinate. Icon Buttons are always stamped in COPY mode. *(v1.54)\_

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 loads the normal `.BMP` directly. When HOT 4096 is enabled and the button is selected, it first tries the paired `.BMH` quietly; any nonzero loader error retries `.BMP`. Successful fallback clears HOT and sets INVERT in that created field, retaining the style record; failure of the normal/fallback load returns an error. All requests use the current palette with mode 2 and fixed SRCCOPY, including when the surrounding effect renderer changes its pen ROP2. See [bitmap palette handling](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap) and the bit-128 finding below. _Evidence: original caller and request captures; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **CLIPBOARD BUTTON (flag 1)** - Uses the current clipboard port's viewport as the base image. An undefined clipboard rejects button creation. Although the inherited draft assigned explicit-port semantics to `<other_port>`, RIPtel 3.1 ignores that wire argument and uses the clipboard pointer. Effects can be applied to the pasted image. _Evidence: original definition, constructor and clipboard renderer; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Button Types
requirements.text: **PLAIN BUTTON (flag 256)** - A plain button is exactly that, plain. No special graphics are used to create the button. The entire button region is simply filled-in with a solid colored rectangle using the `<surface>` color. Any special effects can be further applied to enhance the button's appearance. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<hgt>` and `<wid>` parameters provide fixed dimensions only when **both stored dimensions are nonzero**; the button command's far corner is then ignored. If either is zero, both dimensions come from the command's corners: a single positive style dimension does not independently fix that axis. An empty nonmouse plain button with no complete fixed size and both command far coordinates zero is skipped. RIPtel 3.1 converts the style dimensions from the definition-time world into device units once; creation adds those stored dimensions directly to the converted anchor. A world change after definition does not reconvert them.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: With BEVEL 512, `<bevsize>` is converted once using the definition-time **X** ratio, `floor(bevsize × device_width / world_width)`, stored as a WORD, then its low byte is copied into a created button. The same device size is used on both axes. Without BEVEL the stored size is zero. See [effect coordinate units](#effect-coordinate-units) for chisel, recess, sunken and label insets. _Evidence: original B/U handlers and native scale/mixed-zero matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: There are a large number of flag values that can be combined to achieve a great many effects. There are two flag parameters for the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE command, `<flags>` and `<flags2>`. They are detailed in the two tables that follow in this Section. You may combine any of the flags in the first table together simply by adding the "Value" of each one together and representing that number as a MegaNum.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<dfore>` and `<dback>` parameters are used with the text label. The `<dfore>` parameter is the foreground color for the text. It is always used to determine the color of the text label. The `<dback>` color is the color of the dropshadow (if any). This parameter is only used when you have specified the "Dropshadow" flag in the `<flags>` parameter (see below).

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: NOTE: There are seven (7) color parameters in this command. These parameters are ALWAYS used in Color Map mode. Direct RGB Color Mode cannot be used for these parameters. With Color Map mode, you have up to 256 separate color combinations possible for each color, providing you with a great deal of flexibility. The color parameters always use the Base Math set by the global Base Math setting. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<bright>`, `<dark>` and `<surface>` parameters are used with Plain Buttons and with the Special Effects styles (see `<flags>` below). These colors represent the highlighted color, the shadowed color, and the regular surface color that is used in Special Effects. Typical color combinations for these colors might be White, Dark-Gray and Light-Gray respectively for a "chiseled steel" appearance. Each of these values can contain a two-digit value representing any valid color code that may be used in the [RIP_COLOR](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_color) command.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: In addition to the special effects colors, are two additional colors that can be used, `<uline_color>` which is used for the color of the underline (in the text label), and `<corner_color>` which is used to display the colors of corners for things like the Bevel, Recess, etc.

requirements.heading: Size and Color Parameters
requirements.text: The `<grp_no>` parameter determines which Button Group subsequent RIP_BUTTON commands will be associated with. Button Groups are used to maintain groups of Buttons for things like Radio Buttons and/or Checkbox Buttons. See the section on the BUTTON COMMAND for more information on these modes, and what Button Groups can offer. This value can range anywhere from 0-Z (i.e., 0-35). You should not mix Checkbox and Radio buttons in the same group. -- unpredictable things may happen if you do.

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: The right-most five columns describe the combinations for which each flag has an effect. Use one of Plain, Icon or Clipboard for ordinary content. RIPtel 3.1 accepts multiple type bits and inapplicable flags as described in [Validation and Flag Precedence](#validation-and-flag-precedence); an N is not itself a syntax-error condition.

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: The following table contains the possible flag values for the `<flags>` parameter. Each of these values may be combined to achieve a "composite" group of flags. See the preceding paragraphs for a more detailed explanation of this method.

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: The Icon Button, Clipboard button and Plain flags have already been discussed. Following, will be more discussion of the various flags used in the preceding table: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS INVERTABLE (flag 2)** - This means that the button will be inverted when clicked. This flag is only useful when combined with the "Button is a Mouse Button - flag 1024) flag. Even if the button has special effects, those will be inverted as well as they are considered part of the button - all except for the Recessed effect. The recessed effect is NEVER considered part of the actual button image, and will never be part of the mouse field, button's image or anything - it is just extra graphics. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **RESET SCREEN AFTER BUTTON CLICK (flag 4)** - This flag is used when the button is considered a Mouse Button (flag 1024). What this means is that when the user clicks on the button, the screen will be reset exactly the same as a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command will do. The reset is performed before the host command is processed (if any). _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DISPLAY CHISEL SPECIAL EFFECT (flag 8)** - This displays a special effect on-top of the button image that gives the visual impression of an indented gutter just to the inside of the button's border. The amount of indentation varies depending on the size of the button. See below for a table of indentation values for the Chisel effect. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DISPLAY RECESSED SPECIAL EFFECT (flag 16)** - This places a recessed one-pixel bevel around the exterior of the button. It is never considered part of the button's image. Its purpose is to give the button a more 3D look by making it appear that the button is "poking through" a hole in a dialog box. This effect is accomplished by placing a black outline (one pixel wide) around the exterior of the button's image (including bevel, etc), then placing a one-pixel wide inverted bevel around the black outline. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DROPSHADOW THE LABEL IF ANY (flag 32)** - This flag will instruct RIPscrip to place a dropshadowed version of the text label one pixel to the right and one pixel lower than the original label. This is accomplished by drawing the label first in the `<dback>` color, then drawing the label offset up-left in the `<dfore>`. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **AUTO-STAMP IMAGE INTO CLIPBOARD SLOT (flag 64)** - After rendering the face and effects, but before the label, captures the button image through the current clipboard mechanism. It excludes the recess. RIPtel 3.1 uses the existing clipboard slot or chooses the first free nonzero port; the ignored `<other_port>` field does not select a destination. On capture success it changes both the created field's flags and the **actual current style record's flags** to `(field_flags & 0x7c37) | 1`: ICON, PLAIN, CHISEL, BEVEL, AUTOCLIP and SUNKEN are cleared and CLIPBOARD is set. This write occurs **even if the current style is protected**; protection still rejects an explicit style edit. Other style fields and protection are retained. The initial recess has already been removed from the field's persistent flags, so that field-based write also removes it from the style. On capture failure, drawing returns an error and the style flags remain unchanged; earlier painting or clipboard-port work is not rolled back. Later buttons use the captured face. _Evidence: original renderer and protected/unprotected success/failure fixtures; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS AN ICON BUTTON (flag 128)** - See previous discussions on button types above. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS A PLAIN BUTTON (flag 256)** - See previous discussions on button types above. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DISPLAY BEVEL SPECIAL EFFECT (flag 512)** - When this flag is active, a bevel will be drawn `<size>` pixels thick on the outside of the base image of the button. This makes the button that many pixels wider and taller in each direction. See the RIP*BUTTON for a more detailed description of the affects of the button's final size. *(v1.54)\_
requirements.reason: PR #71 documentation answers are adopted at a9e0c2f490714d82a0827675ffbc074aa5ae00e6; implementation and independent expectations must now be reconciled. Previous blocker review: Issue #27 requests how auto-clip changes a protected current button style and how effect thickness scales across device resolutions. No shipping policy is inferred from the frozen RIP154 implementation.

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS A MOUSE BUTTON (flag 1024)** - When this flag is enabled, the button becomes a clickable mouse region. When this option is in use, the Invert flag and several others are available (see the preceding chart). When a button is a non-mouse button, then it is only used to draw a dialog box or an elaborate "static graphic" image of something that "looks" like a button. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **UNDERLINE HOT-KEYS IN LABEL (flag 2048)** - When this flag is active, the first occurence of the hot-key character in the button's label will be underlined using the `<uline_col>` color. Special care must be taken when underlining the character, taking into consideration if the character has a segment that goes below the "baseline" of the font. Consult the following section to determine what ASCII characters have these "descenders". Characters with descenders have the underline drawn slightly lower than for characters without them. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **MAKE ICON BUTTON USE HOT ICONS (flag 4096)** - A Hot Icon is a button that has an alternative image when the button is "depressed". Normally, when a button is an Icon button, some form of Icon File is used to create the image of the button (eg, EMAIL.BMP). When the Hot Icon flag is in use, whenever that button is depressed, rather than using the normal Icon File for the button's image, a different Icon File is used for the button's image. The filename would be the same filename as the original Icon, but with an extension of .BMH instead of .BMP. When Hot Icon is in use, the alternative Icon is stamped in COPY mode. If the file does not exist, then the original Icon's image is used, but pasted in NOT mode for the duration of the depression. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **ADJ. VERTICAL CENTERING OF LABEL (flag 8192)** - Some Labels may appear non-centered vertically when drawn using some fonts that are rather large. With this in mind, you have the option to adjust the vertical centering. What this does is take into consideration the height of any descenders of the label and calculate those into the overall height of the label before centering. If this flag is not used, then the descenders are not taken into consideration when the vertical centering is calculated. See the Font Metric tables below for more detailed information on font sizes and their associated metrics. This command has no effect if the Label orientation is LEFT or RIGHT of the button. It only applies to an orientation of TOP, BOTTOM or CENTER. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **BUTTON BELONGS TO A RADIO GROUP (flag 16384)** - When this flag is used, then any buttons defined in this button `<group_no>` are considered to be radio buttons where only one of the buttons can be clicked (selected) at any particular time. If a button is not a radio button or a checkbox button, then the "selected" flag of the RIP*BUTTON command is ignored. When a Radio Button is clicked, any other radio button in that button group that is selected is automatically de-selected and the current one selected. Any host command is processed at the time of the button click. If a Radio Button is drawn initally as selected, then that host command is processed at the time of its initial drawing. See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md) for a more complete description of Radio Buttons and how they interact with their Button Group and with each other. *(v1.54)\_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 1
requirements.text: **DISPLAY SUNKEN SPECIAL EFFECT (flag 32768)** - When this option is enabled, a one-pixel inverted bevel is drawn exactly one pixel to the inside of the base image of the button. This and the chisel effect are the only two special effects which physically "overwrite" portions of the base button image. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Chisel Effect Insets
requirements.text: The Chisel effect draws a dropshadowed line around the inside of the button. How far from the borders of the button are determined by this table:

requirements.heading: Chisel Effect Insets
requirements.text: | Height of Button | X inset | Y inset |

requirements.heading: Chisel Effect Insets
requirements.text: The height and both inset columns are **device pixels**, using the face's far-minus-near device height. The 12..74 rows correct the inherited draft's Y values 2/3/5 to the shipped values **3/4/6**. _Evidence: original inset selector, all heights 0..32767 and captured chisel rectangles; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.text: | Quantity | RIPtel 3.1 coordinate rule |

requirements.heading: Effect Coordinate Units
requirements.text: | Style width/height | Converted with the definition-time X/Y ratios and stored in device units |

requirements.heading: Effect Coordinate Units
requirements.text: | Bevel thickness | Converted with the definition-time X ratio once, then copied as a device byte; same value on both axes |

requirements.heading: Effect Coordinate Units
requirements.text: | Chisel | Table selected by device face height; device insets; one-device-pixel pens |

requirements.heading: Effect Coordinate Units
requirements.text: | Sunken | One device pixel inside the face; one-device-pixel pens |

requirements.heading: Effect Coordinate Units
requirements.text: | Recess | Black frame one device pixel outside the bevel, outer inverted bevel two device pixels outside it; does not enlarge the interactive face |

requirements.heading: Effect Coordinate Units
requirements.text: | Left/right label indent | Constants in the world captured at creation, applied after converting face geometry and font metrics to that world, then converted back for output |

requirements.heading: Effect Coordinate Units
requirements.text: For a captured world width W and canvas width D, label LEFT adds **10** world units without chisel or **20** with chisel; RIGHT subtracts label width plus **9** or **19** from the far extent boundary. LEFT wins both flags. The right-edge boundary convention accounts for its one-unit difference from the draft's nominal 10/20 description. For example, at X ratios D/W of 1, 1/2 and 1/4, a left inset of 10 becomes 10, 5 and 2 device pixels for integer-aligned positive fixtures. The chisel/recess/sunken one-pixel strokes remain one device pixel at all three ratios. Default bevel 3 is already a literal device value; an explicitly defined bevel is scaled by the formula above. These rules apply at every device canvas; there is no additional hard-coded 640×350 scaling stage. _Evidence: original helpers and label coordinate consumers, native 1/2/4 ratio matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._
