requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: > **Shipped flags 2 bit 128:** the product history attests an icon-transparency flag added in RIPterm 2.20.01. In the recovered **RIPtel 3.1** driver, this bit is accepted and stored but has **no effect on normal, hot or fallback button-icon loading**. Every such call passes key **-1** (no transparency), current-palette mode **2**, stretch **1** and **SRCCOPY**, with the bit either clear or set. Thus this driver's button path selects no transparent color/index and no special normal/hot palette key. Do not infer the separate [LOAD_BITMAP keyed contract](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap) from this flag. This finding does not establish how RIPterm 2.20.01 implemented its advertised feature. _Evidence: complete original renderer trace and normal/hot/failure request captures; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: Following is a more complete description of the flags described in the `<flags2>` parameter: _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **BUTTON IS IN A CHECK BOX GROUP (flag 1)** - When this flag is selected, then the button `<group_no>` is considered a Check-box group. When in this mode, the Radio Group flag is not accessible - A Button Group can be a Radio Button, a Check-box button or neither, but not more than one at the same time. A Check-box button group is a group of buttons where each button in the group can be either ON or OFF in any combination. In this way, more than one button in the group can be clicked at the same time. See [5.2 Templates & Conditionals](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md) for a complete discussion of how the Host Commands are processed for Check-Box buttons. If a check-box button is drawn as "pre-selected", then the Host Command is processed immediately upon inital drawing of the button (when it is received). _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **HIGHLIGHT HOTKEY CHARACTER (flag 2)** - When this flag is active, then the first occurence of the hotkey character in the label will be hilighted using the `<uline_col>` color. This gives the user a visual impression of what keystroke they need to type in order to activate the button without the mouse. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **EXPLODE (ZOOM OUT WHEN CLICKED) (flag 4)** - This optional flag is designed to "zoom out" from the button when the user clicks on it. What is generally done is a dotted rectangle is drawn initially around the button and it is repeatedly redrawn over itself in XOR mode, constantly getting larger and larger until it hits the full size of the screen. This gives the visual impression that the button is zooming out to another screen. Each time another frame of the zooming rectangle is drawn, the previous rectangle on the inside of the new one is erased by XOR drawing the same rectangle over itself again. This option does not need to be supported in order to be considered a RIPscrip terminal, although it would be nice. In other words, this is not a "make or break" feature. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **LEFT JUSTIFY LABEL (TOP/CTR/BTM) (flag 8)** - If this option is enabled, then any TOP, CENTER or BOTTOM label orientations will be left justified to the left edge of the button. The exact indentation of the label from the interior of the button's base image depends on whether the chisel effect is active. RIPtel 3.1 adds 10 creation-world units without chisel or 20 with chisel; see [effect coordinate units](#effect-coordinate-units). This option can be combined with the Adjust Vertical Centering flag only if the label orientation is CENTER. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **RIGHT JUSTIFY LABEL (TOP/CTR/BTM) (flag 16)** - If this option is enabled, then any TOP, CENTER or BOTTOM label orientations will be right justified to the right edge of the button. The exact indentation of the label from the interior of the button's base image depends on whether the chisel effect is active. RIPtel 3.1 subtracts label width plus 9 creation-world units without chisel or 19 with chisel from the far boundary; see [effect coordinate units](#effect-coordinate-units). This option can be combined with the Adjust Vertical Centering flag only if the label orientation is CENTER. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: Flags Field 2
requirements.text: **DON'T FILL-IN BUTTON INTERIOR** - If this option is enabled and the button is a Plain Button, then the interior of the Button will not be filled in with the surface color. By default, any plain button will have its interior filled in with the surface color. Use this option if you don't want the button face to be drawn. _(v2.A0)_

requirements.text: **FILL-IN INTERIOR IN FILL PATTERN** - If this option is enabled in conjunction with a plain button, then the interior of the button that would normally be filled in with the surface color will instead, use the current Fill Color and Fill Pattern to fill in the interior. requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: _Define a Mouse Button_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `U`                                                   |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `x0:XY y0:XY x1:XY y1:XY hotkey:2 flags:1 res:1 text` |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|1U <x0> <y0> <x1> <y1> <hotkey> <flags> <res> <text>` **Example:** `!|1U2E5O747G2000<>Hotkeys<>`

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Font Style, Viewport, Port (only for "non-mouse" type buttons), Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.3-buttons.md#rip_button)) · HLP (`RIP_Button`; limits label ≤255, hotkey ≤255) · corpus (75 uses in 17 files) · SyncTERM (ripper.c:16764)

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: This command physically creates a new Button using a previously defined [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_button_style) in the current button style. You may have at most 128 different Mouse Buttons (you may have any number of non-Mouse Buttons). The `<slot>` parameter determines which button style slot is used to determine how this button appears. _(v2.A1)_ The ALPHA 4 draft removed the explicit `<slot>` parameters in favor of the current-style model. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<x0>` and `<y0>` parameters for this command designate the upper-left corner of the Button. This (X,Y) location may not be the actual "absolute" corner position of the Button, as it may be adjusted via the Special Effects functions that are part of the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE command (see above).

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<x1>` and `<y1>` parameters are only used for Plain Buttons when you have not specified a specific Height and Width in the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE command. These parameters are used in Dynamically Sized Buttons. If the Height and Width in the RIP_BUTTON_STYLE are non-zero, then these two parameters are set to zero.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The (x0,y0) and (x1,y1) parameters will be modified by the following values for the different special effects:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | Effect Type | X0 Modifier | Y0 Modifier | X1 Modifier | Y1 Modifier |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | Bevel       | -bevel size | -bevel size | +bevel size | +bevel size |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The modifiers above use the [effect coordinate units](#effect-coordinate-units): bevel is the already converted device size, and the additional recess border remains two device pixels outside it. Chisel and sunken overwrite the face without enlarging its bounds. The recess is painted once and excluded from the persistent mouse/button image. _Evidence: original renderer/effect helpers; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<hotkey>` parameter is only used with Mouse Buttons. It is the ASCII code for the keystroke that will activate this Button. It is represented as a two-digit MegaNum. If this character exists in the text label, and the Underline flag or hilight hotkey flag is enabled in the RIP*BUTTON_STYLE, then the character will be underlined in the label. Control codes are allowable, and a value of 255 (decimal) corresponds to "any" key. *(v1.54)\_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<flags>` parameter provides several different functions for each button. The possible "combinatorial" flags for this parameter are listed in the following table. Note that these values may be combined together (by adding their values) to arrive at the final flag parameter's value.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | Value | Description                                   |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | 1     | Draw button as already selected               |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | 2     | Button is "default" when \<ENTER\> is pressed |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Using a flag of 1 means that the Button is already "selected". By selected, we mean that it is already clicked and should be initially drawn as clicked. This is typically used for Radio Buttons and/or Check Boxes. This only affects the image. The Host Command WILL NOT be automatically sent to the host when a selected Button is drawn. If this parameter is set to 0, then the Button will be drawn in normal, unselected mode.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The `<text>` parameter for this command is somewhat different than those found in previously described RIPscrip commands. All other RIPscrip commands only have one text parameter. This command requires anywhere from 0-3 text parameters. The way RIPscrip accomplishes this is by separating each block in the `<text>` parameter with the delimiter `<>`. This text parameter delimiter is not needed before the first text block, but is necessary between the 1st and 2nd blocks, and the 2nd and 3rd blocks. Here is an example of a typical text parameter for this command:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text:
```text
ICONFILE.BMP<>TEXT LABEL<>HOST COMMAND
```

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The actual syntax of this text parameter is as follows:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text:
```text
[icon-file][[<>text-label][<>host-command]]
```

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The block described as ICONFILE.BMP is actually the Icon Filename that will be used for the Button if it is an Icon Button. If it is not an Icon Button, then this block will read `<>` all by itself (a "null" block). _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Note that we actually specified a file extension of ".BMP" for our icon filename. You shouldn't explicitly specify a filename extension like this if it is the default extension of the filename. The reason for this is that some platforms don't use file extensions and their use is not really appropriate. When in doubt, don't specify a file extension. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The .BMP file extension does not need to be included as part of the filename. If omitted, it will automatically be appended to the filename. If an extension is provided, it will be used verbatim. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The "TEXT LABEL" block is actually the text that will be used to descriptively label the Button. You may also specify a "null" block for no label (i.e., `<>`).

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: The final block of the `<text>` parameter is the Host Command. This block contains any text that should be sent to the Host after this Button is clicked. This may contain any Control Characters, Pick-List definitions, Text Variables or Template Definitions. This block might be "segmented" into multiple Host Command segments. See [5.0 Host Commands](5.0-host-commands.md) for additional information on these Host Command features.

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: When this command is stored in-memory, it is converted to global screen coordinates (for internal storage only). This makes it so that if you have mouse button regions defined in multiple different viewports, that each field will be properly inverted at the right location regardless of the currently defined viewport. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: NOTE: All Mouse Fields are scanned in "last in, first out" order. This means that the last-most received Mouse Button will be the first one scanned for a mouse click. _(v1.54)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Not all of the blocks in the `<text>` parameter need to be specified. Here are examples of the valid combinations of text blocks:

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | Parameter Example       | Description of the Text Parameter           |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<>label<>host_cmd` | Specify all three blocks                    |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<>label<>host_cmd`     | 2 blocks specified; no icon                 |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<>label<>`         | 2 blocks specified; no host command         |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<>label`           | 2 blocks specified; no host command         |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<><>host_cmd`          | 1 block specified; no icon or label         |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<>label<>`             | 1 block specified; no icon or host command  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<>label`               | 1 block specified; no icon or host command  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<><>`              | 1 block specified; no label or host command |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon<>`                | 1 block specified; no label or host command |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `icon`                  | 1 block specified; no label or host command |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<><><>`                | A blank text parameter; all blocks omitted  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<><>`                  | A blank text parameter; all blocks omitted  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: | `<>`                    | A blank text parameter; all blocks omitted  |

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: Under RIPscrip 1.54 and earlier versions, button icon filenames ended with .ICN for normal icons, and .HIC for "Hot IcoN". Under 2.0 and later, these file extensions are different. For normal button icons, the extension .BMP is used for a standard bitmap, and .BMH is used for a "hot bitmap". _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: When a button is displayed that uses an icon/bitmap, special care must be taken when dealing with hot bitmaps. If the flag is present in the button style indicating to use hot icons, then when the button is displayed as selected then the hot bitmap (.BMH) file's image is used to display the button. If that file doesn't exist, then the normal bitmap button is displayed in an inverted state. If neither of these files are present, then the RIP*BUTTON command is ignored. *(v2.A3)\_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: If the host command string of the button cannot be parsed properly, then the button is completely ignored. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: RIP_BUTTON
requirements.text: NOTE: The `<res>` parameter is reserved for future use by TeleGrafix Communications, Inc.. It should be set to 0 for compatibility with future releases.

requirements.heading: The shipped 3.x button aesthetic
requirements.text: The 3.x corpus shows how TeleGrafix itself built buttons: rather than 1.54-style chiseled plain buttons, scenes stamp **bitmap skins** with [RIP_LOAD_BITMAP](4.0-icons-and-bitmaps.md#rip_load_bitmap) (TELBUT.BMP, RADIONEW.BMP, CHECKBOX.BMP) and lay `1U` buttons or [`1M` mouse fields](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_mouse) over them; the corresponding `.BMH` files on disk are the pre-rendered **highlight-state** variants automatically shown while a hot-icon button is depressed (they are never named in any script - pairing is by filename convention; see [6.1](6.1-content-file-roles.md#bmh---button-highlight-variants)). `1B` + `1U` with empty `<><>` blocks also serve as pure chisel-frame decorations. The example above is a plain radio-group demo button whose host command is empty - its behavior comes from the button-style flags. _Evidence: corpus (ICONS/\*.BMH pairs; BUTTONS.RIP, TELDEMOS.MNU)._

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: _Switches to a new button style_

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: | **Command**   | `B`            |

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: | **Arguments** | `bstyle_num:2` |

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: **Format:** `!|2B <bstyle_num>` **Example:** `!|2B04`

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: **Attributes used:** Base Math (current setting) **Evidence:** 2.00a4 ([2.0 entry](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.3-buttons.md#rip_switch_button_style)) · HLP (`RIP_SwitchButtonStyle`; button-style slots 0-35, `$SBS$`/`$RBS$` backup variables) - not observed in the RIPtel demo corpus, not in SyncTERM

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: This command physically switches the currently active button style. Any subsequent button operations will use this new button style.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: You are allowed up to 36 separate button styles to switch between. Possible button style slot numbers are from 0-35 (0-Z).

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: When a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) or the global drawing-reset flag of [RIP_HEADER](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) is executed, then all unprotected button style slots are reset to the default button style. Also, the current button style is reset to button style number 0.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE
requirements.text: The demos simply re-send [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](#rip_button_style) before each button group instead of switching slots. _Evidence: corpus (absence)._

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: The Active [Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md) below request synchronous tones. This chapter specifies the requests made by **RIPtel 3.1's original RIPscrip 3.0.7 driver**, including its differences from the inherited [1.54](../../1.54/ripscrip/4.3-tone-and-sound-generation.md) and [2.0](../../2.0/ripscrip/4.4-tone-and-sound-generation.md) recipes. Earlier-version reference and verbatim text remain separate historical records. Exact device waveform reproduction is outside this contract. [WAV playback](4.5-audio-files.md) is a separate capability.

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: A terminal that omits a sound should still recognize its variable and consume it as an action, as explained in [5.1](5.1-text-variables.md). The summary is in [9.1](9.1-text-variable-reference.md#sounds-active).

requirements.heading: 4.4 Tone & Sound Generation
requirements.text: **Primary evidence:** original registered callbacks, numeric validation and synchronous `Beep(frequency,duration)` requests, captured without playing audio. Exact addresses, source hashes, native matrices and controlled-service limits are in the [tone derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md). The inherited draft, help strings and SyncTERM are not executable oracles for these shipped sequences.

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: Frequencies are in **Hz** and durations in **milliseconds**. Successful actions return no characters. Invalid arguments set the variable error and issue no tone: they do **not** play a default effect. In ordinary text expansion the invalid expression remains literal. The callback ignores the audio service's success/failure return; an unsuccessful audio request does not itself make the text variable invalid.

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: | Variable | Argument count | Defaults for omitted trailing arguments | Shipped request |

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: | ALARM | 0 or 1 | count=3 | Two tones per repeat |

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: | BEEP | 0..2 | frequency=1000, length=75 | One tone; no added gap |

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: | BLIP | 0..2 | frequency=1000, length=25 | One tone; no added gap |

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: | MUSIC | 0 or 1 | count=4 | Six tones per repeat |

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: | PHASER | 0..4 | start=2500, stop=50, increment=20, time=2 | Descending sweep |

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: | REVPHASER | 0..4 | start=50, stop=2500, increment=20, time=2 | Ascending sweep |

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: | T | Exactly 2 | None | One tone; no added gap |

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: Supplied numeric fields must fit **0..65535**; negative, nonnumeric, oversized or extra fields reject the action. BEEP/BLIP/T forward zero frequency or duration to the audio service without a macro error. ALARM/MUSIC accept count zero as no requests. Sweep increment and time must instead be **1..65535**, and their strict endpoint ordering is checked before any tone. Defaults apply only to omitted trailing arguments, not to invalid values. _Evidence: original callbacks and exhaustive simple-tone WORD/boundary/arity matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Sound Related Text Variables
requirements.text: The pseudocode uses `tone(hz, ms)` for one synchronous request. It has no implicit trailing silence. The callbacks do not insert the inherited BEEP 75 ms or BLIP 10 ms gaps, nor a separate gap between repeated notes. Actual audio-service timing is not specified.

requirements.heading: $ALARM$
requirements.text: _Warning/failure sound_

requirements.heading: $ALARM$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$ALARM(count)$`

requirements.heading: $ALARM$
requirements.text: **Syntax:** `$ALARM$` or `$ALARM(count)$`, count **0..65535**, default **3**.

requirements.heading: $ALARM$
requirements.text: Each repeat requests **320 Hz for 200 ms**, then **160 Hz for 225 ms**. The inherited second duration 425 ms is not the shipped value.

requirements.heading: $ALARM$
$ALARM$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$ALARM(3)$` is equivalent to `$ALARM$`. **Returns:** nothing.

requirements.heading: $ALARM$
requirements.text: _Evidence: original callback 0x8600 and captured count/default sequences; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: _Beep sound_

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$BEEP(frequency,length)$`

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: **Syntax:** `$BEEP$`, `$BEEP(frequency)$` or `$BEEP(frequency,length)$`; each supplied field **0..65535**. Defaults: **1000 Hz**, **75 ms**.

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
$BEEP$
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 adds **no explicit 75 ms silence** after this request. The inherited draft specifies such a gap, but the original callback has only the single tone call. With both arguments supplied, BEEP and T make identical requests; their difference is that BEEP permits omissions and T does not.

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$BEEP(1000,75)$` is equivalent to `$BEEP$`. **Returns:** nothing.

requirements.heading: $BEEP$
requirements.text: _Evidence: original callback 0x868e and native request captures; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: $BLIP$
requirements.text: _Blipping/barrier sound_

requirements.heading: $BLIP$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$BLIP(frequency,length)$`

requirements.heading: $BLIP$
requirements.text: **Syntax:** `$BLIP$`, `$BLIP(frequency)$` or `$BLIP(frequency,length)$`; each supplied field **0..65535**. Defaults: **1000 Hz**, **25 ms**.

requirements.heading: $BLIP$
$BLIP$
requirements.text: The original driver uses 1000 Hz, rather than the inherited 50 Hz default, and adds **no explicit 10 ms silence**. The inherited example `$BLIP(50,10)$` is a valid custom request but is not equivalent to the parameterless effect. Its default duration is 25 ms.

requirements.heading: $BLIP$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$BLIP(1000,25)$` is equivalent to `$BLIP$`. **Returns:** nothing.

requirements.heading: $BLIP$
requirements.text: _Evidence: original callback 0x873a and native default/argument captures; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: $MUSIC$
requirements.text: _Musical success sound_

requirements.heading: $MUSIC$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$MUSIC(count)$`

requirements.heading: $MUSIC$
requirements.text: **Syntax:** `$MUSIC$` or `$MUSIC(count)$`, count **0..65535**, default **4**.

requirements.heading: $MUSIC$
requirements.text: Each repeat requests these **six** notes, in this order:

requirements.heading: $MUSIC$
requirements.text: | Note | Frequency (Hz) | Duration (ms) |

requirements.heading: $MUSIC$
requirements.text: The requested durations total **90 ms per repeat**. This shipped sequence supersedes the inherited nine-note recipe for this reconstructed v3 reference. SyncTERM's three swept segments are not an equivalent sequence and do not establish RIPtel 3.1 behavior.

requirements.heading: $MUSIC$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$MUSIC(4)$` is equivalent to `$MUSIC$`. **Returns:** nothing.

requirements.heading: $MUSIC$
requirements.text: _Evidence: original callback 0x87e6 and exact native sequence/count captures through count 65535; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: _Descending frequency sweep_

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$PHASER(start,stop,increment,time)$`

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: **Syntax:** **0..4 positional arguments**, with omitted trailing defaults **(2500,50,20,2)**. START/STOP must fit **0..65535**, **START > STOP**, INCREMENT and TIME must be **1..65535**. Thus START is at least 1; STOP may be zero, subject to the shipped wrap defect below.

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: For ordinary inputs that terminate without WORD wrap, the requests are `start, start-increment, ...` while frequency is **≥stop**, each for `time` ms. The stop frequency is included only if a step lands exactly on it. The default makes **123 requests**, **2500,2480,...,60 Hz**, each **2 ms**.

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: Invalid ordering, zero increment, zero time, out-of-range/nonnumeric fields or more than four fields produce a variable error **before any request**. They do **not** fall back to (2500,50,20,2). For example, `$PHASER(1,2)$` and `$PHASER(2500,50,20,0)$` produce no sound. `$PHASER(3000)$` retains the other three defaults.

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$PHASER(2500,50,20,2)$` is equivalent to `$PHASER$`. **Returns:** nothing on success.

requirements.heading: $PHASER$
requirements.text: _Evidence: original callback 0x8892, complete optional-suffix tests and boundary matrices; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: $REVPHASER$
requirements.text: _Ascending frequency sweep_

requirements.heading: $REVPHASER$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$REVPHASER(start,stop,increment,time)$`

requirements.heading: $REVPHASER$
requirements.text: **Syntax:** **0..4 positional arguments**, with omitted trailing defaults **(50,2500,20,2)**. START/STOP must fit **0..65535**, **START < STOP**, INCREMENT and TIME must be **1..65535**. START may be zero; STOP is at least 1.

requirements.heading: $REVPHASER$
requirements.text: For ordinary inputs that terminate without WORD wrap, the requests are `start, start+increment, ...` while frequency is **≤stop**, each for `time` ms. The stop frequency is included only if a step lands exactly on it. The default makes **123 requests**, **50,70,...,2490 Hz**, each **2 ms**.

requirements.heading: $REVPHASER$
requirements.text: Invalid inputs set the variable error before any tone, with **no fallback to defaults**, just as for PHASER. The inherited descending description and START>STOP requirement are incorrect for REVPHASER.

requirements.heading: $REVPHASER$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$REVPHASER(50,2500,20,2)$` is equivalent to `$REVPHASER$`. **Returns:** nothing on success.

requirements.heading: $REVPHASER$
requirements.text: _Evidence: original callback 0x89d2 and native ordering/default/boundary captures; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: Shipped Sweep Arithmetic Defect
requirements.text: Both callbacks use an **unsigned 16-bit frequency accumulator**, including their update and loop comparison:

requirements.heading: Shipped Sweep Arithmetic Defect
Shipped Sweep Arithmetic Defect
requirements.text: A step can wrap rather than finish a sweep. With descending STOP=0, or ascending STOP=65535, the loop cannot pass its exit test. Other steps can also cycle if their modulo-65536 progression never reaches a value beyond the stop. This is a shipped implementation defect, not fallback-to-default behavior. Native verification bounds execution after 65536 requests; implementors should bound this defect rather than reproduce an endless audio loop. The usual default sweeps terminate without wrapping. _Evidence: original WORD instructions and bounded modular sequence captures; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: $T$
requirements.text: _Play one audio tone_

requirements.heading: $T$
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A4._

requirements.heading: $T$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$T(frequency,length)$`

requirements.heading: $T$
requirements.text: **Syntax:** **Exactly two required parameters**, each **0..65535**. The inherited optional/default syntax is not implemented: `$T$` and `$T(1000)$` set the variable error and issue no tone.

requirements.heading: $T$
$T$
requirements.text: T adds no explicit trailing silence. In RIPtel 3.1, `$T(1000,75)$` and `$BEEP(1000,75)$` request the same one tone, and the latter is also the default BEEP request. Their documented older-client gap distinction is not present in this driver's callbacks.

requirements.heading: $T$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$T(1000,75)$`. **Returns:** nothing on success.

requirements.heading: $T$
requirements.text: _Evidence: original callback 0x8b0d, original registration and full expansion/arity/WORD-boundary tests; [derivation](../research/issue-28-tone-variable-contract.md)._

requirements.heading: 4.5 Audio Files (WAV)
requirements.text: Digitized audio files: Microsoft **WAVE** (`.WAV`) PCM audio, played in the background while graphics and command processing continue - triggered from the command stream with [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](#rip_play_audio) or at the host-command layer with the `$)FILE.WAV$` playback prefix ([5.3 Local File Playback](5.3-local-playback.md#local-audio-playback---filewav)), and distinct from the terminal's own speaker-tone generation ([4.4 Tone & Sound Generation](4.4-tone-and-sound-generation.md)), which needs no files at all.
requirements.reason: Complete 1w command bodies now reach read-only MEDIA resolution, WAV decoding and the existing mixer through a public void parser entry. Independent PCM and nonfatal syntax/service recovery are covered. Raw framing/unescaping, host-prefix expansion, reset/header orchestration, settings/capability binding, delivery/query/deletion and active session integration remain pending.

requirements.heading: 4.5 Audio Files (WAV)
requirements.text: > **Editor's note - provenance:** WAV audio is not a 3.x innovation. RIP_PLAY_AUDIO entered the 2.0 specification at ALPHA 3 ("Added the RIP_PLAY_AUDIO command to playback a WAVE file" - 2.00a4 changelog) and **shipped** in RIPterm Professional 2.0 (January 1995): its manual introduces "digitized sound, in the form of .WAV files" (RIPTERM.DOC §4.3) with an Audio Setup screen for 19 sound boards (Sound Blaster, Pro Audio Spectrum, Gravis, etc.) and a `-A` command-line switch to disable digitized audio (RIPTERM.DOC §2.3), and the install carries HMI "Sound Operating System" drivers and a `RIPTERM.WAV` - both preserved (see the [RIPterm 2.30 audio assets](../../2.0/assets/audio/README.md)). TeleGrafix's December 1995 "RIP-2 Internet Multimedia" press release advertised the same "digital WAV sound". Like several other "3.x" features, it belongs to the RIPterm 2.30 product era that 3.x inherits (see the [revision history](1.0-introduction.md#revision-history)).

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: RIPscrip permits the support of digitized audio to be played in the background whild graphics and other operations are being performed. This includes playing sounds while graphical commands are being received from the host (without interruption).
requirements.reason: Complete 1w command bodies now reach read-only MEDIA resolution, WAV decoding and the existing mixer through a public void parser entry. Independent PCM and nonfatal syntax/service recovery are covered. Raw framing/unescaping, host-prefix expansion, reset/header orchestration, settings/capability binding, delivery/query/deletion and active session integration remain pending.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: The format of audio data used by RIPscrip is formally defined as straight audio data in the Microsoft WAVE file format. When dealing with host systems and downloading digitized audio data, or being told to play back audio data, RIPscrip will assume that you are working with WAVE files. For example, you might be told to playback a file named SOUND.WAV. If you are not internally supporting the actual WAVE format, but some other format, then you need to translate the name of the file to the correct name in your environment (if necessary) and perform the playback.
requirements.reason: Complete 1w command bodies now reach read-only MEDIA resolution, WAV decoding and the existing mixer through a public void parser entry. Independent PCM and nonfatal syntax/service recovery are covered. Raw framing/unescaping, host-prefix expansion, reset/header orchestration, settings/capability binding, delivery/query/deletion and active session integration remain pending.

requirements.heading: Audio (Sound & Music) Formats
requirements.text: When dealing with the [RIP_FILE_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query) command, you need to be careful if you're not dealing with true WAVE files. The RIP_FILE_QUERY command is used to "detect" if a particular file is present on the target system and if so, if it is the right date/time and file size as the file on the host. The file on the host will be in WAVE format so if you're translating the files as they're received, you need to translate the RIP_FILE_QUERY information returned to the host so that it thinks that the file you have on your local hard disk is actually a WAVE file (ie, translate the file size to a WAVE equivalent). If the sizes and, or the time/date don't match, the host could download a new file to you (via the [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) command) thinking that your's is out of date.

requirements.heading: RIP_PLAY_AUDIO
requirements.text: This command will physically start a local .WAV file to play back on the user's remote terminal. The audio file must already exist in the user's hard disk in the same location as their bitmapped icons. If the file doesn't exist, then this command does nothing. If you specify the `<filename>` parameter as `$OFF$` then you will in effect be shutting off any currnetly running sound file. If a sound is already playing when this command is received, the older file that was playing will be terminated in place for the new file. You may use [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) to transfer audio files to the user's computer for subsequent playback.

requirements.heading: Stopping, resets, and capability negotiation
requirements.text:
- **Stopping playback** - issue [RIP_PLAY_AUDIO](#rip_play_audio) with `$OFF$` as the filename, or the [`$RESET(SOUND)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#reset) text variable, which aborts any playing digitized sound immediately (the DLL string table names a dedicated `resetKeywordSOUND` handler). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
- **Reset interaction** - the shipped [`RIP_HEADER`](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) uses type-7 segment flag 1 to stop waveform playback, with no audio table slot. Global header flag 2048 belongs to the superseded Alpha 4 layout and is rejected by this driver. A hard reset also stops waveform playback. See the [audio header action](7.1-data-tables.md#audio-header-action-new-in-3x). During a [`$D(time)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#d) delay, sound-related activity continues while everything else pauses. _Evidence: DLL ([header derivation](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md)); 2.00a4 (delay behavior)._
- **Terminal-side switch** - the RIPtel installer creates the master toggle **`AUDIO=TRUE`** in the `[CONFIG]` section of `RIPscrip.ini`; the driver also exposes a `RIP_AudioSupport` client-API entry point. _Evidence: HLP._
- **Capability negotiation** - before relying on audio, query [`$IFS(WAV)$`](5.1-text-variables.md#ifs): the terminal answers `1` if it can play WAVE files, `0` if not. `$IFS(LIST, _AUDIO)$` lists every audio format the terminal supports. The `$IFS$` processor is present in the 3.0 DLL's variable table. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._
- **Delivery and housekeeping** - hosts deliver `.WAV` files with [RIP_ENTER_BLOCK_MODE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_enter_block_mode) (or a UU-encoded block), check freshness with [RIP_FILE_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_file_query), and clean up with [`$FILEDEL$`](5.1-text-variables.md#filedel); audio files live alongside the icon files in the [connection directory](../../glossary.md)/default-directory family - see [6.2 Asset Delivery & Storage](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 5.0 Host Commands
requirements.text: The **Host Command Language (HCL)**, as the RIPscrip 3.0 White Paper names it - the action language that mouse regions, buttons, hotkeys and query expressions speak back to the host, divided into five areas: control characters, pop-up picklists, local playback directives, template directives, and text variables. A [host command](../../glossary.md) is, at its simplest, raw text transmitted to the host when a button or mouse field is clicked; every HCL directive is something the terminal interprets _before_ (or instead of) transmitting.

requirements.text: _Evidence: WP; 2.00a4._

requirements.text: _The 2.0 record this generation inherits is [5.0 of the v2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/5.0-host-commands.md) (1.54 lineage in the [v1.54 page](../../1.54/ripscrip/5.0-host-commands.md)); the flowed-text/overflow machinery the HCL pagination variables drive is the [Column Text System](3.1-column-text-system.md)._

requirements.heading: Where Host Commands Run
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; SyncTERM (ripper.c:11884-12001); HLP._

requirements.heading: Where Host Commands Run
requirements.text: A host-command string may be attached to:

requirements.heading: Where Host Commands Run
requirements.text:
- **Buttons** (`1U`) - the command block of the Text Parameter segment, executed when the button is clicked. Template groups are associated with buttons; the [shipped common processor](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order) also accepts template-enabled blocks without a button association.
- **Mouse fields** (`1M`) - the host command executed when the field is clicked.
- **Queries** (`1` + ESC) - the query text itself is a host-command string, executed or deferred per the mode digit (below); full entry at [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query).
- **Keystroke macros / hotkeys** - hotkey-triggered buttons execute their command block exactly as if clicked.

requirements.heading: What Can Go Where
requirements.text: The following chart records the inherited 2.00a4 design. For shipped RIPtel behavior, use the [consumer/pass contract](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order): its common host processor can accept template-enabled blocks without a button association, and angle preprocessing is separate from these ordinary host features.

requirements.heading: What Can Go Where
requirements.text: RIPtel’s ordinary host response expansion makes **two passes**, while its angle preprocessor has distinct rescan rules. Template insertion and local-file playback must not be collapsed into one unlimited recursive expansion model; see the [exact processing order and shipped defects](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order). SyncTERM’s separate `handle_command_str` recursion cap of 64 is implementation evidence for SyncTERM, not a recovered RIPtel limit.

requirements.heading: What Can Go Where
requirements.text: RIPtel additionally exposes a **Command Mode** menu option that executes any typed HCL string directly - TeleGrafix's own recommended way to test host commands interactively. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: _Evidence: original RIPtel 3.1 response executor 0x4acd9, ordinary conversion 0x4b394 and [native notation derivation](../research/issue-53-host-control-brackets.md#original-stages-and-first-native-checkpoint); inherited 2.00a4/HLP conventions._

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 converts caret (`^`) and backquote (`` ` ``) pairs during the **second ordinary host-response pass**, after bracket-template segmentation. For the shipping default ASCII locale, the conversion rules are:

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | Following character | Result |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `A`..`Z` or `a`..`z` | Uppercase the letter, then subtract 0x40: bytes 1..26 |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | The same prefix as the first character | One literal prefix: `^^`→caret, doubled backquote→backquote |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | Caret after a backquote | Byte 30 (RS); `^^` instead means literal caret |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | Any other non-NUL ASCII character | Preserve both bytes unchanged |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | End of text immediately after the prefix | Preserve the trailing prefix unchanged |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: Thus `^m` and `^M` both produce CR, `^?` sends the two literal bytes 5e 3f rather than DEL, and **`^@` sends 5e 40 rather than NUL**. The inherited “following character minus @” formula applies only to the accepted letters/punctuation above. Invalid/unrecognized pairs and trailing prefixes do not reject the response. A decoded literal prefix is skipped rather than decoded again: `^^M` sends literal `^M`. Non-ASCII character classification depends on the CRT locale and is not specified by this ASCII contract.

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: **Individual control characters**

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | Sequence     | Transmitted byte | Conventional meaning         |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `^H`         | 08               | Backspace                    |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `^L`         | 0c               | Form feed                    |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `^M` or `^m` | 0d               | Carriage return              |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `^C`         | 03               | Break, host-dependent        |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `^[`         | 1b               | Escape                       |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `^S` / `^Q`  | 13 /11           | Pause/resume, host-dependent |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: **Special keystroke notation** uses the same ordinary conversion; there is no atomic whitelist of key strings. Only the first `^[` becomes ESC; subsequent raw bytes retain their values unless the earlier template parser recognizes a complete directive.

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | Sequence | Transmitted bytes (hex) | Conventional key |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `^[[L` | 1b 5b 4c | Control-Home |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `` `[[A `` | 1b 5b 41 | Same bytes as `^[[A` |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: | `^[[Z` | 1b 5b 5a | Unlisted example; still converted and transmitted |

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: The unclosed bracket+Mega-letter forms above also produce a **nonfatal `Invalid MegaNum` diagnostic** while the earlier stage looks for a closing template delimiter. RIPtel nevertheless transmits the bytes shown; malformed template syntax is not universally rejected before partial execution. Remote host interpretation of those escape sequences is separate from the bytes sent.

requirements.heading: Control Characters
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** `^M` is notation for a byte, not two transmitted characters. RIPscrip wire commands themselves (for example [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query)) use a real ESC byte, not the `^[` host-command notation.

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: The earlier blanket claim that every raw `$` or `[` must start a directive, attributed to a SyncTERM source comment, does **not** describe shipping RIPtel 3.1. Its bracket stage searches for **complete recognized template delimiters** before ordinary dollar/control expansion. It neither tests for a preceding ESC nor treats special-key sequences atomically. See [template processing order](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order) and the [original derivation](../research/issue-53-host-control-brackets.md).

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | Host-command source | Result with template 3=`THREE`, template A(10)=`TEN` |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | Lone raw `[` | Transmit literal byte 5b; no template action or diagnostic |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | `^[[A` | Transmit ESC+`[A`; nonfatal incomplete-template diagnostic |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | `^[[A]` | Invoke template A; transmit ESC+`TEN` |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | Raw ESC followed by `[A]` | Invoke template A; transmit ESC+`TEN` |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | `^[x[3]` | Invoke template 3; transmit ESC+`xTHREE` |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | `[3]` | Invoke template 3; transmit `THREE` |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | `\[3]` | Still invoke template 3; backslash does not hide a delimiter from the earlier scan |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | `[3` | Transmit literal `[3`; nonfatal `Invalid MegaNum` diagnostic |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: | `x[A:]TAIL` | Transmit x, store TAIL as template A |

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: An emitted ESC does **not** suppress bracket interpretation. Complete directives in the original source are processed earlier; an expression that returns the literal string `[3]` after segmentation is not restarted through that stage and can transmit those bytes literally. Unrecognized bracket syntax such as `[?]` also passes as ordinary text. These facts do not create a universal quote for an otherwise valid bracket directive.

requirements.heading: Literal Dollars and Brackets
requirements.text: Backslash handling is stage-specific. In the full two-pass host path, `\$SHIFT\$` transmits literal `$SHIFT$` without evaluating SHIFT, whereas quoting only its opening dollar (`\$SHIFT$`) still lets the earlier pass evaluate the variable. Both forms are verified through the original pipeline. These examples are **host-command input bytes**; preserve the separate [wire quoting rules](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#escaping-in-text-parameters) when carrying them inside RIP commands. Caret/backquote doubling quotes only its own prefix and is unrelated to bracket segmentation.

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: _Evidence: SyncTERM (ripper.c:14996-15013); 2.00a4; corpus (MENU.MSE, DEMO-01.COL); HLP._

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: The query command `1` + ESC ([RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query)) takes a leading mode digit, a window number and two reserved digits. The shipping RIPtel 3.1 behavior is:

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: | Mode | Effect |

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: | `0` | Execute the command text immediately upon receipt |

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: | `1` | Store a floating viewport expression; clicks do not execute it |

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: | `2` | Store a floating text-window expression; clicks do not execute it |

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: | `3` | Store an expression on the numbered viewport; clicks do not execute it |

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: | `4` | Store an expression on the numbered text window; clicks do not execute it |

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: | `5` | Store a mouse-field entry expression; execute on pointer entry |

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: | `6` | Store a mouse-field exit expression; execute on pointer exit |

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: Modes 1–4 retain the storage/copy/reset machinery, but the original driver has no click-dispatch loop for them and the original client adds none. There is **no shipping numbered/floating click order or same-click live/snapshot mutation rule** to implement for RIPtel 3.1. The inherited A4 numbered-viewport→numbered-text-window→floating-viewport→floating-text-window sequence and contrary A1 sentence are explicitly separated as historical intent in [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query). This finding does not change earlier-version references. _Evidence: original query definition, event dispatch, client forwarding and [72,972 native query checks](../research/issue-51-deferred-query-order.md#event-path-and-native-checkpoint)._

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: Sending case-insensitive `$OFF$` in a stored-query mode cancels that mode/target's stored expression. “Resident” covers stored strings, including floating/numbered and entry/exit queries; it does not split the historical ordering into two classes.

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: The RIPtel corpus makes constant use of mode 0 as an immediate command carrier - nearly every `.DEF` configuration file is a stack of `!|1<ESC>0000$-=NAME=value$` lines that silently set variables. MENU.MSE also contains:

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text:
```text
!|1^[5000$MCURSOR(4)$$>menu.ent$
!|1^[6000$MCURSOR(0)$$>menu.ext$
```

requirements.heading: Query Deferral Modes
requirements.text: TeleGrafix comments describe mouse entry/exit status-line and cursor changes. Original pointer-movement dispatch confirms the numbering: **5=entry, 6=exit**. These are working hover paths, separate from the stored-but-unexecuted click modes 1–4. _Evidence: corpus; original hover 0x4035, native positive controls and [derivation](../research/issue-51-deferred-query-order.md#event-path-and-native-checkpoint)._

requirements.heading: Mouse-Field Identities - `ID=n:`
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (DEMO-01.COL, MENU.MSE, MENU.ENT); HLP._

requirements.heading: Mouse-Field Identities - `ID=n:`
requirements.text: RIPscrip 3.x lets a [mouse field](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md)'s host command begin with an identity prefix, `ID=` followed by a number and a colon:

requirements.heading: Mouse-Field Identities - `ID=n:`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1M000G7Y8ICC1000000ID=2:$-=RETURN=>NEWSPAPR.RIP$$>TWEATHER.RIP$
!|1M000GCG8GGU1000000ID=3:$>N2_HORO.RIP$
```

requirements.heading: Mouse-Field Identities - `ID=n:`
requirements.text: The prefix is not transmitted; it assigns the field a numeric identity that the pre-defined data variable `$FIELDID$` ("current mouse field ID" - RIPTEL.HLP) reports back. Combined with entry/exit queries this produces per-field behavior from a _single_ shared handler. RIPtel's main menu is the canonical example: nine fields carry `ID=1:` through `ID=9:`, the entry query plays MENU.ENT, and MENU.ENT draws a status line with:

requirements.heading: Mouse-Field Identities - `ID=n:`
requirements.text:
```text
!|@HSKA$&MSG<<FIELDID>>$
```

requirements.heading: Mouse-Field Identities - `ID=n:`

requirements.heading: Setting & Reading User Variables from Host Commands
requirements.text: If the user cancels a non-required prompt, the value `NULL` is inserted. Limits per RIPTEL.HLP: variable names up to **20 characters** (letters, digits, underscore; must start with a letter; auto-uppercased), questions and defaults up to **100 characters**, values up to **255 characters**. SyncTERM's reconstruction diverges on the name limit - its `rip_user_var` struct allows only 12 characters (`ripper.c:7774-7789`) - and RIPtel's help lists `%` where the 2.00a4 draft used `=` for the memory-table directive. The corpus shows `=` still accepted (below), so `%` and `=` are best read as synonyms for the memory directive _(hypothesis)_.

requirements.heading: The Set-Syntax: `$-=NAME=value$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (122 distinct occurrences; NEWSPAPR.RIP, MENU.DEF, TELLISTS.MSE)._

requirements.heading: The Set-Syntax: `$-=NAME=value$`
requirements.text: The single most common HCL construct in the RIPtel corpus - 122 distinct forms - is the silent assignment:

requirements.heading: The Set-Syntax: `$-=NAME=value$`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1^[0000$-=MAIN_STORY=story01.txt$|!     Filename containing main story
!|1^[0000$-=MAIN_AUTHOR=Jeff Reeder$|!    Author of main story
!|1^[0000$-=RETURN=>TELDEMOS.RET$
```

requirements.heading: The Set-Syntax: `$-=NAME=value$`
requirements.text: This is not new syntax but a _composition_ of the directive characters above: `-` (set without prompting) + `=` (memory table) + `=value` (default supplying the value). Nothing is prompted, nothing is transmitted - the variable is simply defined. MENU.DEF confirms the decomposition by writing the same two directives in the opposite order: `$=-MSG1=Visit your favorite Telnet sites$`. Whole `.DEF` files are nothing but these lines, turning scene scripts into configurable applications.

requirements.heading: The Dereference: `$&NAME$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (SHOWFONT.FN, NEWSPAPR.RIP, MENU.ENT); 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: The Dereference: `$&NAME$`
requirements.text: The `&` directive was defined in 2.0 as _transparent retrieval to the host_. The 3.x corpus shows its far more powerful role: **inline interpolation into command arguments**. A `$&NAME$` expands to the variable's value wherever it appears - including inside the argument block of drawing commands:

requirements.heading: The Dereference: `$&NAME$`
requirements.text:
```text
!|@I064$&FONT_NAME$:                    (text argument of RIP_TEXT_XY)
!|y0000010X000000001S1a000000Marin
!|@4L2L$&MAIN_TITLE$                    (headline drawn from a variable)
!|1R00000000$&MAIN_STORY$               (RIP_READ_SCENE filename from a variable)
```

requirements.heading: The Dereference: `$&NAME$`
requirements.text: Even the outline-font _name_ argument of `y` (RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE) can be `$&FONT_NAME$`. Together with the set-syntax this is the parameter-passing mechanism of the whole RIPtel demo: a scene sets variables, then calls a generic `.FN` "function" scene that dereferences them.

requirements.heading: Defining Variables from the Wire - RIP_DEFINE (`1D`)
requirements.text: _Evidence: SyncTERM (ripper.c:15899-16089, 7843-7895); HLP._

requirements.heading: Defining Variables from the Wire - RIP_DEFINE (`1D`)
requirements.text: The host can also create variables with the level-1 `D` command rather than through a host command - full entry at [RIP_DEFINE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define). SyncTERM's handler quotes what appears to be original TeleGrafix specification prose: the definition text is

requirements.heading: Defining Variables from the Wire - RIP_DEFINE (`1D`)
requirements.text:
```text
variable-identifier[,field-width]:[?question-text?][default-value]
```

requirements.heading: Defining Variables from the Wire - RIP_DEFINE (`1D`)
requirements.text: e.g. `FULL_NAME,30:?What is your full name?John Doe`, with field width defaulting to 60, and a flags word of `001` (save persistently), `002` (blank response not allowed), `004` (non-interactive). Where persistent variables are stored is up to the implementation (see [5.1 Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md)). The host may also _delete_ variables; RIPtel confirms with the prompt _"The host wants to delete the variable %s. Proceed?"_, and protected variables trigger a "Data Security Activated" message - the data-security concern the 2.x specification urged implementors to address.

requirements.heading: Launching Web URLs - `$GOTOURL(NAME)$`
requirements.text: _Evidence: corpus (TELLISTS.MSE); HLP._

requirements.heading: Launching Web URLs - `$GOTOURL(NAME)$`
requirements.text: New to the 3.x era - and pure 1997 - is web integration from a mouse field. `$GOTOURL(NAME)$` launches the URL held in user variable `NAME` in the system browser. RIPtel's Telnet Site Listings screen wires six fields this way:

requirements.heading: Launching Web URLs - `$GOTOURL(NAME)$`
requirements.text:
```text
!|1M000ZACBSE41000000ID=1:$-=WEBURL=http://duke.usask.ca/~scottp/free.html$$GOTOURL(WEBURL)$
!|1M00CDACNAE41000000ID=2:$-=WEBURL=http://library.usask.ca/hytelnet$$GOTOURL(WEBURL)$
```

requirements.heading: Launching Web URLs - `$GOTOURL(NAME)$`
requirements.text: Each click silently sets `WEBURL` with the set-syntax, then invokes the launcher - a two-step idiom that keeps `$GOTOURL$` itself generic.

requirements.heading: Things to Take Special Care With Host Commands
requirements.text: Special care must be taken when executing host commands or query commands that contain local file playback or active text variables. Either of these operations could instruct the terminal to destroy all mouse fields by performing a [RIP_RESET_WINDOWS](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_reset_windows) command (`$RESET$`), a [RIP_KILL_MOUSE_FIELDS](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_kill_mouse_fields) command (`$MKILL$`), a restore mouse fields text variable (`$RMF$`) or other such things.
requirements.reason: Immediate queries own their complete text before effects and retain it across D suspension, caller-buffer mutation/reuse, bounded yields and EOF; cancellation/destruction release it. This establishes buffer lifetime independently of reference effects. Mouse-field/button destruction, local playback and their complete host-expression orchestration remain unimplemented, so the broader host-buffer requirements are not claimed complete.

requirements.heading: Things to Take Special Care With Host Commands

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_REFRESH
requirements.text: This command sets a host command sequence in the terminal that can be sent to the host to refresh the current display screen. This refresh option would be chosen by the user to redisplay the screen in case line noise or some kind of corruption caused the screen to become distorted or corrupted. It can only be altered (or cleared) by another RIP_SET_REFRESH command or via a reset. To completely clear a refresh state, call this command with a `$OFF$` text variable as its host command or use the text variable `$NOREFRESH$`.

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_REFRESH
requirements.text: The host command portion of this sequence can contain any kind of host command information including control characters, [pick lists](5.4-popup-lists.md), text variables or many other things (but not [templates](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md)).

requirements.heading: RIP_SET_REFRESH
requirements.text: Local demo scenes have no host to refresh from - hence the command's absence from the RIPtel corpus - but the 3.0 driver's refresh machinery is well attested in HLP (`$REFRESH$`/`$NOREFRESH$` variables, "refresh expressions", the `RIP_RefreshSend` DLL export). _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: 5.1 Text Variables
requirements.text: `$NAME$` [text variables](../../glossary.md) - sequences usable in [host commands](5.0-host-commands.md), [queries](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query), button commands and keystroke macros: **data** variables substitute a value, **active** variables perform an action on the terminal. The 2.0 engine carries into 3.x intact; the 3.x inventory is known from three overlapping sources - RIPtel 3.1's help files (roughly 60 data-returning and 60 command-performing variables), the demo corpus (**269 distinct `$…$` forms** actually used in shipping scripts), and SyncTERM's **103-entry built-in table** - and where the sources disagree, the divergence is called out on the entry.

requirements.heading: 5.1 Text Variables
requirements.text: If you are implementing a client terminal and do not intend on supporting 100% of all pre-defined text variables, you SHOULD at least recognize them and do nothing - so that an unsupported sound variable, for example, is ignored instead of popping up a dialog asking the user to enter data for `$MUSIC$`. _(v1.54)_ Many of the text variables like `$PCB$` are very important to GUI design and should be implemented; if you omit any, do not omit the active text variables - they are critical to implementing a full GUI system using RIPscrip 2.0. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Text Variables
requirements.text: A special feature of RIPscrip allows it to understand what a Text Variable is. A text variable is a piece of text that both RIPaint and RIPterm know something about. For example, the Text Variable `$DATE$` is known to represent the current Date on your PC. The host may ask your system what the values of one or more of these variables are, and if your terminal knows these particular Text Variables, it will tell the host.

requirements.heading: Variable Resolution in 3.x
requirements.text: The shipped RIPtel 3.1 driver registers 179 built-in callbacks. It handles special directives and then looks up permitted built-ins case-insensitively; a missing name can enter the user-variable engine when the caller permits it. A known built-in rejected for invalid arguments does not fall back to a user variable of the same name. The user-variable path can prompt or retrieve stored data according to its directives; SyncTERM’s unconditional empty-string fallback for unknown names is not the shipped driver’s universal rule. [`$P$`](#p) illustrates the distinction: it has no paste built-in and follows the user-variable path.

requirements.heading: Variable Resolution in 3.x
requirements.text: The caller controls which callback classes and user-variable operations are allowed. Ordinary graphic text permits data callbacks and user variables; the recovered [`RIP_TEXT_METRIC`](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_text_metric) ordinary pass permits data callbacks but does not enable user-variable fallback. Its preceding angle preprocessor can still dereference a user name through `<<NAME>>`. Stateful getter/setter callbacks such as HOSTDIR retain their own argument-dependent actions. These are fixed consumer behaviors, not a wire-level option mask. The [processing-order contract](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md#shipped-processing-order) distinguishes preprocessing, ordinary text and host commands.

requirements.heading: Variable Resolution in 3.x
requirements.text: Empty parentheses supply zero arguments. Empty comma fields are omitted: `$RAND(9,,2)$` is the two-argument form `$RAND(9,2)$`, not a third-argument minimum with an omitted width. Unquoted argument text preserves spaces for the handler to normalize; a quoted empty argument such as `$HOSTDIR("")$` is rejected by the parser. The parser permits at most 40 nonempty arguments, each at most 20 bytes, in its fixed argument slots. Apply these rules before counting required/optional arguments in the recovered entries below.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Creation and Query
requirements.text: As previously mentioned, Text Variables were described as either pre-defined variables, or as User Variables. Pre-defined variables are variables that RIPscrip products know things about "out of the box". They will always know what the variables mean, from the day you install the software. User Variables are variables that the user of RIPscrip products defines, and teaches the software new things it doesn't already know.

requirements.heading: Pre-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: A pre-defined text variable is either a data text variable, or an active text variable. A data text variable is a text variable that inserts a piece of text wherever the text variable is used. For example, the sequence `$DATE$` might get replaced with 09/19/94. This is a simple example of a data text variable. An active text variable on the other hand does something (usually). They normally don't get replaced with other text information. For example, the text variable `$SAVE$` saves the contents of the screen to a disk file that can later be restored with `$RESTORE$`. In these situations, active text variables are removed from whatever text message they are present in (they are still activated though).

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: A User Variable is a Text Variable that RIPscrip doesn't know exists. They are custom-defined text variables that contain information that the terminal user will fill in. If a variable already contains information, a host will be automatically told (if told to do so) what that variable contains without the user having to intervene (i.e., transparent information exchange).

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: Examples of Text Variables might be:

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: | Variable         | Question                            |

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: | `$FULL_NAME$`    | What is your full name?             |

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: | `$COMPANY_NAME$` | What company do you work for?       |

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: | `$AGE$`          | How old are you?                    |

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: | `$DATEOFBIRTH$`  | What is your Date of Birth?         |

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: | `$PHONENUMBER$`  | What is your Day-time phone number? |

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: User Variables will "keep track" of these responses for you, in the terminal program database. You can tell the terminal to store these values permanently, or they may be active only during the current session, or they may be defined as temporary where they are not stored for more than a brief moment.

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: > **NOTE:** This ability is configurable so that information exchange can be either interactive, or automatic. Automatic transfer of information does NOT prompt the user with the information unless the variable has not yet been defined. If it has not been defined, a pop-up question will appear asking the user a particular question, thus defining the text variable.

requirements.heading: What Are User Variables?
requirements.text: If the exchange is interactive, the data is displayed in a pop-up editor box, asking you if the information is correct. If it is, press ENTER and the retrieved information is sent to the host for you. If it is not correct, or it has not been created yet, just type it in and press ENTER and it will be saved automatically, and sent to the host all at once.

requirements.heading: How Can User Variables Be Important?
requirements.text: Lets take an example. You are the system operator of a large RIPscrip host. As you have read, RIPscrip can take advantage of database-like ability on the terminal end. If you can alter your host to ask questions with RIPscrip Text Variables built in, you can have the terminal calling your host automatically fill in questionnaires. Imagine if a user could sign-up on your host without having to type more than a single keystroke (i.e., "YES, this information is correct"). With User Text Variables, you can do this very thing.

requirements.heading: Creating User Variables
requirements.text: There are two ways of defining User Text Variables in RIPscrip. You can use either the [Define Text Variable command](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define), or you can use Text Variable Queries, as described in the next section.

requirements.heading: Defining Text Variables
requirements.text: The RIPscrip command Define Text Variable is by definition, an interactive command with the user. The RIPscrip command will attempt to define a User Variable. This variable is some piece of information that the system operator deems important. You may specify a question, a default response, and how many characters long the response may be.

requirements.heading: Defining Text Variables
requirements.text: Once the terminal has received a define command, the terminal pops up an appropriate question box on the user's screen, asking him the desired question that should be saved to a particular Text Variable. If you did not specify a question, a default question is used (i.e., "Enter <name of text variable>").

requirements.heading: Defining Text Variables
requirements.text: Once the user has entered his response, it is recorded and saved. How long it is stored depends on what the host told the terminal. The host can tell the terminal "save this on your hard disk forever". The host may also tell the terminal "don't save this to disk, but remember this value until you exit RIPterm". You also have the option of saying "don't remember this value at all, just pop up a question, and send the value to me NOW" - i.e., don't save it at all, just enter it and send it to the host).

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE in 3.x
requirements.text: The wire command [RIP_DEFINE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define) (`!|1D`) creates a variable. SyncTERM's handler quotes what appears to be original TeleGrafix specification prose in its comments, giving the definition-text grammar:

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE in 3.x
requirements.text:
```text
variable-identifier[,field-width]:[?question-text?][default-value]
```

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE in 3.x
requirements.text: Example (from the in-source spec quote): `FULL_NAME,30:?What is your full name?John Doe`. Field width defaults to 60 when omitted. The command's numeric flags are `001` save to the [persistent variable store](../../glossary.md), `002` a blank response is not allowed, `004` non-interactive query. When a definition is interactive - or a non-interactive one finds no stored value - the terminal raises an input dialog honoring the field width and no-blank flag.

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE in 3.x
requirements.text: _Evidence: SyncTERM (ripper.c:15899-16089) handler with spec-quoted comments; SyncTERM (ripper.c:7843-7895) `parse_define_text`; SyncTERM (ripper.c:15924-15928) flags; SyncTERM (ripper.c:11325-11354) input dialog._

requirements.heading: Querying Text Variables
requirements.text: Now that you know how to define information on the terminal, you need to know the last method of asking the terminal about text variables. This feature is called "Data Query". Data Query is a generic query command that can ask the terminal one or more questions, and tell it how to transmit the information back to the host. This command is for use in non-button situations where you do not want to wait until the user clicks on a button to get your data back.

requirements.heading: Querying Text Variables
requirements.text: [Data Query](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query) is a special RIPscrip command that can be used to ask the contents of one or more Text Variables.

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text: Lets take a simple example. You wanted to ask the terminal program some address information. You could do this with the following query (remember, the query also tells the terminal HOW to send the data back to the host):

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text:
```text
$FULL_NAME$^m$COMPANY$^m$ST_ADDR$^m$CITY$, $STATE$ $ZIP^m
```

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text: This would query the terminal the contents of 6 text variables, and format them in a manner similar to any normal address on an envelope. The results of this query might send the following back to the host :

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text:
```text
Joe Sixpack
ACME Corporation
13631 Palindrome Parkway
Surf City, CA 92649
```

requirements.heading: Examples of Text Variable Query
requirements.text: If a text variable is queried, and it has not been defined yet, a pop-up question will appear asking the user to fill in the information.

requirements.heading: Defining Permanent Variables
requirements.text: Under normal situations you reference text variables by simply placing dollar signs (`$`) around the variable name. Anywhere where that text variable occurs in a Host Command, Query, or other related place that can contain text variables will have its contents replaced with the associated information. A RIPscrip command exists in the specification to define text variables for permanent storage. Since this is an actual RIPscrip command, it is not well suited for using in a Host Command directly. In fact, you couldn't use that in the Host Command's return string definition.

requirements.heading: Defining Permanent Variables
requirements.text: If you reference a Text Variable in a Host Command that hasn't been defined yet (eg, `$FIRST_NAME$`), then the user will be presented with a pop-up dialog box asking them to:

requirements.heading: Defining Permanent Variables
requirements.text:
```text
Please enter FIRST_NAME:
```

requirements.heading: Defining Permanent Variables
requirements.text: When the user enters some information, this data is inserted where the `$FIRST_NAME$` variable was located, and the contents of that variable are lost after that moment. What is truly needed is an ability to preserve that information (either on Disk, or in memory) so that it can be used later on. To accomplish this, we will form some variations on the text variable syntax.

requirements.text: There are six basically different text variable references, each of them take a single command character added between the first dollar sign and the beginning of the variable name. Those characters and their significance is:

requirements.heading: Directive Characters in 3.x
requirements.text:
- `*` ... An answer is required
- `+` ... Save variable to database permanently
- `=` ... Save to internal memory table (lost when RIPterm hangs up)
- `#` ... Do not echo keystrokes (show #'s instead). This is useful for things like entering passwords.
- `-` ... Used in conjunction with a default response (see below). When this option is used, the value of the variable is set to the default value and the user is not prompted for any data entry (transparent data variable define). Nothing is returned to the host in this mode (unless transparent retrieval mode is used - see below). _(v2.A1)_
- `&` ... Transparent data variable retrieval. This allows the host to retrieve a text variable from the terminal and the user is not prompted to modify the information. _(v2.A1)_
