requirements.heading: User Defined Variables and Data Security
requirements.text: When working with user-defined text variables, a topic arises which may or may not be addressed by the RIPscrip software developer: security! What if you had credit card information stored in a permanent text variable named `$CredCardNo$` and the host system asked your terminal for that information? Obviously the user should be informed about this request. Situations might arise where security is not a concern - like in a closed environment like an internal office system using RIPscrip. With these situations in mind, the designer of a RIPscrip terminal might wish to include some kind of "data security" feature into the software package.
requirements.reason: Historical/evidence/navigation, table heading or optional security discussion; shipping 3.x executable behavior is tracked in the corresponding individual requirements. Legacy SyncTERM divergences are not the v3 contract.

requirements.heading: User Defined Variables and Data Security
requirements.text: Data security can be in many forms. You could implement complete "tight" security which would overide all transparent forms of text variable operations - in effect, always making the user approve the request. A lighter security might be desirable - one where any action working on permanent database text variables requires the user's approval, but memory variables don't have to be approved. This kind of a situation would let allow a host system to have control over memory variables (which it presumably created anyway), but let access to permanent variables be under strict control. The exact form of data security that you offer your software's users is unimportant - but knowing that security is a concern is. You do not have to implement data security on your system - it is not an actual part of RIPscrip (per se), but it could be useful to your customers if security is an issue.

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: Below are some examples of user defined text variables as might be used in a real world situation:

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text:
```text
$*+20,50:NAME(ToName),30@What's your name?=John Doe$
```

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: _(example as of v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: This is about as complex as they get. Going from left to right, lets look at what all the codes mean. First, the "\*" means that a response to this request is required (they cannot hit ESC or CANCEL to get out of it). The "+" means to save the response to the internal database permanently. The sequence "20,50:" means to place the dialog box's upper left corner at location (20,50) on the screen. The "NAME" is the name of the data variable. The format option "(Name)" means that this should be a formatted name field where the first letter of any word should be capitolized and the remaining characters should be set to lower case. The value ",30" after the variable name/format indicates that this field is up to 30 characters in length. "@What's your name?" indicates that the question "What's your name?" should be displayed when the user is prompted for the information. Finally, the "=John Doe" indicates that if the field doesn't exist, it should be filled in with "John Doe" before any editing is allowed. This gives the user the ability to choose a default name if they wish.

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text:
```text
$*#20,10:PASSWORD,10@Please enter your password$
```

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: This example is a required data variable that echos #'s in place of the keystrokes you entered. The field is placed at (20,10) on the screen with a variable name of PASSWORD. The field is 10 characters wide and the prompt is "Please enter your password".

requirements.heading: Examples of User-Defined Text Variables
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP - both examples above appear verbatim in the RIPtel help file._

requirements.heading: Persistence
requirements.text: Variables defined with the `+` directive (or [RIP_DEFINE](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_define) flag `001`) are saved to a client-side persistent store and survive across sessions. Functionally this is nothing more than a **persistent key/value store** - variable name (≤ 20 characters) → string value (≤ 255 characters) - and that is all an implementation needs to provide. **How** it is stored is an implementation detail, not part of the protocol - RIPtel used a local database file, SyncTERM mirrors the behavior with `save_persistent_var`/`load_persistent_vars`, reloading persistent variables during interpreter startup; a new implementation may use any key/value-capable storage it likes so long as persistent variables survive across sessions and honor host deletion/protection semantics.
requirements.reason: The key/value backend, owned snapshots/import and optional atomic client file adapter are implemented. Separate writer/reader processes verify disk persistence, including byte lengths, replacement and deletion; malformed loads preserve live tables. Directive selection, host approval/deletion protection, session lifetimes and interpreter startup/wire integration remain pending.

requirements.heading: Silent Set & Dereference
requirements.text: The user-variable system is 3.x's client-side data store in action: the host defines named variables, the terminal prompts the user (or not), and later `$NAME$` references expand to the stored value - including as arguments _inside RIPscrip commands_ (the demo corpus passes `$&FONT_NAME$` as a font name and `$&MAIN_STORY$` as a filename).

requirements.heading: Silent Set & Dereference
requirements.text:
- **`$-=NAME=value$`** assigns a value without prompting. This is the workhorse of the demo corpus - 122 distinct set-forms observed, wiring menu state: `$-=RETURN=>NEWSPAPR.RIP$`, `$-=WEBURL=http://…$`, `$-=TITLE=Telnet Site Listings$`.
- **`$&NAME$`** expands the stored value without any prompt, usable inline in command arguments: `$&FONT_NAME$` as the font-name field of an extended-font-style command, `$&MAIN_STORY$` as a read-scene filename, even computed names via macro expansion (`$&MSG<<FIELDID>>$`).

requirements.heading: Silent Set & Dereference
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP (`-` and `&` directives); corpus (TELLISTS.MSE, SHOWFONT.FN, NEWSPAPR.RIP)._

requirements.heading: Template-Slot Dereference (`$?N$`)
requirements.text: `$?N$` - where `N` is one of the 36 slot characters `0`-`9`/`A`-`Z` - expands to the stored [template](5.2-templates-and-conditionals.md) text for that slot. _(SyncTERM (ripper.c:11918-11923))_

requirements.heading: Host Deletion and Data Queries in 3.x
requirements.text: The host may delete a variable; RIPtel asks the user to confirm ("The host wants to delete the variable %s. Proceed?"). A _data query_ is simply a host-sent template of variable references - e.g. `$FULL_NAME$^m$ST_ADDR$^m$CITY$, $STATE$ $ZIP$^m` - which the terminal returns filled in; protected variables trigger a "Data Security Activated" notice (see [User Defined Variables and Data Security](#user-defined-variables-and-data-security) above). _(HLP)_

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Each text variable's description details the exact syntax of that variable. The syntax is described in concise detail so that you can easily spot at the glance of an eye exactly what parameters are allowed, and if omitted, what the default values are for those parameters. You can also determine what text variables have optional parameters, and what parameters are required.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: There are two basic text variables - those that take parameters, and those that don't. Those that don't use any parameters are the simplest of all to describe syntactically. If a text variable does not require any parameters, then its syntax description would be nearly identical to the following:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR$
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: This simply states that in order use this text variable in an expression, you insert the text `$TEXTVAR$` in your host command.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: For text variables that require parameters though, more detailed descriptions are necessary. Here is an example listing of a text variable requiring one parameter and having an optional second parameter:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: You should notice the text "req:" and "opt:". The "req:PARAM1" text indicates that the parameter named "PARAM1" is required. The second piece of text is "opt:PARAM2", which means that the parameter named "PARAM2" is optional.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: But what values can PARAM1 or PARAM2 be? It's not mentioned at all what values they can obtain. This is where the parameter value notation comes in. Suppose that PARAM1 can be set to "TRUE" or "FALSE", and that PARAM2 can be set to "BLUE" and "RED". To describe these values our new syntax description would be:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: From the above description, it is quite simple to determine what parameters are required, which ones are optional, and which ones can be set to what values. Now, let's add a new color to PARAM2, called "GREEN", and let's say that it can only be used as PARAM2 when PARAM1 is equal to "TRUE". We denote this like the following:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                                  GREEN:PARAM1=TRUE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Notice the "GREEN:PARAM1=TRUE". This means that PARAM2 can be set to "GREEN" only if PARAM1 is equal to TRUE. What if we added another value to PARAM1 that could also be green, called "MAYBE". Then our example would look like this:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN:PARAM1=TRUE,MAYBE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Now the description of GREEN has "PARAM1=TRUE,MAYBE". This means that PARAM2 can be set to "GREEN" only if PARAM1 is equal to TRUE or MAYBE. Pretty simple. This same situation could be written more shortly (in this case) with the "not equal" expression <> as in the following:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN:PARAM1<>FALSE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: This means that PARAM2 can be set to GREEN only if PARAM1 is not equal to FALSE. If PARAM2 could only be set to GREEN if PARAM1 was equal to TRUE, we could list this (using a previously described notation):

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN:PARAM1<>FALSE,MAYBE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Optional parameters do not need to be specified. If they are not, then some "suitable" default value will be used for that parameter. Let's take a variation of our previous example:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN
                                  ──────
                              def=BLUE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: This says that if PARAM2 is omitted, that BLUE will be the default. What if BLUE is only the default when PARAM1 is set to TRUE, and RED is default all the other times? Then you would have the following syntax description:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, opt:PARAM2)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN
                                  ──────
                              def=BLUE:PARAM1=TRUE
                                  RED:PARAM1<>TRUE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Lastly, a number of text variables have a variable number of parameters. This means that one of the parameters can be repeated more than once, but it must be specified at least once. This is represented in the actual text variable "short description" with an ellipse "..." shown in the parameter list like the following:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
$TEXTVAR(param1,param2,...)$ - Perform some kind of operation
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: In the syntax description, it is also shown as an ellipse "...". The parameter immediately preceding the ellipse is the one that is repeated and all subsequent instances of that parameter use the same syntax as the first one repeated. Here is an example if we allowed PARAM2 to be repeated multiple times:

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text:
```text
Syntax:  $TEXTVAR(req:PARAM1, req:PARAM2, ...)$
                      ──────      ──────
                      TRUE        BLUE
                      FALSE       RED
                      MAYBE       GREEN
                                  ──────
                              def:BLUE
```

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: Notice how PARAM2 is set to "req:". This means that PARAM2 must be specified at least once, but can be repeated. It is also possible that the repeated parameter itself may be optional (eg, "opt:"). If this is the case then there can be zero or more occurrences of that parameter.

requirements.heading: Text Variable Syntax Descriptions
requirements.text: If no specific default value is allowed for an omitted parameter (ie, it has special significance if it is omitted), then the default value would be listed as "\<none\>".

requirements.heading: Version Number and Vendor Text Variables
requirements.text: These text variables are for version number, vendor determination, and software features of a RIPscrip package. These are used heavily for "detecting" what kind of RIPscrip software a host is connected with. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Version Number and Vendor Text Variables
requirements.text: 3.x adds the bookmark-identity variables [`$USERNAME$`](#username) and [`$PASSWORD$`](#password) and the random-value variable [`$RAND$`](#rand). _Evidence: HLP (RIPTEL.HLP text-variable chapter; RIPSCRIP.HLP tvarProc string table); 2.00a4; SyncTERM (ripper.c:8055)._

requirements.heading: $IFS$
requirements.text: Because the number of features supported by a software package can get quite extensive, they are categorized for the purposes of this command. This allows the host to be able to query particular sub-sets of information (eg, what file transfer protocols are supported, etc). These categories are simple keyword names just like the keyword names used to identify particular features, but with one slight difference. Categories begin with an underscore character (_) to differentiate them from actual feature keywords. These categories are used in conjunction with a special `$IFS$` directive called LIST. This will list out all keywords for a specific category, or if no category is specified, it will list out all categories. The basic categories and their corresponding sub-items are as follows: _(v2.A4)\_

requirements.heading: $NULL$
requirements.text: This text variable is a special variable. It always returns nothing to the host system. It doesn't prompt the user or any information and it doesn't set anything. It is intended to be a place-holder for commands that require a text parameter ([RIP_MOUSE](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_mouse), [RIP_BUTTON](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) and [RIP_QUERY](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md#rip_query)). When you have this text variable all by itself in a host command, it makes the host command do absolutely nothing, but has something defined for the host command to satisfy the RIPscrip interpreter (which expects something to be defined in host command text parameters).

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: _Return a random decimal value, with optional zero padding_

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$RAND(maximum[,length[,minimum]])$`

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: One to three nonempty decimal-digit arguments are required after empty fields have been omitted. For ordinary range-valid inputs, maximum is 1..32767, length is 0..5 (default 0), and minimum is 0..maximum-1 (default 0). Bare `$RAND$` and `$RAND()$` reject; the former help-only syntax did not describe an executable zero-argument query.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: The handler obtains a random integer `r` in 0..32767 and computes:

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text:
```text
minimum + ((maximum - minimum + 1) * r) / 32767
```

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: For normal inputs division truncates toward zero. The decimal result is left-padded with zeroes to at least `length` characters and is never truncated to that width. **Shipped endpoint defect:** `r=32767` returns maximum+1. For `$RAND(9,3,2)$`, normal results are `002` through `009`, with `010` possible at that endpoint. Hosts must not assume the declared maximum is an absolute upper bound in this client.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: For exact driver compatibility, decimal conversion wraps modulo 2^32. The converted maximum must be 1..32767; length is checked with signed `<=5`, and minimum with signed `<maximum`, so oversized positive tokens can wrap into accepted values. Checked examples: maximum `4294967297` becomes 1; length `4294967295` becomes -1 and causes no padding; minimum `4294967295` becomes -1 and returns `-1` when r=0. Arithmetic follows the original 32-bit operations. These quirks do not add a signed-token syntax: a literal minus is not accepted by this handler’s digit validator.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: The original CRT generator updates `state = state*214013 + 2531011` modulo 2^32 and returns `(state >> 16) & 32767`. This identifies the shipped generator; no portable initial seed or cross-session sequence is promised by the variable grammar.

requirements.heading: $RAND$
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL, callback RVA `0x28e96–0x2902f`, generator `0x68fc0`; [derivation and native range/parser oracles](../research/issue-6-macro-evaluation.md)._

requirements.heading: $RIPVER$
requirements.text: _Return the RIPscrip identification phrase_

requirements.heading: $RIPVER$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$RIPVER$` or `$RIPVER()$`

requirements.heading: $RIPVER$
requirements.text: The shipped driver returns **`RIPSCRIP030001`**, exactly 14 ASCII bytes with no CR/LF. It accepts no arguments; extra arguments reject. Autosense default/0 and RIPVER share the same literal, not separate short and long versions. A containing host command can add its own control characters after expansion.

requirements.heading: $RIPVER$
requirements.text: The format is `RIPSCRIPxxyyvs`: major 03, minor 00, generic vendor 0, vendor subversion 1. Vendor codes are 0 generic/unspecified, 1 RIPterm/TeleGrafix and 2 Qmodem Pro. This is a language/identity phrase, not product version RIPtel 3.1 or driver build 3.0.7. The [version reference](9.2-versions.md) supplies exact autosense terminators and permits the generic profile `RIPSCRIP030000` for a new compatible implementation.

requirements.heading: $RIPVER$
requirements.text: The HLP example `RIPSCRIP015300` is stale documentation, and its FAQ’s `RIPSCRIP03000` quote is incomplete; neither overrides the original producer. SyncTERM independently emits the same 14-byte 3.0 phrase.

requirements.heading: $DATETIME$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$DATETIME$` **Syntax:** `$DATETIME$`
requirements.reason: PR #71 documentation answers are adopted at a9e0c2f490714d82a0827675ffbc074aa5ae00e6; implementation and independent expectations must now be reconciled. Previous blocker review: Reported in #18: YEAR Syntax incorrectly names DOY; DATETIME has an inconsistent weekday/date example and does not establish single-digit day padding or trailing newline. DATETIME remains recognized/unsupported without propagating an error; YEAR uses its explicit canonical name and two-digit meaning.

requirements.heading: $DATETIME$
requirements.text: Returns the current **local** date and time as exactly **17 ASCII characters**, `MM/DD/YY HH:MM:SS`. All six fields contain exactly two decimal digits with leading zeroes: month 01–12, day 01–31, year 00–99, hour 00–23, minute 00–59 and second 00–59. Separators are literal `/`, one ASCII space between date and time, and `:`. There is no weekday, month name or four-digit year, and **no trailing newline or carriage return**. The driver's C-string NUL terminates storage; it is not part of the expanded value. No arguments are accepted.

requirements.heading: $DATETIME$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$DATETIME$` **Returns:** `12/05/93 14:38:50` for Sunday December 5, 1993 at 14:38:50 local time. December 19 at the same time returns `12/19/93 14:38:50`.

requirements.heading: $DATETIME$
requirements.text: > **Correction to the inherited description:** RIPtel 3.1's original driver formats `%c` using its built-in numeric date/time templates. It does not return Unix/asctime-style text; none of `Sun Dec  5 …`, `Sun Dec 05 …` or `Sun Dec 5 …` matches its output. The inherited `Sat Dec 19 14:38:50 1993` example also had the wrong weekday (that date was Sunday). Merely correcting Sat to Sun would still give the wrong output format. For this variable, Monday is considered to be the first day of the week.

requirements.heading: $M$
requirements.text: _Mouse Button Status: LMR_

requirements.heading: $M$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$M$` **Syntax:** `$M$`

requirements.heading: $M$
requirements.text: This Text Variable returns a 3-character code representing the status of each mouse button. This variable works with two button and three button mice. The format of the code is LMR where L=Left, M=Middle (if any), and R=Right. If any button is clicked, the code for that button is "1". If the button is not depressed, it is "0". "100" would mean the left mouse button is depressed, but none of the others are.

requirements.heading: $M$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$M$` **Returns:** `001`

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: _Set the mouse cursor style number_

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$MCURSOR(cursor_no)$`

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: **Syntax:**

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text:
```text
$MCURSOR(opt:CURSOR_NO)$
             ─────────
             0-6
             ─────────
         def=0
```

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: This command changes the current mouse cursor style to one of the pre-defined mouse cursor styles as defined in the [RIP_SET_MOUSE_CURSOR](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_set_mouse_cursor) command. The cursor_no parameter is identical to the cursor style numbers permitted for the RIPscrip command to alter the cursor. If you omit the CURSOR_NO parameter, the default "pointer" cursor is activated.

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: **RIPtel 3.1 ownership/protection:** this changes the current environment's mouse number and refreshes its presentation; it changes no graphics-style record. The variable accepts 0..7 (or no argument for zero) and bypasses environment protection. The corresponding wire command checks environment protection; protecting a graphics style does not block either path. _Evidence: [original setter and native matrix](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#ownership-and-switching-observations)._

requirements.heading: $MCURSOR$
requirements.text: The demo scripts switch cursors on field entry/exit - `$MCURSOR(4)$` busy, `$MCURSOR(6)$` hand, `$MCURSOR(0)$` arrow. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP (`tvarProcMCURSOR`); corpus (DEMO-01.COL, MENU.FN)._

requirements.heading: $X$
requirements.text: _X Mouse location_

requirements.heading: $X$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$X(domain)$`

requirements.heading: $X$
requirements.text: **Syntax:**

requirements.heading: $X$
requirements.text:
```text
$X(opt:DOMAIN)$
       ──────
       WORLD
       DEVICE
       ──────
   def=WORLD (except under "text mode query - see below)
```

requirements.heading: $X$
requirements.text: This Text Variable returns the current X coordinate of the mouse pointer. This can be used interactively (for example, by on-line games) to determine the location of the mouse pointer. Only the X value of the mouse (X,Y) is returned. The value is 0000-9999 depending on what the current position is.

requirements.heading: $X$
requirements.text: If this text variable is used inside a "text window query", then the X coordinate is returned in text cell coordinates based on the internal dimensions of the text window. This kind of result cannot happen unless the user clicks inside a text window's display area that has a text window query command in it, so there's no possibility for the coordinate to be out of bounds for that text window's dimensions. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $X$
requirements.text: The results are in current world coordinates if no parameter is specified. If TYPE is "DEVICE" then the result is in raw video device coordinates. If TYPE is "WORLD" then the result is in desktop world coordinates. If the domain parameter is specified when this text variable is used in a text mode query, then it is explicitly overiding the "text coordinate" defaults of this command and returning the mouse coordinate information in the desired coordinate system. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $X$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$X(WORLD)$` - equivalent to `$X$` **Returns:** `0523`

requirements.heading: $XY$
requirements.text: _Return the captured mouse position in world, device or text-cell coordinates_

requirements.heading: $XY$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$XY([domain])$` **Domain:** WORLD or DEVICE, case-insensitive; at most one argument.

requirements.heading: $XY$
requirements.text: Outside a text-window query, omission means WORLD. WORLD converts the captured device coordinates using the current world/device dimensions, with integer truncation; DEVICE returns the captured device coordinates directly. Both return zero-padded **decimal** `XXXX:YYYY` using signed 16-bit values and a minimum width of four, independently of Base Math. With captured position (297,321), DEVICE returns `0297:0321`; with world/device ratios of 2, WORLD returns `0594:0642`.

requirements.heading: $XY$
requirements.text: Inside a text-window query, omission instead returns cell coordinates for the query’s text window as decimal `XX:YY`, minimum width two. The original cell helpers clamp positions to the window’s bounds. Explicit WORLD or DEVICE overrides this cell-coordinate default. For (297,321) in an 80×25 window with 8×16 cells at origin, bare XY returns `37:20`. The format widths are minimum padding, not universal 99/9999 limits. Other domains or extra arguments reject.

requirements.heading: $XY$
requirements.text: SyncTERM’s hexadecimal readback differs from the shipped RIPtel driver; the decimal-versus-hexadecimal question is resolved by the original `%04hd:%04hd` and `%02hd:%02hd` formats and native oracles.

requirements.heading: $XY$
requirements.text: _Evidence: DLL, callback RVA `0x34c36–0x34d2c`, cell helpers `0xe2e9`/`0xe34d`; [derivation](../research/issue-6-macro-evaluation.md)._

requirements.text: _X, Y & button status_

requirements.heading: $XYM$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$XYM(domain)$`

requirements.heading: $XYM$
requirements.text: **Syntax:**

requirements.heading: $XYM$
requirements.text:
```text
$XYM(opt:DOMAIN)$
         ──────
         WORLD
         DEVICE
         ──────
     def=WORLD (except under text mode query - see below)
```

requirements.heading: $XYM$
requirements.text: This Text Variable returns the X and Y coordinates of the mouse pointer, and which mouse buttons are pressed (if any). A colon (:) separates the three values. The X and Y values may range from 0000-9999. LMR stands for Left/Middle/Right. If any of these buttons are depressed (clicked), then the corresponding position will contain a 1. If a button is NOT depressed, then it will contain a 0. The format that this value uses is: XXXX:YYYY:LMR

requirements.heading: $XYM$
requirements.text: If this text variable is used inside a "text window query", then the X/Y coordinates are returned in text cell coordinates based on the internal dimensions of the text window. This kind of result cannot happen unless the user clicks inside a text window's display area that has a text window query command in it, so there's no possibility for the coordinate to be out of bounds for that text window's dimensions. The format that the coordinates are returned in is XX:YY:LMR where XX and YY can range from 00-99. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $XYM$
requirements.text: This means that the (X,Y) location of the cursor is (0123,0297), and that the Left and Middle buttons are depressed, but that the Right Mouse Button is not depressed.

requirements.heading: $XYM$
requirements.text: The results are in current world coordinates if no parameter is specified. If TYPE is "DEVICE" then the results are in raw video device coordinates. If TYPE is "WORLD" then the results are in desktop world coordinates. If the domain parameter is specified when this text variable is used in a text mode query, then it is explicitly overiding the "text coordinate" defaults of this command and returning the mouse coordinate information in the desired coordinate system. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $XYM$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$XYM(WORLD)$` - Equivalent to `$XYM$` **Returns:** `0123:0297:110`

requirements.heading: Text Window Related Text Variables
requirements.text: The window-introspection group (`$TWX0$`/`$TWY0$`/`$TWX1$`/`$TWY1$`/`$TWW$`/`$TWH$`/`$TWIN$`/`$TWFONT$`) is confirmed for 3.x by SyncTERM's `rv_termstat` handler group; `$CURX$`/`$CURY$`/`$CURSOR$`/`$ISEXTWIN$` rest on the spec and help files, the management variables (`$ATW$`, `$MTW$`, `$TWGOTO$`, `$TWHOME$`, `$TWERASEEOL$`) are attested by the RIPTEL.HLP command-variable table, and the erase pair `$ETW$`/`$EGW$` by SyncTERM's `rv_erase`. The parameter grammar (window, type `BOUND`/`TEXT`/`CELL`, domain `WORLD`/`DEVICE`/`COLS`/`ROWS`) carries into 3.x unchanged as far as the evidence shows. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; SyncTERM (ripper.c:8734 `rv_termstat`; 8696 `rv_erase`)._

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: _Activates a text window definition_

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$ATW(window1,window2,...)$`

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: **Syntax:**

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text:
```text
$ATW(opt:WINDOW1, ...)$
         ───────
         ALL
         CUR
         0-35
         ───────
     def=CUR
```

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: This command does the exact opposite of the [`$DTW$`](#dtw) text variable which deactivates a text window. When a window is activated, it no longer discards raw ANSI text that is sent to it. This does not make any visual changes on the screen immediately unless the current text window is the one activated, whereby the cursor might appear all of a sudden.

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: You may specify one or more parameters to indicate that you wish to activate more than one text window in the same `$ATW$` statement. If any one of them fails to match the proper parameters, then the entire command is considered a syntax error and none of the parameters are processed.

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: If the text window being activated is protected, then it is not changed (ie, activated).

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: You may activate more then one window by specifying multiple text window slot numbers (0-35). You may also specify the following:

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: | Keyword | Description                           |

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: | `ALL`   | Activate all text windows at once     |

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: | `CUR`   | Activate only the current text window |

requirements.heading: $ATW$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$ATW(CUR)$` **Returns:** nothing

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: _Disable the Text Cursor_

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$COFF(window1,window2,...)$`

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: **Syntax:**

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text:
```text
$COFF(opt:WINDOW1, ...)$
          ───────
          ALL
          CUR
          0-35
          ───────
      def=CUR
```

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: This Active Text Variable turns off the text cursor in the specified text window(s). If that text window(s) is undefined or disabled, this this command does nothing for that parameter. If the window parameters are omitted, then the cursor in the current text window is displayed. If the window parameter(s) are specified, then they can be a value from 0-35 to indicate a specific text window data table entry, the value "CUR" to indicate the current text window, or the value of "ALL" to indicate that you wish to turn off the cursor in all text windows simultaneously. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: If you attempt to turn off a cursor in a text window that isn't defined, or that is deactivated, then that parameter does nothing. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: If any one of the parameters is invalid, then the entire command is considered a syntax error and none of the parameters are processed. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: If you turn off the cursor in a text window other than the current text window, then only the internal cursor status of that text window is altered. Since the cursor wouldn't be visible in that text window anyway, you wouldn't expect anything to visually happen on the screen. If you switch to that text window though, the cursor would not be displayed upon switching to it (normally it would). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$COFF$` **Returns:** nothing

requirements.heading: $COFF$
requirements.text: `$COFF$$DTW$` is the standard demo-scene prologue. _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP; SyncTERM (ripper.c:8801 group); corpus (BLUEBACK.FN)._

requirements.heading: $CON$

requirements.heading: $CON$
requirements.text: **Format:** `$CON(window1,window2,...)$`

requirements.text: **Syntax:**

requirements.heading: $CON$

```text
$CON(opt:WINDOW1, ...)$
         ───────
         ALL
         CUR
         0-35
         ───────
     def=CUR
```

requirements.heading: $CON$
requirements.text: This Active Text Variable turns on the text cursor in the specified text window(s). If that text window is undefined or deactivated, this command does nothing. If the window parameter(s) are omitted, then the cursor in the current text window is displayed. If the window parameter is specified, then it can be a value from 0-35 to indicate a specific text window data table entry, the value "CUR" to indicate the current text window, or the value "ALL" to indicate all defined text windows (ie, in use). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $CON$
requirements.text: If you attempt to turn on a cursor in a text window that isn't defined, or that is deactivated, then that parameter does nothing. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $CON$
requirements.text: If any one of the parameters is invalid, then the entire command is considered a syntax error and none of the parameters are processed. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $CON$
requirements.text: If you turn on the cursor in a text window other than the current text window, then only the internal cursor status of that text window is altered - it will not be turned on until you switch to that text window. In this respect, only altering the current text window's cursor will actually make any immediate visible effect on the screen. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $CON$
requirements.text: **Example:** `$CON$` **Returns:** nothing

If you specify the window number parameter, then you can specify a value from 0-35 to indicate a specific text window data table entry, or a value of "CUR" to indicate the current text window. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: $CURX$
requirements.text: This Text Variable returns the X coordinate of the text cursor in the specified text window, relative to the upper left of the Text Window. The location is "one based", so the first column of data is a value of "1", not "0". Typical return values for valid cursor locations could easily range from 1-91. If the specified text window is not defined, or is currently deactivated (via the [`$DTW$`](#dtw) command for example), then this text variable returns a value of "0" to indicate that the information isn't available. _(v2.A4)_
