requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: The coordinate illustrations below describe the intended port-relative model. For exact RIPtel 3.1 behavior after an explicit viewport command, the [original producer](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport) stores directly converted context coordinates without adding the screen-port origin or intersecting with port bounds. [POINT uses that stored origin; PIXEL omits it](2.1-lines.md#rip_point). Newly created ports still begin with their default port-sized viewport. _Evidence: [original driver and native checks](../research/issue-11-pixel-pen-units.md)._

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: Each drawing port has an associated viewport, or clipping rectangle. A viewport is a rectangle inside the port that defines the drawing limits inside that port. It's similar in concept to a coloring book with invisible lines. You can draw all you want, but you can't go outside the lines. If any operation would extend beyond the edge of this clipping rectangle, it will be truncated. For example, if you have a drawing port that is 100x100 pixels in size, and you define the viewport to be from (25,25) to (74,74), you would have a 50x50 drawing area right in the center of the drawing port. If you then draw a circle in the exact center of the drawing port with a radius of 60 pixels, you would have pieces of the circle that extend beyond the top, left, bottom and right borders of the viewport. What you would see would be four arcs in each corner of the viewport as in the following example:

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: If you notice in the above diagram, the rectangle inside the port defines the viewport. The solid squares (█) denote pixels inside the viewport that would actually be drawn, and the shaded squares (░) show pixels that will not be drawn because they are outside the viewport.

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: You can alter the location and size of the viewport inside any given drawing port. By default, the viewport is set to the full size of the drawing port when the port is created. If you attempt to make the viewport go outside the actual port, it will be adjusted to fit so that it is completely within the port. If an attempt is made to define a viewport that is completely outside the boundary of its port, then the definition is ignored as an error condition. If the lower-right corner is outside the boundary of the port, then the lower-right corner of the newly defined viewport is set to the lower-right corner of the port itself.

requirements.heading: Ports and Viewports
requirements.text: Just like drawing ports, a viewport also "adjusts" drawing coordinates. When you alter the location of a viewport inside of a drawing port, the origin (0,0) for drawing operations relates to the upper-left corner of the viewport itself, not the actual underlying drawing port. All drawing operations pertain to a port's viewport, not the port itself. The port is considered the maximum limits for the viewport inside - just like the screen, you can only draw to areas inside the screen; the same applies to viewports and ports.

requirements.heading: Observed Usage in the 3.x Era
requirements.text: The port system is the workhorse of TeleGrafix's own 3.x demo material. The RIPtel demo corpus contains **9,104 uses of `2C` (RIP_PORT_COPY)** - by far the most frequent command after RIP_LINE - almost all of them in the WIPE00-WIPE24 "wipe" transition library: each wipe composes the next scene in an offscreen port, then reveals it with a sequence of narrow port-to-screen copies to animate slides, splits, and dissolves. The supporting pattern (define port 1 full-screen, copy the screen into it, switch, draw, copy back) appears throughout the `.FN` function scenes, with TeleGrafix's own comments narrating it: "Create a port for the status line backup area, and copy the area where the status line will go into that drawing port."

requirements.heading: Observed Usage in the 3.x Era
requirements.text: The corpus uses only four level-2 port commands - `2P` (define), `2p` (delete), `2s` (switch), `2C` (copy) - confirming these as the practical core of the port system on the wire. (SyncTERM's `RIPSCRIP030001` mode implements **no level-2 commands at all** - the single largest gap between the open-source reconstruction and shipped 3.x content.)

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: The `<port-num>` parameter determines which entry in the master Port Table you wish to define. When working with ports, you need to be concerned about the port number you're working with - that's the location of the port, and that's how you access it when you need to switch ports - by port number. You are allowed up to 36 separate graphical ports (0-35 in decimal). Port #0 cannot be re-defined because it is always defined as the Screen Port. You can however, alter the viewport for Port #0 to make a sub-area on the screen to draw in (and clip). The viewport for Port #0 may also be deactivated as can the viewport on any other graphical Port. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: Port geometry uses **extent boundaries** in the current world coordinate system, without an extra inclusive pixel. For a screen port, convert both corners to device coordinates, then use `width = device_x1 - device_x0` and `height = device_y1 - device_y0`. For an offscreen port, the effective near corner is **(0,0)**: send x0=y0=0, and interpret x1/y1 as the far extent boundaries from that origin. The protocol's flag-1 rule treats supplied nonzero x0/y0 as zero; they do not reduce the requested offscreen dimensions. With equal world/device dimensions, an offscreen request (2,1)–(6,4) therefore means a **6×4** port at (0,0); its canonical form is (0,0)–(6,4). A sender needing a 4×3 port sends (0,0)–(4,3). _Evidence: ALPHA 4 §3.4.3.1, coordinate paragraph and flag-1 definition; [origin/extent derivation](../research/issue-72-define-port-contract.md#offscreen-origin-and-extents)._

requirements.heading: RIP_DEFINE_PORT
requirements.text: On successful definition, initialize the viewport to cover the whole port, then apply the requested initial state. Flag 4 makes that viewport inactive; flag 8 protects the new definition; flag 2 selects the new port. These are independent postconditions, so setting protection does not prevent the same command from establishing its requested viewport state. For example, decimal flags 15 create an offscreen port that is current, has an inactive viewport and is protected. You may later change an unprotected port's viewport with [RIP_VIEWPORT](1.3-world-view-virtual-canvas.md#rip_viewport).

requirements.text: The example above is the corpus's standard form (TELPORT.FN, FONTS.RIP, DRAGON.RIP): it requests the full **world extent** 1280×960 (`ZKQO`) with flags `0003` (offscreen + switch). At world 1280×960 and device 640×480, its translated corners are (0,0) and (640,480), and the original allocator creates a **640×480 physical bitmap**. Its last pixel is (639,479). There is no 641×481 extra edge and it is not a physical 1280×960 bitmap. Offscreen allocations are not clamped to the display: endpoints 2560,1920 under the same conversion create a 1280×960 bitmap, subject to the ordinary pixel budget. _Evidence: corpus for the wire example; [original allocation instructions and native observations](../research/issue-10-port-geometry.md#native-allocation-and-copy-checkpoint) for physical dimensions._

requirements.heading: Resource-failure guarantees
requirements.text: The documented protected-target rejection above is distinct from a failure to allocate a new port. The source describes unprotected replacement as deletion followed by creation, but supplies **no atomic-replacement or rollback guarantee**. An allocation failure therefore does not guarantee that the old target definition or its pixels survive. The resulting target definition, current selection and clipboard assignment after a resource failure are implementation-defined; applications cannot assume a particular recovery state.

requirements.heading: RIP_SWITCH_PORT
requirements.text: **Failure is not transactional.** Source flags run before selection and remain applied if creation fails. Destination flags refer to the actual fallback port 0 in that case; they do not target the still-undefined requested entry or return to the old source. Port 0 ignores them. In particular, destination-unprotect cannot rescue a protected-but-undefined target: the constructor has already failed before that action runs. An out-of-range target (36 or above), or disabled graphics processing, returns before any protection writes.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELETE_PORT
requirements.text: This command physically deletes one or more graphical ports. The exact port depends on the `<port_num>` parameter. If the port number specified is between 1-35, then the given port is deleted (providing of course that it is unprotected). If you attempt to delete a protected port, then this command will fail. If you attempt to delete port #0 (the screen port), then you will be activating a special case of this command - all unprotected ports from 1-35 are automatically deleted. This is a good garbage collection command mode when you want to start with a new slate of ports without the overhead of sending many delete port commands.

requirements.heading: RIP_DELETE_PORT
requirements.text: The `<dest_port>` parameter defines the port number that will be switched to after the delete operation is finished. Typically, this will be set to port #0 (switch to screen port), but it need not be. If the destination port is undefined, then it will automatically switch to port #0. If you instruct this command to delete all ports, then the destination port may or may not be set to the screen port - it all depends on whether or not the destination port both exists, and is protected - remember, a protected port cannot be deleted with this command without first being unprotected. So, if you delete all ports and switch to another port that isn't port #0, and that port is protected, then that protected port is selected as the new active port. If however, that port doesn't exist (ie, it did exist at the beginning of this command, but wasn't protected), then the screen port #0 will be selected.

requirements.heading: RIP_PORT_COPY
requirements.reason: Reconciled with adopted PR #71 / issue-10 port geometry. 2C projects WORLD boundaries once in wide arithmetic, resolves all-zero source/destination and destination zero-ending forms after projection, and gives full-destination precedence. requirements.text: This command copies graphics data from one port to another (or possibly even the same port). The area copied is a rectangular area based on the (sx0,sy0)..(sx1,sy1) parameters in the `<source_port>` and the (dx0,dy0)..(dx1,dy1) parameters in the `<dest_port>`. The `<source_port>` and `<dest_port>` parameters specify which port numbers are to be used for the source and destination respectively. They may be set to the same port number which signifies that a bit-blit operation is to occur from one location of the current port to another. Both the source and destination ports are specified as port numbers from 0-35. If either port doesn't exist (or is deactivated) then this command will do nothing.

requirements.text: For an initially **equal-size** copy, clip the source and destination against their respective viewports, shortening the other rectangle's right/bottom by the same amounts. The original no-scale branch remains selected, preserving one source pixel per destination pixel. For an initially **unequal-size** copy, clip the two rectangles independently, then scale the surviving source into the surviving destination. A rectangle wholly outside its viewport produces no copy. The driver does not reclassify an initially unscaled copy as scaled merely because clipping shortened its destination. This also applies to explicitly sized equal rectangles, not only the zero-endpoint shorthand. _Evidence: original handler 0x46372, compositor 0x134d0, coupled trim 0x13456 and [native geometry matrix](../research/issue-10-port-geometry.md#native-allocation-and-copy-checkpoint)._

requirements.text: By use count this is _the_ RIPscrip 3.x command: the WIPE00-24.FN transition library is almost nothing but port-copy animation, sliding successive slices of a pre-rendered offscreen scene onto the screen. Between the wipes and the `.MSE` status-line backups ("Copy the screen image to the port"), 46 of the 116 corpus files depend on it. _Evidence: corpus._

requirements.heading: 7.1 Data Tables
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 7.1 Data Tables
requirements.text: Data tables - the mechanism, inherited from 2.0 and confirmed throughout the 3.0.7 driver's error strings, that turns nearly every piece of drawing state into a numbered, switchable, protectable table entry: six general tables of 36 entries each, plus the special 128-entry mouse field table.

requirements.heading: 7.1 Data Tables
requirements.text: _The switch commands live with their subject matter - [RIP_SWITCH_PORT](7.0-drawing-ports.md#rip_switch_port) in 7.0, [RIP_SWITCH_PALETTE](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md#rip_switch_palette) in 2.0, [RIP_SWITCH_TEXT_WINDOW](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md#rip_switch_text_window) in 1.4, [RIP_SWITCH_BUTTON_STYLE](4.3-buttons.md#rip_switch_button_style) in 4.3 - while the graphical-style and environment switches are documented here._

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: RIPscrip 2.0 was different from its previous versions architecturally on a number of levels, and one of the key fundamental differences - the data table - carries into 3.x unchanged. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: A data table is a table of information used in RIPscrip. Data tables may be the color palette table (where each table entry is a complete color palette definition), graphical style tables, button style tables, [drawing port](7.0-drawing-ports.md) tables, text window definition tables, mouse field tables, or environment data tables. Some data tables have an entry that is "currently active". This might be the currently active text window in the text window data table, or the currently active color palette in the palette data table. Every data table has one or more entries in it, in which each entry is a specific piece of data. Data table entries can be "in use" and/or protected (see below). _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: Data can be moved from one table entry to another (in effect, making a copy of one table entry to another); this doesn't apply to all data tables (eg, mouse field data table). Also, most tables' entries can be protected so that the contents of a particular entry cannot be modified or deleted until either an unprotect entry function is executed, or a hard reset is performed (a hard reset completely resets the entire RIPscrip environment to ground zero). Again the mouse field data table cannot have individual entries protected. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: Host commands manipulate tables through the [`$CUR$`](5.1-text-variables.md#cur), [`$COPY$`](5.1-text-variables.md#copy), [`$PROT$`](5.1-text-variables.md#prot), [`$UNPROT$`](5.1-text-variables.md#unprot), [`$ISPROT$`](5.1-text-variables.md#isprot) and [`$INUSE$`](5.1-text-variables.md#inuse) [text variables](../../glossary.md).

requirements.heading: Data Tables - A Fundamental Concept
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver's error strings confirm the table architecture directly: every general table has **36 entries, numbered 0-35** ("Invalid … entry number (0-35)", "Invalid button group number (>35)"), entries can be PROTECTed and unprotected, and data can be copied from one entry to another. Entry contents survive until overwritten, cleared by a reset, or removed by a hard reset. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Entry 0 - the Common Modifiable Entry
requirements.text: _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Entry 0 - the Common Modifiable Entry
requirements.text: Entry 0 of each table is special: it is the always-present working entry that **cannot be deleted or protected**. The driver enforces this per table - "Cannot protect current text window slot when it is #0", "Can't protect environment data table entry #0", "Can't protect graphics style data table entry zero", "Can't protect color palette zero", and for ports, "Can't delete graphics port #0". Entry 0 is thus the common, freely modifiable entry every scene can rely on; protection is reserved for entries 1-35.

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: There are six different data tables for general data storage: the drawing port table, color palette table, graphical style table, text window table, the button style table and the RIPscrip environment data table. There are backup areas for these data tables so you can make complete backup copies for re-use later after some operation is performed (eg, executing a dialog box, running a door, etc). There are actually more data backup areas than there are data tables - see [7.2 Data Backup Areas](7.2-data-backup-areas.md). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: The `RIP_Switch*` command family in the 3.0 command inventory covers the switchable tables (`RIP_SwitchButtonStyle`, `RIP_SwitchEnvironment`, `RIP_SwitchPalette`, `RIP_SwitchPort`, `RIP_SwitchStyle`, `RIP_SwitchTextWindow` - plus `RIP_SwitchDirectory`, level-2 ESC, which belongs to the [storage model](6.2-asset-delivery-and-storage.md#rip_switch_directory) rather than a drawing table). _Evidence: DLL; HLP._

requirements.heading: Types of Data Tables
requirements.text: The general table groups are described in more detail as follows: _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: One of the most fundamental aspects of the language is the concept of a [drawing port](7.0-drawing-ports.md). Any drawing of graphics occurs inside a drawing port. There may be up to 36 ports [defined](7.0-drawing-ports.md#rip_define_port) simultaneously. Port number 0 is always defined as the screen. Its dimensions are that of the screen. The remaining 35 ports may be sub-sections of the screen or may be offscreen memory drawing ports (ie, clipboard ports). At any one moment in time, only one port may be the current port - the port that will receive graphical drawing operations. If the current port is an offscreen clipboard port, then any drawing operations will not appear on the screen. The only way that those graphics can be viewed by the user is if the contents of the port are copied to a screen port. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: All ports, when defined, are defined using the current [world coordinate](../../glossary.md) system. From those coordinates, the port's actual physical pixel dimensions are determined and those dimensions are remembered by the port. Any graphical operation that bypasses the viewport system pays close attention to coordinates and the boundaries of the drawing port. If any coordinate would go outside of the port, it is adjusted to fit inside. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table
requirements.text: Each port entry remembers its own drawing state - the full list is in [7.0](7.0-drawing-ports.md#the-port-table). The entire drawing port data table also keeps track of the "current viewport" query expression (otherwise known as a floating viewport query). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: In RIPscrip there is a graphical color palette. The color palette is a group of 256 separate color RGB values, also known as a color lookup table. This color palette is used to map a particular color number to some combination of red, green and blue color components. For example, color 0 is usually black (no red, green or blue), and color 255 is typically white (full intensity red, green and blue). This color palette is normally written directly into the video hardware of your computer to activate the colors. So when you try to draw in color 255, you see a white line appear on the screen. _(v2.A3)_
requirements.reason: Reference adoption reopens this claim: the containing document changed in PR #71. Existing implementation/tests are historical evidence, pending reconciliation with the new contract. Previous review: 36 independently owned 256-color palettes, one current selection, indexed-pixel cycling and complete palette-table snapshots/restoration including current/defined/protection state. Backup slots/stack, wire/variable handling and reset lifecycle remain separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: Up to 36 separate color palettes may be held at once. Only one entry in the color palette table may be current at any one moment in time. An entry in the color palette table is a complete 256 color palette. When you switch from one color palette entry to another, the colors on the screen will typically change instantly. This gives you the ability to quickly and easily switch from one color scheme to another without sending a large amount of information to the terminal every time you wish to switch color schemes. _(v2.A3)_

Existing implementation/tests are historical evidence, pending reconciliation with the new contract. Previous review: 36 independently owned 256-color palettes, one current selection, indexed-pixel cycling and complete palette-table snapshots/restoration including current/defined/protection state. Backup slots/stack, wire/variable handling and reset lifecycle remain separate requirements.

requirements.heading: Color Palette Table
requirements.text: The language allows for two forms of color modes, color palette mapping mode (the default) and direct RGB color encoding - see [2.0 Color Modes & Palettes](2.0-color-modes-and-palettes.md). Under 24-bit configurations, a real hardware color palette is not possible; the palette is used as an RGB lookup table for subsequent drawing, and switching palettes will not change colors already on the screen. _(v2.A3)_

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: _Evidence: original RIPtel 3.1 reset/select/copy/status consumers; [native derivation and reproduction tool](../research/issue-16-table-lifecycle.md). These findings concern complete palette slots, not individual colors within a palette._

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: A slot's RGB values, defined/in-use state, protection and current selection are distinct. Selecting an unused palette defaults its RGB values and marks it defined. Resetting it restores RGB defaults and clears the nonzero slot's definition flag. It does not automatically change its current index or make another palette current. Slot zero remains defined and unprotectable.

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: | Operation | Unprotected nonzero slot | Protected nonzero slot | Palette selection |

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: | `$RESET(PAL,n)$` / current-slot PAL reset | Default RGB; undefined afterward, including if already undefined | Reject unchanged, with protection error | Retained |

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: | `$RESET(PAL,TBL)$` | Default RGB; undefined afterward | Skip unchanged | Retained |

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: | SOFT / ordinary drawing reset | Default RGB; undefined afterward | Skip unchanged | Retained, even if now undefined |

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: | HARD reset | Default RGB; undefined and unprotected afterward | Remove protection; default RGB; undefined afterward | Select zero |

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: | `$CUR(PAL,n)$` on an unused slot | Default RGB and define it | Protection is a separate flag; selecting does not itself unprotect | Select n |

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: Thus, after selecting/modifying slot 5, a specific or soft reset leaves `$INUSE(PAL,5)$` false unless protection caused it to be skipped/rejected. Numeric `$ISPROT(PAL,5)$` then returns `-1` because the slot is undefined; `$CUR(PAL)$` can still be `5`. Reselecting slot 5 defines it with defaults again. The ISPROT CUR branch has no definition check and reports the current protection bit directly; it is not interchangeable with the numeric-slot query in this state.

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: Live-entry [`COPY`](5.1-text-variables.md#live-entry-copy-validation-and-protection) rejects an undefined source or any protected destination before modifying any destination. PAL/STYLE/TW/ENV copies carry source protection into writable nonzero destinations; BUT copies instead clear destination protection. Copies to zero always leave zero unprotected. Whole-table backup restoration has its own saved-state/protection rules.

requirements.heading: Palette reset lifecycle
requirements.text: Palette header flags 64/128 **do not initialize default RGB values**: their helper uploads existing current colors. Flag 128 additionally has an invalid current-sentinel guard; see the [corrected header contract](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#button-graphics-style-palette-and-environment-flags). Do not use those flags as a substitute for PAL reset.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1. Evidence: DLL; [ownership/default derivation](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md). The following corrects the inherited 2.00a4 ownership lists for RIPtel 3.1._

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: There are 36 graphical style entries. Initially, entry 0 is current. Each entry owns drawing/background/fill colors, fill pattern and user rows, line pattern/thickness/user mask/odd rule, write mode, border setting, classic font/size/direction/justification, and the [extended font fields](3.0-text-output-and-fonts.md#rip_extended_font_style).

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: **Drawing X/Y and image style belong exclusively to ports. Color mode and mouse pointer number belong exclusively to environments.** These are not additional copies in the style record. Changing style does not capture, restore or alter them; changing port does not select a different style. Environment selection does not select a different style or port either.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table
requirements.text: For example, give port 1 cursor (10,20)/image A under style 1, then port 2 cursor (30,40)/image B under style 2. Switching only to style 1 leaves port 2 active with (30,40)/B. From port 2/style 2, switching only to port 1 exposes (10,20)/A while retaining style 2. There is no last-switch-wins conflict between duplicate cursor/image records. [Backups](7.2-data-backup-areas.md#graphical-style-table-save-area) follow the same ownership, with specific restore defects noted there.

requirements.heading: Initial and per-slot defaults
requirements.text: Normal driver initialization, reset of an unprotected style, and first selection of an unused style use the same fixed record. These are exact stored values, independent of which palette entries currently look white:

requirements.heading: Initial and per-slot defaults
requirements.text: | Attribute | Default |

requirements.heading: Initial and per-slot defaults

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: Button style data table entries contain a complete button style definition as defined by a [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style) command. Having multiple button style slots defined at the same time allows you to have many commonly used button styles defined at once, so that you can simply reference an already defined button style rather than having to transmit a rather lengthy button style command each and every time you wish to define a button.

requirements.heading: Button Style Table
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 initially selects slot 0 and defines only that slot; all 36 records hold the same fixed PLAIN+BEVEL default. Selecting an undefined slot installs that default, rather than copying the previous style. The [complete default fields and reset behavior](4.3-buttons.md#initial-and-reset-style) include the shipped current-reset metadata corruption; [auto-clip](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style) can also mutate the current style's flags even when protected. _Evidence: original initialization, selection, reset and rendering; [derivation](../research/issue-27-button-style-contract.md)._

requirements.text: _Added in RIPscrip v2.A1._

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4._

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: A [text window](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) is simply a region on the screen where raw, non-RIPscrip text is routed once it is received from the host. Initially, the text window is full screen, using the MicroANSI font #2 (80x25) - different from 1.54, whose initial setting was font #0 (80x43); 80x25 is more aesthetically pleasing to most people so it was made the default. A text window typically supports ANSI and VT-102 screen control codes. Each of the 36 text window table entries stores:

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text:
- The upper-left and lower-right corner definitions for the text window (coordinates are in text coordinates, not graphical screen coordinates).
- The MicroANSI screen font number for the given window.
- The current ANSI color attributes
- The current cursor X/Y location
- The status of the cursor (is it on or off)
- The current vertical scrolling margins (ANSI formatting)
- Whether the window is activated or deactivated.

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: A text window can also be deactivated. If the current text window slot is deactivated then any raw text that is received from the host will be discarded (ie, not shown on screen at all). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Text Window Table
requirements.text: Having multiple defined text windows allows you to quickly switch from one text window configuration to another without losing any previously used information (color, location, cursor, etc). Note that the text contained inside the current text window is not stored as part of the text window definition - only the window's raw definition is preserved. See [1.4 Terminal & ANSI View](1.4-terminal-ansi-view.md) for the extended (resolution-independent) text window added in the 3.x era.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: The environment data table is a central table for the maintenance of critical values that define the characteristics of the RIPscrip environment. This data table holds up to 36 separate environments. For RIPtel 3.1, world dimensions, Base Math, coordinate width, RGB precision and mouse pointer number belong to the environment. The inherited draft also describes baud-rate emulation in this table. **Current STYLE, BUT, PORT, TW and PAL selections are separate state:** the driver's environment selector does not save or restore those selections, their records, or mouse fields. The draft's proposed whole-context-swap example is not the shipped behavior. _Evidence: DLL; [activation derivation](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#ownership-and-switching-observations)._

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: Wire color-mode and mouse-pointer commands check the current **environment's** protection, independently of the current style's protection. A protected style does not block those changes, and neither change modifies the style. [`COLORMODE`](5.1-text-variables.md#colormode) can edit an already defined noncurrent environment without changing active mode; the new value becomes active when that environment is selected. That variable and [`MCURSOR`](5.1-text-variables.md#mcursor) bypass environment protection, unlike their wire commands.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: **Environment activation order and defect:** the selector reads the target's Base Math, RGB precision and coordinate width, invokes their active setters, activates target world dimensions, requests a mouse refresh if the number differs, and finally changes the current environment index. Because those first three setters run before the index changes, they also overwrite the **departing environment's** Base Math, RGB precision and coordinate width, even if it is protected. They do not overwrite its saved world dimensions or mouse number. Target protection does not prohibit selection.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: For example, start with environment 0 = base 36, two-character coordinates, palette mode, world 640×480, cursor 2; environment 5 = base 64, four-character coordinates, RGB 8, world 1280×960, cursor 6. Switching 0 → 5 activates 5's values and leaves every other table's current selection unchanged. Switching back to 0 activates **base 64 / width 4 / RGB 8**, because 0's three fields were overwritten, but restores **640×480 / cursor 2**, whose stored values survived. Mouse presentation uses the newly current environment at its next refresh. Implementations targeting this client must distinguish this sequencing defect from independent, correctly preserved records.

requirements.heading: Environment Table
requirements.text: The environment table is central to the 3.x backup/dialog system: HLP confirms the 36 slots, the unprotectable slot #0, the `$SENV$`/`$RENV$` backup variables, and environment header segments carrying coordinate-size and RGB-bit settings (below). _Evidence: HLP._
requirements.reason: All environment record fields, explicit entry definition/selection, slot-zero/protection rules, per-canvas frames and independently owned whole-table backups are implemented. requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table
requirements.text: The mouse field data table is unlike the other data tables. It can hold up to 128 separate mouse field definitions and does not have a "current mouse field" entry number. Each mouse field that is defined gets added to the mouse field data table at the very end until 128 fields are defined, or the table is deleted and things start over. Mouse fields only pertain to drawing port #0, so they can only be on the screen, not on an offscreen drawing port. See [RIP_MOUSE](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md#rip_mouse), [RIP_BUTTON_STYLE](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button_style) and [RIP_BUTTON](4.3-buttons.md#rip_button) for more details on this special data table.

requirements.heading: Mouse Field Table
requirements.text: The 3.0 driver adds the `ID=n:` prefix convention for assigning numbered identities to mouse fields, readable back through `$FIELDID$` and used by the `.MSE` overlay scenes' entry/exit queries ([4.2](4.2-mouse-fields-and-pointer.md)). _Evidence: HLP; corpus._

requirements.heading: Audio header action (New in 3.x)
requirements.text: Header type 7 has a two-character flags field and **no slot number**. Flag 1 stops waveform playback; it is not an audio data table or an instruction to stop independent MIDI playback. Audio behavior is covered in [4.4](4.4-tone-and-sound-generation.md) and [4.5](4.5-audio-files.md).

requirements.heading: Scene Header Segments and Table State
requirements.text: [`RIP_HEADER`](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#rip_header) supplies typed operations for button/style/port/text-window/palette/environment tables, mouse fields, audio and the screen. The reference now gives the byte grammar, current versus supplied-slot operations, reset/backup/protection effects, validation defects and checked examples. Table segments run in wire order after global header operations; they do not declare new table dimensions. Audio is a single stop action. A malformed character-set descriptor is also present but has no consistently usable standalone wire framing. The demos’ explicit prologue commands remain valid alternatives.

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Data table entries by themselves have quite a bit of usefulness in short-term situations where a lot of different configurations need to be switched between fairly often. Their usefulness becomes even more powerful with the concept of protected data table entries. A protected entry is one that cannot be cleared by a normal reset operation or a clear table entry operation until the entry is unprotected, or until a "hard reset" operation is performed. In addition, they cannot be modified while they are protected (see below). _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: A "hard reset" is a complete reset of the RIPscrip environment. Typically, a hard reset should only be performed immediately after connection to a RIPscrip compatible host system to clear the slate so to speak. Other uses for a hard reset are when the RIPscrip environment is hopelessly corrupted due to line noise, or when a complete re-synchronization of the environment is about to commence. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Protected entries become quite powerful when you look at a larger host system. For example, let's say that throughout your system you use five different graphical style configurations all over the place, all of which require quite a bit of transmitted RIPscrip code. If you define each of these styles as separate entries and then protect them, you don't need to re-transmit those blocks of data again unless a hard reset operation is performed! This can mean quite a bit of saved data transmission, and consequently faster transmission times. The same concept applies to text windows, ports, button styles, graphics style, palette and environment tables. When taken from a system-wide perspective, where many sections of the system may be made by other manufacturers (eg, doors, BBS modules, etc), you may not be able to count on whether a section of the system uses one style or another, or does one kind of reset or another. Having protected entries gives you the ability to protect your data configurations so that these sub-sections do not destroy your data. When you return from the sub-section, simply re-activate your table configuration(s) and away you go. _(v2.A1)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: We just described that a protected data table entry cannot be deleted. We also mentioned that they cannot be modified. Let's clarify what we mean by not modifiable. A data table entry that is protected cannot be modified by any of the normal RIPscrip commands or [text variables](5.1-text-variables.md) that alter their basic configuration (eg, you cannot alter the foreground drawing color in a protected graphical style data table entry, etc). It should be noted however, that normal drawing operations like rectangles, circles, etc, can still be performed to a port that is protected. In this case, the port is protected from having its "configuration" modified (eg, the viewport cannot be modified nor can the actual port's orientation). The same applies to text windows (eg, you can output text to a text window, perform ANSI/VT-102 operations to it, erase it, etc, but you cannot redefine it or delete it). One tiny exception rests with text windows that support VT-102. VT-102 has an ANSI escape sequence that allows you to alter the wrap/chop setting of text windows. Since ANSI operations are allowed on protected text windows, this is permissible even though it seemingly violates the nature of modifying a text window's protected status. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: Terminal emulation modes are also unaffected by a text window's protection status. If a text window is enabled, VT-102 mode can be turned on or off because this is a "global" setting, not a text window specific setting. Also, RIPscrip processing can be disabled via a special ANSI escape sequence ([1.1](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md)). This does not affect protection of text windows or drawing ports either. _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: With these things in mind, performing operations like "copying a port's data to another port" where one or both are protected is allowable because you are not altering the basic configuration of the ports in question, you are simply altering their data contents. This applies to "clipboard" related commands too which might dynamically pick and choose ports to define. Since a clipboard related command will auto-define a new port if one doesn't already exist, it will pick a currently undefined drawing port and define it (if it's not defined, then it cannot be protected). _(v2.A4)_

requirements.heading: Protected Data Table Entries
requirements.text: The 3.0.7 driver's PROTECT machinery is confirmed by its error strings, including the entry-0 exclusions listed above, and by the `$PROTECT$`/`$ISPROT$`/`$UNPROT$`-family text-variable processors present in its string table. _Evidence: HLP._

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A data backup area is a backup area that composes one base save area and ten data save regions for specific data table types. The data save regions are broken collectively up as a set of individually addressable data save slots (like an array in most programming languages), and a data save stack. Each data backup area can contain up to eleven separate, complete data tables of one particular type - one in the base save area, and up to ten other data tables in the data save slots or the data save stack, or in some combination of the two (save slots or stack).

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Each data backup area can store only one particular type of [data table](7.1-data-tables.md). For example, the color palette data backup area can only store color palette data tables (remember a color palette data table consists of 36 separate color palette definitions).

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A data save slot is a backup area that is large enough to store an entire specific data table, or other object (graphics screen, mouse fields, etc). Each data backup area's save slots can hold one entire data table of the type designated for the data backup area. Each data save slot has a specific slot number associated with it (0-9). When the data in a data save slot is restored back to the actual RIPscrip drawing environment, that slot is deleted (cleared), providing that it isn't protected (see below).

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A base save area is very similar to a data save slot, except that a base save area does not have a specific "slot number" associated with it. Unlike data save slots, when you restore a data table object from a base save area, the base save area is not cleared (ie, deleted) so it can be restored multiple times without losing the saved data (the base save area cannot be protected like data save slots can be - see below for more details).

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Finally, we have stack save areas. Stack save areas are like a stack of plates - you put plates on top of the stack, and when you want one, you take one off the top of the stack. The plate at the bottom of the stack was the first plate placed on it, and to get to it, you need to take off each of the plates above it. When you place a data table onto a save stack, it is like placing a plate on top of our stack of plates. This is extremely useful (in fact, critical) to creating dialog boxes that overlap menus, and when you close the dialog box, you restore the menu's environment. The act of placing a data table onto a data save stack is called "pushing" a table onto the stack. The act of removing a table from the top of the stack is called "popping" a table from the stack. In order to remember where the "top" of the stack is (ie, how many layers are on the stack), a thing called a "stack pointer" is maintained internally which is simply a count of the number of items on the stack. Each time you add a new data table onto the stack, the pointer is increased by one (we have one more item on the stack).

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: Notice how there are ten different data save slots, and ten different data save stack "locations". What this means is that individually, either one of these may hold ten complete data tables. But combined, they cannot both contain more than 10 complete data tables. What this means is that you can have 4 separate tables saved in the data save slots, and 6 data tables pushed onto the stack, but then you wouldn't be able to store one more data table into an "open" data save slot, or push it onto the save stack (the slot/stack system is effectively "full"). requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: A stack restore (also known as a "pop") is a method of restoring a data object from the data save stack into a data table. When you perform a stack pop, the data table at the top of the stack (the entry just below the stack pointer) is removed from the stack and placed in the appropriate data table (which one is based on the type of data that is stored in the data backup area). Once the restore operation is complete, the entry in that location of the stack is deleted (cleared), and the stack pointer is decremented by one, thus making room for one more entry in the data save slot/stack system to hold a new data table. (Popping an empty stack is an error - the 3.0 driver's "No stack to pop".)

requirements.heading: Data Backup Areas
requirements.text: All totalled, a data backup area can store eleven separate data tables, and each data table in a data backup area is of the same type of information (eg, text window, color palette, etc). If a data table has 36 separate data table entries in it, then a data backup area for that data table would hold 396 separate data table entries in it! This makes for a lot of backup storage. requirements.text: Push and pop operations are vital to the concept of multiple overlapping windows and dialog boxes in RIPscrip. requirements.heading: Protection and Restoration
requirements.text: When you restore a data table from a data save slot back into the actual data table on the other hand, that data save slot is deleted (cleared) unless it is protected from deletion. Only a data save slot that is actually "in use" can be protected - it is pointless to protect a data save slot that isn't holding a data table because what would you do with it? You couldn't store anything in it and you couldn't read anything from it, so this situation is not allowed.

requirements.heading: Graphical Style Table Save Area
requirements.text: **RIPtel 3.1 scope and restore defect:** STYLE saves only the current style index and all 36 style records; it contains no port cursor/image state or environment color-mode/mouse state. Its restore reads the saved index into the current style's foreground word, then immediately overwrites that word when restoring the table. The pre-restore current style index therefore survives and is reactivated. For example, saving while style 5 is current and restoring while style 7 is current restores all records but leaves style **7** current. _Evidence: DLL; [original save/restore and native case](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#backups)._

requirements.heading: Drawing Port Table Save Area
requirements.text: **RIPtel 3.1 cursor exception:** PORT owns and saves the image rectangle/flags, separately from STYLE; restore reinstates those image fields without touching style/environment records. Screen-port cursor X/Y are written to the backup stream, but restore reads them into a local buffer and never copies them to the port. Thus an existing screen port retains its live cursor rather than its saved cursor: saving (515,616), changing to (717,818) and restoring leaves **(717,818)**. Offscreen ports do not serialize cursor X/Y in this path. The saved current port selection and resident queries do restore. Do not infer cursor restoration from the fact that the stream contains it. _Evidence: DLL; [original serializer/restore and native screen-port case](../research/issue-24-drawing-state-ownership.md#backups)._

requirements.heading: Screen Save Area
requirements.text: The screen operation ignores the selected port's viewport and protection when choosing its **capture/restore target**: that target is port zero's screen DC. It does not restore port zero's viewport, the saved current port's viewport, all viewports, or an independent viewport setting. If port 1 was current at save and port 35 is current at restore, 35 remains current. Deleting, redefining or protecting port 1 between those operations does not change that result. Restore does not resize the canvas. The original calls are specified here; native fixtures use an unclipped indexed GDI model and do not establish exact Windows clipping/raster behavior.

requirements.heading: Palette binding example
requirements.text: Suppose palette **5** is current at SAVE, its index 15 is red, and the screen contains pixels of index 15. Before RESTORE select palette **17**, make its index 15 green, and protect entry 17. RESTORE writes 5's saved RGB values into **17**, leaves 17 current/protected, and presents the saved pixels using that restored mapping. It neither selects palette 5 nor restores the whole palette table. Its direct RGB overwrite does not change the target's defined/protected flags. In the original private stream the palette occurs twice—an outer RGB block and the bitmap codec's included palette—and both copies target the same live palette entry, causing two uploads. Private in-memory storage need not duplicate an identical palette to reproduce the resulting state.

requirements.heading: Palette binding example
requirements.text: [`RESTOREALL`](5.1-text-variables.md#restoreall) differs because it subsequently restores the **whole palette table**: all 36 entries/flags and saved current index 5 return. The screen phase's temporary overwrite of 17 is then replaced by 17's saved table contents, and saved palette 5 becomes current. This order is observable; the combined operation is not a single atomic snapshot restore.

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: | Form | Destination/source and lifetime |

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: | `SAVE` / `SAVE(BASE)` | Replace screen base backup; reusable until replaced/deleted |

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: | `RESTORE` / `RESTORE(BASE)` | Restore base without consuming it |

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: | `SAVE(n)` / `SAVEn`, n = 0..9 | Same numbered backup; a protected existing snapshot blocks overwrite |

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: | `RESTORE(n)` / `RESTOREn`, n = 0..9 | Same restore followed by delete; unprotected snapshot is consumed, protected snapshot is restored and retained |

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: | `SAVE(PUSH)` / `RESTORE(POP)` | Per-family stack; successful POP restores and consumes the top snapshot |

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: Numbered aliases accept **no arguments**; all SAVE0..9 and RESTORE0..9 are registered in RIPtel 3.1. Parameter keywords are case-insensitive. Snapshot protection is separate from protection of a live palette or port. **Numeric restore requests deletion even if restoration fails**, so an unprotected snapshot can be consumed after a failed read; POP instead requires successful restoration before removing the stack entry. These action callbacks do not propagate the manager's success/failure as a value or variable error; invalid arguments do set the variable-error flag. Lower-level error reporting remains separate.

requirements.heading: Aliases, protection and lifetime
requirements.text: RIPtel 3.1 uses generated files in the configured engine directory, named **`%03hu%05hu.$$$`** from instance number and an incrementing counter, not RIPTERM.SAV or RIPTERM0.SAV..RIPTERM9.SAV. It closes but retains a reusable snapshot's file, unlinks on overwrite/consumption/deletion, and clears backups during normal manager teardown. These are client-owned backing files, not filenames named by the host command. A memory-backed implementation can preserve the same state/lifetime semantics without creating either the inherited RIPTERM*.SAV names or the driver's private generated files.

requirements.heading: SAVEALL / RESTOREALL composition
requirements.text: Numeric RESTOREALL attempts all eight restores, then all eight deletes in that same order. Base backups remain reusable. PUSH/POP use each family's independent stack. A failed/protected family does not stop subsequent families and there is no rollback; snapshot protection and consumption apply independently per family.

requirements.heading: SAVEALL / RESTOREALL composition
requirements.text: The **PORT** component supplies the saved current port and viewport definitions of saved defined ports, unlike screen-only SAVE. Saved definitions replace even protected live targets; a deleted saved port is redefined. Initial PORT cleanup skips protected live ports, however, and an undefined saved slot does not overwrite them, so a protected live port absent from the snapshot can survive. The [PORT cursor exception](#drawing-port-table-save-area) and [STYLE current-index defect](#graphical-style-table-save-area) still apply to RESTOREALL. Status-bar state is not added by any of these families: its owner is separate engine/host state. Thus “all” means this exact eight-family composition, not every client/UI setting.

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: Every command of the reconstructed RIPscrip 3.x inventory with its [command level](../../glossary.md), command type character, argument summary, lineage/evidence status, and one-line purpose, each symbol linked to its full entry.

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: Argument notation follows [1.1 Protocol & Command Hierarchy](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#how-commands-are-documented): `name:width` fields are fixed-width numbers in the current [Base Math](../../glossary.md); `:XY` marks a variable-width coordinate (2 digits by default, adjustable via [RIP_SET_COORDINATE_SIZE](1.2-math-and-coordinates.md#rip_set_coordinate_size)); `:CM` marks a color parameter that follows the current color mode; `text`/`filename` is a trailing text parameter; `...` marks variable-length commands; `<esc>` denotes the actual Escape character (ASCII 27).

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: TeleGrafix never published a 3.x language reference, so this inventory is an editorial reconstruction assembled from the 2.00 ALPHA 4 specification, the RIPSCRIP.HLP command-name inventory (~90 `RIP_*` names recovered from the RIPtel 3.1 help files and DLL string tables), the 116-script RIPtel demo corpus, and SyncTERM's open-source RIP 3.0 implementation - the **Added/Status** column carries both lineage and evidence status per the legend below.

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text: **Added/Status legend:**

requirements.heading: 9.0 Command Reference
requirements.text:
- blank - carried from 1.54 or earlier into the 2.0 engine that 3.x inherits.
- `v1.54`, `v2.A0`-`v2.A4` - spec revision that introduced the command (2.00 ALPHA draft revisions; 3.x inherits the 2.0 engine).
- `3.0 (corpus)` - 3.x-era command recovered from the RIPtel demo-script census; documented in no published specification.
- `3.0 (HLP; corpus)` - 3.x-era command attested by the RIPSCRIP.HLP name inventory and the corpus, absent from the 2.00a4 draft.
- `DLL` - grammar and behavior traced in RIPtel 3.1’s RIPscrip 3.0.7 driver, with derivation/probe links in the full entry.
- `outside DLL contract` - a SyncTERM descriptor with no entry in the original driver’s complete dispatch table; explicitly excluded from this driver’s executable contract below.
- `deprecated v2.A2` - deprecated in that revision; still implemented by every shipping driver, so authors should avoid it and implementers still have to handle it. The linked page explains why.
- `obsolete v2.A1` - declared obsolete in that revision but still parsed by clients.
- (\*), (†), (‡), (¶) - footnotes for special cases, listed [at the end of the page](#footnotes).

requirements.heading: Footnotes
requirements.text:
- (\*) The 2.00a4 draft assigns letter `b` to **both** RIP_SET_BASE_MATH and RIP_EXTENDED_TEXT_WINDOW - an unresolved collision in the draft. The shipping 3.0 driver moved base math to **`J`** (90 of 116 corpus files open with `!|J10|n2000|M08|fZKQO`, and ONLINE.RIP annotates `J10` inline as "Set base math to MegaNums"), leaving `b` to the extended text window, exactly as SyncTERM's descriptor table also has it. _Evidence: corpus; SyncTERM._
- (†) The command name is an editorial hypothesis reconstructed from census evidence (demo comments, on-screen titles, or layout analysis); TeleGrafix's own name is unrecovered. The six skewed-oval names, by contrast, come verbatim from TeleGrafix's NEWCMDS.RIP comments and are not so marked; RIP_POLY_POLYGON's name, initially inferred from its demo title, is now confirmed by the [original driver's error literal](../research/issue-13-polygon-counts.md).
- (‡) The RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory lists this command under the 3.0 name `RIP_BeginEncodedStream`, and its error strings reference "encoded stream" file types - the mechanism survived into 3.x under the new name.
- (¶) RIP_EXTENDED_FONT_STYLE uses 26 fixed UltraNum characters plus a font name, superseding the draft’s 13-character list. The [DLL derivation](../research/issue-3-extended-font-style.md) resolves the crib’s field roles: `OO` is shadow distance, `BB` is baseline displacement, the second `CC` is spacing percentage, and `WW` is ignored. `s` and `f` are stored compatibility bytes unused by the renderer. The 26-character form predates 3.x; semantic claims here are verified for driver 3.0.7.

requirements.heading: Announced but never specified
requirements.text: **RIP_FILE_DELETE** appears in the 2.00a4 v2.A3 revision history ("to remove unneeded JPEG or WAVE files off the user's hard disk") but received no command entry, opcode or argument list, and no such command name appears in the RIPSCRIP.HLP inventory. The capability is implemented as a text variable instead: `RIPSCRIP.HLP` carries the handler symbol `tvarProcFILEDEL` (the `tvarProc` prefix marking a text-variable processor), and `FILEDEL` is present in the shipping RIPterm 2.0/2.20.01/2.30 executables. Hosts use [`$FILEDEL(file,…)$`](9.1-text-variable-reference.md); see [5.5](5.5-file-transfer-and-queries.md). _Evidence: 2.00a4; HLP._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - every claim carries an evidence tag; see [Contents](README.md) for the legend._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: Every pre-defined [text variable](../../glossary.md) known for RIPscrip 3.x, with its parameter form, type, effect, and evidence status, linked to its full entry. **Value** variables return text to the host; **Active** variables perform an action on the terminal (some also return data when used to query). Parameters shown in parentheses are optional unless the full entry says otherwise; the 2.0 parameterized forms supersede the 1.54 fixed names (`$SAVE(8)$` vs `$SAVE8$`). The 3.x inventory combines the original driver’s 179 registrations with the RIPtel help files (roughly 60 data-returning and 60 command-performing variables), the demo corpus (269 distinct `$…$` forms in shipping scripts), and SyncTERM's 103-entry built-in table.

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference
requirements.text: _User-defined variables - any `$IDENTIFIER$` with the `*`/`+`/`%`/`#`/`-`/`&` directives, positioning, questions, defaults and format options - are covered in [5.1 Text Variables](5.1-text-variables.md#text-variable-creation-and-query); variables removed or renamed since 1.54 are listed in [5.1's rename note](5.1-text-variables.md)._

requirements.heading: 9.1 Text Variable Reference

requirements.heading: 9.2 Version Identification Reference
requirements.text: _Reconstructed edition - original-driver findings and the generic compatibility profile are distinguished below. [Primary derivation and native probes](../research/issue-7-framing-identification.md)._

requirements.heading: Identification phrase
requirements.text: The inherited format is **`RIPSCRIPxxyyvs`**, totaling 14 ASCII bytes: `xx` is the two-digit language major version, `yy` the two-digit minor version, `v` a vendor code and `s` that vendor’s subversion digit. Vendor 0 is generic/unspecified, 1 RIPterm/TeleGrafix, 2 Qmodem Pro. These last two digits are not a two-digit language revision. [1.54 identity history](../../1.54/ripscrip/9.2-versions.md) and the [2.0 record](../../2.0/ripscrip/9.2-versions.md) preserve the earlier evidence.

requirements.heading: Engine replies and terminators
requirements.text: | `$RIPVER$` or `$RIPVER()$` in an allowed macro context | Return the phrase `RIPSCRIP030001`, no ending | Not an autosense request; expansion depends on the caller context |

requirements.heading: Engine replies and terminators
requirements.text: Default/0 phrase bytes are **`52 49 50 53 43 52 49 50 30 33 30 30 30 31`**. Selector 3 appends **`0d`**. No NUL is sent: the C-string storage terminator is not a wire byte. RIPVER accepts no arguments and adds no CR/LF; a surrounding host command can supply its own control characters. The original client may translate a supplied CR to CRLF according to its output setting, as recorded in the [reply-path trace](../research/issue-5-scene-headers.md#entry-point-effect-probes-and-client-reply-trace); default/0 have no CR to translate.

requirements.heading: Engine replies and terminators
requirements.text: The autosense callback uses the first ANSI parameter only, ignores later parameters and sends no reply for other selector values; private-prefix `?0!` is a different ANSI dispatch. The ordinary ANSI decimal accumulator wraps to 16 bits. Enable/disable changes the emulation flag without resetting buffered parser state; [checked stream examples](1.1-protocol-and-command-hierarchy.md#esc-priority-and-resumption) distinguish this from a scene reset.

requirements.heading: Generic Implementation Profile
requirements.text: **Allowed by this reconstructed specification:** an independent implementation supporting the 3.0 contract may identify itself as **`RIPSCRIP030000`**: language 03.00, generic vendor 0, vendor subversion 0. It need not claim TeleGrafix vendor code 1 or copy a product name. This is an explicit interoperability policy using the inherited generic-vendor allocation, not a newly discovered historical response or a distinct RIPscrip language version.

requirements.heading: RIPscrip 3.0 - Language Reference (reconstructed record)
requirements.text: **RIPscrip 3.0** - the third-generation Remote Imaging Protocol scripting language (TeleGrafix Communications, Inc., 1996-1997), as shipped in **RIPtel Visual Telnet 3.1** (RIPscrip driver 3.0.7), the only client that ever shipped it. Chapter numbers align with the [2.0 reference](../../2.0/ripscrip/README.md) the generation evolved from, with the 3.x-era changes flattened into their proper sections and sections unique to this generation marked; the official [3.0 Technical White Paper](../text/RIPScrip-3.x-technical-whitepaper.txt) (December 1996, by Jeff Reeder - prose only, the sole TeleGrafix document for the generation) is preserved separately as a faithful conversion.

requirements.heading: Fill Defects (delta)
requirements.text: The [legacy flood-fill record](../../2.0/techspecs/2.1-fill-defects.md) distinguishes the inherited seed-stack limitation, the adopted patterned-flood claim and the withdrawn manual pie/chord leak attribution. This page records the evidence specific to RIPtel 3.1 / driver 3.0.7.

requirements.heading: Fill Defects (delta)
requirements.text:
- **Pie/chord source correction:** original I/i helpers invoke GDI Pie, _ invokes GDI Chord, and skewed filled variants submit Polygon contours. The [native derivation](../research/issue-14-arc-sweeps.md) contradicts this repository's earlier adoption of RIPlib `§BUG.6` as an observed arc-plus-radii flood construction. That attribution is withdrawn; it must not be generalized to earlier clients or new skewed commands merely from engine lineage.
- **Actual curve quirks:** original angle reduction, O/V separation, full-turn degeneracy and skewed pie center closure are now traced directly. The [angle reference](../ripscrip/2.2-curves.md#angle-ordering-and-sweeps) and [consumer contract](2.1-arc-consumer-contract.md) state those findings with API boundaries, separately from Windows rasterization.
- **Legacy RIP_FILL survives:** the original DLL retains its legacy border-color flood path despite the language's removal declaration and absent help/corpus uses. RIPlib `§DEAD.7` reports its patterned brush is not applied, producing a solid flood; this separate adopted claim does not describe ordinary GDI-filled pies or polygons.
- **Earlier-client scope:** 2.x behavior requires evidence from a 2.x binary. Shared resource magic and ancestry do not establish identical angle or fill defects.

requirements.heading: Axis-aligned endpoint rays
requirements.text: For a geometric adapter, Arc/Pie/Chord use the intersections of the center-to-endpoint rays with the ellipse and advance counterclockwise. This is a **radial-bearing** construction; converting to ellipse parameter angles may be necessary for a renderer whose arc API uses parametric angles. Microsoft's [Arc](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-arc), [Pie](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-pie) and [Chord](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-chord) contracts define that boundary. Their complete-ellipse cases do not override the driver's earlier identical-integer-endpoint branches. Consequently 0..360 and 450..810 do not reach a full-ellipse GDI call in A/V/I/i/_.

requirements.heading: Axis-aligned endpoint rays
requirements.text: For a kernel using ellipse-parameter angles, a nonzero ray vector `(dx,dy)` maps to `theta = atan2(-dy/ry, dx/rx)` in degrees modulo 360, with positive device radii rx/ry. The counterclockwise span between distinct curve intersections is `(theta_end-theta_start) mod 360`; the API's coincident-intersection/full-ellipse cases apply when that span is zero. Apply the driver's integer-endpoint shortcuts **before** this conversion. Pie center closure and chord endpoint closure remain separate topology operations. A ray collapsed to the center by integer quantization remains an API degeneracy, outside a claim of exact pixel reproduction.

requirements.heading: Standing and scope
requirements.text: This documents RIPtel 3.1's RIPscrip 3.0.7 integer Bézier generation and the arrays its drawing consumers actually submit. The [language reference](../ripscrip/2.2-curves.md#rip_bezier) defines Z and the recovered z/t/x wire grammar. The [derivation](../research/issue-15-bezier-contracts.md) identifies the original DLL, hashes, RVAs, reproducible native probe and controlled services. These findings describe this shipped driver, without claiming an earlier client's numeric kernel or Windows rasterization parity.

requirements.heading: Ideal geometry and conversion order
requirements.text: For four control points P0..P3, the ideal curve is the cubic Bernstein polynomial `(1-t)^3*P0 + 3*t*(1-t)^2*P1 + 3*t^2*(1-t)*P2 + t^3*P3`. Three rounds of linear interpolation give that polynomial directly. P0/P3 are endpoints; P1/P2 are intermediate controls. This corrects the inherited X*4/Y*4 typographical error and generic B-spline label.

requirements.heading: Ideal geometry and conversion order
requirements.text: RIPtel first converts the four world control points to device coordinates through original **0x31084**, then samples those integer controls. For ordinary nonnegative, non-overflowing inputs, conversion is `floor(x*device_width/world_width)` and equivalently for y; no final sample can recover a fractional control position discarded here. The poly consumer takes a cubic endpoint from the next record's first pair, or the first record for a terminal closed cubic, and zero-extends that converted endpoint's low 16 bits before calling the generator. Standalone Z passes its converted controls directly. Point-class records are stored as zero-extended low-16-bit device coordinates.

requirements.heading: Original integer interpolation
requirements.text: Generator **0x2c9e0** uses signed 32-bit arithmetic with eight fractional bits. For an interior sample i/N, evaluate each axis independently. `wrap32` retains the low 32 bits and interprets them as signed, `trunc0` is signed division toward zero, and `signed16` retains the low 16 bits and interprets them as signed:

requirements.heading: Original integer interpolation
requirements.text:
```text
q[j] = wrap32(P[j] << 8), j=0..3
for level = 3,2,1:
    for j = 0..level-1:
        difference = wrap32(q[j+1] - q[j])
        product = wrap32(difference * i)
        q[j] = wrap32(q[j] + trunc0(product / N))
output = signed16(floor(q[0] / 256))
```

requirements.heading: Original integer interpolation
requirements.text: The original first level accumulates i times each fixed difference rather than multiplying anew; modular arithmetic makes the expression above equivalent. The probe also covers extreme signed-16-bit controls where intermediate products wrap, so floating-point interpolation plus one final rounding is not an exact substitute. The first output is P0's input integer directly; the final output is P3 narrowed to signed 16 bits. Interior outputs use the fixed-point sequence above. Bounds are accumulated from generated outputs, rather than the ideal curve's extrema.

requirements.heading: Written and submitted counts
requirements.text: For N>=2, the generator writes **N points**:

requirements.heading: Written and submitted counts
requirements.text:
```text
P0,
fixed-point samples at i/N for i=1..N-2,
P3
```

requirements.heading: Written and submitted counts
requirements.text: The expected `(N-1)/N` sample is missing. With N=2 only endpoints are generated. A unit-scale example with controls `(0,0),(0,0),(0,0),(64,0)` and N=4 yields **(0,0), (1,0), (8,0), (64,0)**, omitting (27,0) at t=3/4. This observed historical sampling defect is separate from the valid ideal cubic equation.

requirements.heading: Written and submitted counts
requirements.text: For N=0/1 the generator skips all interior division and still writes two scratch endpoints. Standalone Z forwards the requested N to Polyline: zero/one submitted points cannot draw a curve under that API's two-point minimum. It does not reject or replace N. Its full two-digit base-64 range reaches 4095 submitted points.

requirements.heading: Written and submitted counts
requirements.text: The poly consumer rejects zero N if any cubic is present. With N=1, each cubic advances its output index by only one; the extra written scratch endpoint may be overwritten by the next record, or lie outside the submitted array for a final cubic. Thus one cubic contributes only its start to drawing at N=1. Point records contribute one point each. For N>=2, a cubic includes the next record's start as its endpoint, then that record supplies its start again: join duplicates remain in the submitted array.

requirements.heading: Expansion budget and topology
requirements.text: For C cubic records and L point records, the common poly consumer checks `C*N + L + 1 <= 4095`. If exceeded, it sets **N=floor((4094-L)/C)** for every cubic, rejecting if this becomes zero. The resulting submitted count is **C\*N+L**, so the maximum is **4094**, often slightly lower because the shared N is integral. The original 80,000-byte workspace allocation does not define this usable limit.

requirements.heading: Expansion budget and topology
requirements.text: Input collection remains independently bounded by **8193 numbers**, including headers and type digits. The [record grammar and rejection rules](../ripscrip/2.2-curves.md#counts-limits-and-rejection) specify its accounting; an input count is not permission to expand to `num*count` points.

requirements.heading: Expansion budget and topology
requirements.text: Open t rejects a terminal cubic before any drawing. Closed z and filled x permit a terminal cubic and use the first record's start as its P3. A terminal point need not explicitly return to the start. z/x submit Polygon contours and t submits Polyline; this consumer appends no extra closure vertex. Polygon provides the final straight closing edge when needed. Fill/border passes preserve that array and count; the native fixture captures arguments and pass counts without emulating GDI pixels.

requirements.heading: Verification boundary
requirements.text: `run/riptel-bezier-probe DLL [ORIGINAL_CORPUS_FILE]` executes the original byte parser, state setters, numeric generator, common validation/expansion, world conversion and standalone handler. It tests all encoded base-64 counts 0..4095, selected negative/fractional/overflow profiles, both bases, all XY widths, seven record types, all modes and borders, input truncation, generated reduction, malformed-vector rejection and original corpus vectors. Host framing/state, memory services, object selection and GDI calls are controlled. The source DLL stays byte-exact, no GUI is started, and temporary executables are removed automatically.

requirements.heading: Bitmaps, masks and legacy-icon conversion in RIPtel 3.1
requirements.text: This is the RIPtel 3.1 / RIPscrip driver 3.0.7 delta to the [inherited Windows BMP icon formats](../../2.0/techspecs/3.0-icon-formats.md). It resolves [issue #8](https://github.com/bbs-land/remote-imaging-protocol/issues/8) from the unchanged shipped driver; the [derivation and reproducible native probe](../research/issue-8-bmm-masks.md) distinguish original instructions from controlled drawing services. These findings do not establish behavior in earlier RIPterm clients.

requirements.heading: A BMM is an explicitly loaded BMP
requirements.text: **The client does not automatically load a same-named BMM alongside an image.** The bitmap loader, legacy icon loader, local bitmap playback and icon-button renderer pass one image filename to the common BMP renderer. Buttons choose the normal BMP or hot BMH; they do not fetch an attached BMM. An explicitly supplied MSK extension is normalized to BMM. BMM is a filename role for a mask raster used by explicit stamping, with the ordinary BMP decoder and put modes; it has no special Boolean pixel interpretation. _Evidence: DLL filename/renderer/button audit in the [research note](../research/issue-8-bmm-masks.md#completed-routing-audit)._
requirements.reason: 1b/1I request only the explicit image, and the tested 1b BMP loads ignore a malformed same-name BMM companion. Explicit BMM inputs use the ordinary decoder/key/mode route. Complete MSK-to-BMM role normalization, button rendering and local playback integration remain pending; no attached-mask or nonzero-index Boolean interpretation is introduced.
